ccumulation rate on the margin and that permeability barriers and lithological changes within the stratal architecture maintain each failure event some- what “conﬁned” within a discrete clinotheme. 6. conclusions the mtcs of the pb foredeep, investigated through a 3d geomor- phological approach coupled with a 2d seismic facies analysis and rollover trajectory analysis, have revealed that: • mtes can occur at any sea level position; the sea level does not ap- pear to act as a triggering mechanism in this framework. • the morphology of the mtc reﬂects the stratigraphy of the failed sec- tion and their source sedimentary environment (i.e., subaqueous delta, contouritic deposit, advection-dominated open slope depocenter). • the sediment failures are always conﬁned within a discrete clinotheme. the depth of rooting of each mass transport deposit is a further important controlling factor in the resultant deposit morphology, even within the same mass transport complex. in the pb foredeep, the main predisposing factor for the mtes ini- tiation is represented by a major increase in accumulation rate along the margin, which can occur irrespective of sea level variations. acknowledgments the authors would like to thank eni — exploration and production division, san donato milanese (italy) for sponsorship of this work and for the permission to publish these outcomes. we thank jasper knight (editor), michael strasser and an anonymous reviewer for their reviews that greatly improved the quality of the paper. references armitage, d.a., romans, b.w., covault, j.a., graham, s.a., 2009. the inﬂuence of mass transport deposit surface topography on the evolution of turbidite architecture: the sierra contreras, tres pasos formation (cretaceous), southern chile. journal of sedimentary research 79, 287–301. bull, s., cartwright, j., huuse, m., 2008. a review of kinematic indicators from mass transport complexes using 3d seismic data. marine and petroleum geology 26, 1–20.

o the 1929 grand banks incident (heezen & ewing, 1952), when a magnitude 7.2 earthquake set off a sequence of events that led to an orderly progression of submarine cable breaks south of newfoundland. following the event, the scientiﬁc community began a discussion that has continued to the present concerning exactly what caused the cable breaks and how the resulting processes related to the initial earthquake loading. terzaghi (1956) proposed a mechanism that is now known to be almost certainly false: that the cable breaks resulted from an advancing front of liquefaction within the seaﬂoor sediment. that is, the sediment did not move but rather a liquefac- tion wave passed through the sediment. heezen & ewing (1952) presented the more convincing argument that the earthquake ‘jarred the con- tinental slope and shelf, setting landslides and slumps in motion’. these mass movements ‘raced downward, and by the incorporation of water, the moving sediment was transformed into turbidity currents’. the currents started in different submarine canyons; as the ﬂows down each canyon joined, the currents grew larger. ultimately the combined current covered the ﬂoor of a 300-km-wide bight. the currents easily snapped the cables and pro- ceeded toward the south for at least 600 km. the model suggested by heezen & ewing (1952) has generally withstood the test of time, but the details of the event are not yet fully understood. at one point scientists thought that the initial failure might have been one or two very large landslides. heezen & drake (1964) found what appeared to be a 500-m-thick displaced block on the upper part of the laurentian fan, and emery et al. (1970) found a similar scale feature 40 km to the west. later investigations (piper & normark, 1982) showed that these features were not displaced blocks at all, but were parts of eroded terrain that only appeared to be blocks when viewed along indi- vidual tracklines.

o the 1929 grand banks incident (heezen & ewing, 1952), when a magnitude 7.2 earthquake set off a sequence of events that led to an orderly progression of submarine cable breaks south of newfoundland. following the event, the scientiﬁc community began a discussion that has continued to the present concerning exactly what caused the cable breaks and how the resulting processes related to the initial earthquake loading. terzaghi (1956) proposed a mechanism that is now known to be almost certainly false: that the cable breaks resulted from an advancing front of liquefaction within the seaﬂoor sediment. that is, the sediment did not move but rather a liquefac- tion wave passed through the sediment. heezen & ewing (1952) presented the more convincing argument that the earthquake ‘jarred the con- tinental slope and shelf, setting landslides and slumps in motion’. these mass movements ‘raced downward, and by the incorporation of water, the moving sediment was transformed into turbidity currents’. the currents started in different submarine canyons; as the ﬂows down each canyon joined, the currents grew larger. ultimately the combined current covered the ﬂoor of a 300-km-wide bight. the currents easily snapped the cables and pro- ceeded toward the south for at least 600 km. the model suggested by heezen & ewing (1952) has generally withstood the test of time, but the details of the event are not yet fully understood. at one point scientists thought that the initial failure might have been one or two very large landslides. heezen & drake (1964) found what appeared to be a 500-m-thick displaced block on the upper part of the laurentian fan, and emery et al. (1970) found a similar scale feature 40 km to the west. later investigations (piper & normark, 1982) showed that these features were not displaced blocks at all, but were parts of eroded terrain that only appeared to be blocks when viewed along indi- vidual tracklines.

(2007). by sorbonne universite user 59 interplay of mass-transport and turbidite-system deposits mixed contourite and debris-flow deposition, that take place during later glacial deposition. multichannel seismic reflection profiles in wilkes land show that extensive mass transport deposits at the base of the paleoslopes develop above a regional unconformity, wl-u3. on the continental shelf, wl-u3 truncates 300 to 600 m of strata and has been interpreted to separate preglacial strata below from glacial strata above (eittreim et al., 1995; escutia et al., 1997; escutia et al., 2005). extensive mass transport deposits in the wilkes land have irregular upper surfaces and commonly lens-shaped or wedge-shaped external geometries (fig. 18). internally, the mass transport deposits are mainly structureless, characterized by chaotic seismic facies and hyper- bolic reflections. their minimum run-out distances are 15 to 50 km, their width ranges from 5 to 13 km, and their thicknesses vary from 200 to 450 ms (about 170 to 380 m) (table 1; escutia et al., 2007). multi-event mass transport deposits at the base of the slope are observed and include deposits from wl-s4 to wl-s6, and possibly wl-s7 (figs. 18, 19). seismic units above the wl-u7 unconformity are not involved in any of the mass transport deposits, as indicated by downlap of prograding slope wedge clinoforms (i.e., seismic units wl-s8 and wl-s9) in the proximal parts of the mass transport deposits (fig. 18).

ge from 100 m to 200 m. headward escarpments are well imaged in both map and cross-section views. proximal facies of the mass transport deposits includes rotated blocks and large angular glide blocks. these pass distally into smaller glide blocks and chaotic seismic facies inferred to be debrites. intermediate parts of the mass transport deposits have longitudinal linear features parallel to inferred flow direction. distal patterns consist of transverse compressive ridges. other mass transport deposits too large to be completely imaged within the 3d survey show internal facies, consisting of large angular glide blocks in a matrix of seismically visible smaller blocks and chaotic facies inferred to be debrites. multiple causes of mdts in this area are probable. in possible order of importance, these include tilting and oversteepening of sediments because of tectonic uplift, high sedimentation rates at the mouth of the canyon, and eustatic falls of sea level. key words: upper quaternary, seafloor, mass-transport deposits, mass transport deposits, base of slope, offshore niger delta, deepwater nigeria, leveed- channel deposits, sediment waves, seismic facies, debrites, digital enhancement, volume rendering, pressure ridges, lateral flow lines, shear zones, fault scarp, rotated blocks, thrust blocks mass-transport deposits in deepwater settings sepm special publication no. 96, copyright © 2011 sepm (society for sedimentary geology), isbn 978-1-56576-287-9, p.

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

top_chunks.text: oor ( fig. 1). submarine channels are common features associ- ated with the nile delta and subsurface examples have been previously described from the deepwater western nile (samuel et al., 2003 ). 2. dataset and methodology the 3d seismic dataset used in this study was acquired in 2000 by bg group and partners. the data was migrated with a single pass 3d post-stack time migration to generate a 12.5m by 12.5m grid with a 1 ms sampling interval. the seismic data are processed to near zero phase and is displayed using seg normal polarity, with an increase in acoustic impedance being represented by a positive amplitude (red) on seismic sections. the plio-quaternary sedi- mentary section overlying the messinian evaporites has a dominant frequency of 50 hz, with the estimated vertical and lateral resolu- tion for this interval being 10 and 40 m, respectively. this was determined using an average interval velocity of 2000m s /c0 1 derived from velocity checkshot data ( frey-martinez et al., 2005 ). the messinian evaporites are characterised by a lower dominant frequency of 30 hz, although the frequency within the messinian is variable and this results in changes in vertical resolution within this unit (bertoni and cartwright, 2006 ). the channel levee systems in this study were characterised qualitatively using isochron maps of channel intervals. using these, the thickness and areal extent of the channel levees and channel axis can be assessed and compared to the surrounding structures. the base of the levee package in such maps is deﬁned as the surface against which the internal levee reﬂections downlap. the base of the channel is deﬁned as the lowermost erosive surface associated with incision into the pre-channel sequence (fig. 2 , deptuck et al., 2003; mayall et al., 2006 ). in order to quantitatively characterise the submarine channels in this study, the following morphometric parameters were measured (fig.

grooves across the levee (see figures 7 and 8 for location of grooves). sediment waves have been markedly deformed by local normal faulting of the synclinal axes of the waves, forming a series of rotated blocks. the listric faults appear to sole out along a detachment surface at the base of the levee. younger sediments of the levee system above the interpreted unit have also been folded and faulted. this pattern is consistent with early stages of mass-transport activity. a later phase of erosion by a mass-transport deposit is evident with its base eroding upper- most parts of the sediment waves (to be discussed below). as a summary map for leveed-channel complex 1, a volume- rendered image is composed over an interval that includes both channel-fill and levee deposits (fig. 13). this map allows a comparison of the high amplitudes of the channel-fill reflections with the slightly lower amplitudes of the sediment waves. the high-amplitude reflections of the channel-fill sediments (yellows, greens, and reds) contrast with the slightly lower ampli- tudes of the sediment waves. this character extends eastward from the channel axis for more than 8 km, before passing into the brown amplitudes of the thin levee flank. these contrasts are possible using volume-rendering techniques within a time inter- val of seismic data whereby the data are partially transparent. the highest amplitudes are weighted highest, and low ampli- tudes and zero crossings are weighted lowest, allowing emphasis on differing stratigraphic elements. individual channel-fill me- anders in the channel fairway as well as sediment waves in the levee system are evident. sediment waves have been studied in detail for both seafloor examples and ancient turbidite systems (normark et al., 1980; top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

top_chunks.text: diment waves developed on the outer levee of a westward bend of the channel (fig. 7). presumably the sediment waves were formed by turbidity flows that overflowed the levee of the outer channel bends. the sediment waves are largest in the proximal edge of the levee and decrease in amplitude away from the channel to the south. imbricate slumping of individual sediment waves accentuates the wave patterns, especially in two narrow grooves cutting from north to south across the levee. an isopach map of levee thickness for leveed-channel com- plex 1 (fig. 8, located in inset area of fig. 7) shows details of the highly asymmetric thickness development of the outer levees on channel bends, both at the westward bend described above, and the slight southern bend down-channel from the western bend, as turbidites overflow the outer levees during deposition. levees on the inner flanks of the bends are thinner than those on the outer flanks, and are marked by arcuate slump patterns as the levee walls are eroded. the slumped material probably contributes to mass transport deposits in the channel-fill itself. narrow grooved patterns are very evident in the thick eastern levee system. they may represent headward develop- ment of slumping along narrow detachment surfaces, possibly augmented by overbank channel splays. a seismic profile across leveed-channel complex 1 (fig. 9) shows a central channel area that is filled by irregular high-amplitude reflections interpreted as coarse channel-fill deposits. an overlying level of high- amplitude channel fill occurs between low-amplitude fill zones. this zone may be an mass transport deposit formed by slumping of the adjoining levee. the wedge-shaped levees flanking the channel thin away from the channel axis. leveed-channel complex 1 is bounded on either side and below by several older leveed-channel com- plexes and possible interbedded mass transport deposits.

top_chunks.text: oor ( fig. 1). submarine channels are common features associ- ated with the nile delta and subsurface examples have been previously described from the deepwater western nile (samuel et al., 2003 ). 2. dataset and methodology the 3d seismic dataset used in this study was acquired in 2000 by bg group and partners. the data was migrated with a single pass 3d post-stack time migration to generate a 12.5m by 12.5m grid with a 1 ms sampling interval. the seismic data are processed to near zero phase and is displayed using seg normal polarity, with an increase in acoustic impedance being represented by a positive amplitude (red) on seismic sections. the plio-quaternary sedi- mentary section overlying the messinian evaporites has a dominant frequency of 50 hz, with the estimated vertical and lateral resolu- tion for this interval being 10 and 40 m, respectively. this was determined using an average interval velocity of 2000m s /c0 1 derived from velocity checkshot data ( frey-martinez et al., 2005 ). the messinian evaporites are characterised by a lower dominant frequency of 30 hz, although the frequency within the messinian is variable and this results in changes in vertical resolution within this unit (bertoni and cartwright, 2006 ). the channel levee systems in this study were characterised qualitatively using isochron maps of channel intervals. using these, the thickness and areal extent of the channel levees and channel axis can be assessed and compared to the surrounding structures. the base of the levee package in such maps is deﬁned as the surface against which the internal levee reﬂections downlap. the base of the channel is deﬁned as the lowermost erosive surface associated with incision into the pre-channel sequence (fig. 2 , deptuck et al., 2003; mayall et al., 2006 ). in order to quantitatively characterise the submarine channels in this study, the following morphometric parameters were measured (fig.

grooves across the levee (see figures 7 and 8 for location of grooves). sediment waves have been markedly deformed by local normal faulting of the synclinal axes of the waves, forming a series of rotated blocks. the listric faults appear to sole out along a detachment surface at the base of the levee. younger sediments of the levee system above the interpreted unit have also been folded and faulted. this pattern is consistent with early stages of mass-transport activity. a later phase of erosion by a mass-transport deposit is evident with its base eroding upper- most parts of the sediment waves (to be discussed below). as a summary map for leveed-channel complex 1, a volume- rendered image is composed over an interval that includes both channel-fill and levee deposits (fig. 13). this map allows a comparison of the high amplitudes of the channel-fill reflections with the slightly lower amplitudes of the sediment waves. the high-amplitude reflections of the channel-fill sediments (yellows, greens, and reds) contrast with the slightly lower ampli- tudes of the sediment waves. this character extends eastward from the channel axis for more than 8 km, before passing into the brown amplitudes of the thin levee flank. these contrasts are possible using volume-rendering techniques within a time inter- val of seismic data whereby the data are partially transparent. the highest amplitudes are weighted highest, and low ampli- tudes and zero crossings are weighted lowest, allowing emphasis on differing stratigraphic elements. individual channel-fill me- anders in the channel fairway as well as sediment waves in the levee system are evident. sediment waves have been studied in detail for both seafloor examples and ancient turbidite systems (normark et al., 1980; top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

top_chunks.text: oor ( fig. 1). submarine channels are common features associ- ated with the nile delta and subsurface examples have been previously described from the deepwater western nile (samuel et al., 2003 ). 2. dataset and methodology the 3d seismic dataset used in this study was acquired in 2000 by bg group and partners. the data was migrated with a single pass 3d post-stack time migration to generate a 12.5m by 12.5m grid with a 1 ms sampling interval. the seismic data are processed to near zero phase and is displayed using seg normal polarity, with an increase in acoustic impedance being represented by a positive amplitude (red) on seismic sections. the plio-quaternary sedi- mentary section overlying the messinian evaporites has a dominant frequency of 50 hz, with the estimated vertical and lateral resolu- tion for this interval being 10 and 40 m, respectively. this was determined using an average interval velocity of 2000m s /c0 1 derived from velocity checkshot data ( frey-martinez et al., 2005 ). the messinian evaporites are characterised by a lower dominant frequency of 30 hz, although the frequency within the messinian is variable and this results in changes in vertical resolution within this unit (bertoni and cartwright, 2006 ). the channel levee systems in this study were characterised qualitatively using isochron maps of channel intervals. using these, the thickness and areal extent of the channel levees and channel axis can be assessed and compared to the surrounding structures. the base of the levee package in such maps is deﬁned as the surface against which the internal levee reﬂections downlap. the base of the channel is deﬁned as the lowermost erosive surface associated with incision into the pre-channel sequence (fig. 2 , deptuck et al., 2003; mayall et al., 2006 ). in order to quantitatively characterise the submarine channels in this study, the following morphometric parameters were measured (fig.

grooves across the levee (see figures 7 and 8 for location of grooves). sediment waves have been markedly deformed by local normal faulting of the synclinal axes of the waves, forming a series of rotated blocks. the listric faults appear to sole out along a detachment surface at the base of the levee. younger sediments of the levee system above the interpreted unit have also been folded and faulted. this pattern is consistent with early stages of mass-transport activity. a later phase of erosion by a mass-transport deposit is evident with its base eroding upper- most parts of the sediment waves (to be discussed below). as a summary map for leveed-channel complex 1, a volume- rendered image is composed over an interval that includes both channel-fill and levee deposits (fig. 13). this map allows a comparison of the high amplitudes of the channel-fill reflections with the slightly lower amplitudes of the sediment waves. the high-amplitude reflections of the channel-fill sediments (yellows, greens, and reds) contrast with the slightly lower ampli- tudes of the sediment waves. this character extends eastward from the channel axis for more than 8 km, before passing into the brown amplitudes of the thin levee flank. these contrasts are possible using volume-rendering techniques within a time inter- val of seismic data whereby the data are partially transparent. the highest amplitudes are weighted highest, and low ampli- tudes and zero crossings are weighted lowest, allowing emphasis on differing stratigraphic elements. individual channel-fill me- anders in the channel fairway as well as sediment waves in the levee system are evident. sediment waves have been studied in detail for both seafloor examples and ancient turbidite systems (normark et al., 1980; o the 1929 grand banks incident (heezen & ewing, 1952), when a magnitude 7.2 earthquake set off a sequence of events that led to an orderly progression of submarine cable breaks south of newfoundland. following the event, the scientiﬁc community began a discussion that has continued to the present concerning exactly what caused the cable breaks and how the resulting processes related to the initial earthquake loading. terzaghi (1956) proposed a mechanism that is now known to be almost certainly false: that the cable breaks resulted from an advancing front of liquefaction within the seaﬂoor sediment. that is, the sediment did not move but rather a liquefac- tion wave passed through the sediment. heezen & ewing (1952) presented the more convincing argument that the earthquake ‘jarred the con- tinental slope and shelf, setting landslides and slumps in motion’. these mass movements ‘raced downward, and by the incorporation of water, the moving sediment was transformed into turbidity currents’. the currents started in different submarine canyons; as the ﬂows down each canyon joined, the currents grew larger. ultimately the combined current covered the ﬂoor of a 300-km-wide bight. the currents easily snapped the cables and pro- ceeded toward the south for at least 600 km. the model suggested by heezen & ewing (1952) has generally withstood the test of time, but the details of the event are not yet fully understood. at one point scientists thought that the initial failure might have been one or two very large landslides. heezen & drake (1964) found what appeared to be a 500-m-thick displaced block on the upper part of the laurentian fan, and emery et al. (1970) found a similar scale feature 40 km to the west. later investigations (piper & normark, 1982) showed that these features were not displaced blocks at all, but were parts of eroded terrain that only appeared to be blocks when viewed along indi- vidual tracklines.

o the 1929 grand banks incident (heezen & ewing, 1952), when a magnitude 7.2 earthquake set off a sequence of events that led to an orderly progression of submarine cable breaks south of newfoundland. following the event, the scientiﬁc community began a discussion that has continued to the present concerning exactly what caused the cable breaks and how the resulting processes related to the initial earthquake loading. terzaghi (1956) proposed a mechanism that is now known to be almost certainly false: that the cable breaks resulted from an advancing front of liquefaction within the seaﬂoor sediment. that is, the sediment did not move but rather a liquefac- tion wave passed through the sediment. heezen & ewing (1952) presented the more convincing argument that the earthquake ‘jarred the con- tinental slope and shelf, setting landslides and slumps in motion’. these mass movements ‘raced downward, and by the incorporation of water, the moving sediment was transformed into turbidity currents’. the currents started in different submarine canyons; as the ﬂows down each canyon joined, the currents grew larger. ultimately the combined current covered the ﬂoor of a 300-km-wide bight. the currents easily snapped the cables and pro- ceeded toward the south for at least 600 km. the model suggested by heezen & ewing (1952) has generally withstood the test of time, but the details of the event are not yet fully understood. at one point scientists thought that the initial failure might have been one or two very large landslides. heezen & drake (1964) found what appeared to be a 500-m-thick displaced block on the upper part of the laurentian fan, and emery et al. (1970) found a similar scale feature 40 km to the west. later investigations (piper & normark, 1982) showed that these features were not displaced blocks at all, but were parts of eroded terrain that only appeared to be blocks when viewed along indi- vidual tracklines.

mulder & cochonat, 1996) and shallow mass-transport deposits (e.g. slide blocks, sediment slides and slumps, debris ﬂows; evans et al . 1996; mulder & cochonat, 1996), to assess possible links between gravity tectonics and mass-transport processes on the amazon fan. data and methods the available seismic data comprise about 15 000 km of 2d multichannel seismic reﬂection proﬁles (fig. 1). the seismic data include a super-regional seismic grid of 100 km spacing and an industrial seismic grid of 10–20 km spacing (fig. 1): the ﬁrst consists of the leplac survey lines collected at 13 s recorded time interval by the brazilian navy and by petrobras (vertical resolution between 5 and 10 m); (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (2015) studied the stratigraphic interval of interest, deﬁning seven seismic facies that were used to infer a number of sedimentary subenviron- ments (i.e. channel-ﬁll, levees, lobes and mtcs). these subenvironments were then grouped into seven seismic units. ortiz-karpf et al. (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (a) (b) fig. 1. location and tectonic setting.

(2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (a) (b) fig. 1. location and tectonic setting.

(2007). by sorbonne universite user 59 interplay of mass-transport and turbidite-system deposits mixed contourite and debris-flow deposition, that take place during later glacial deposition. multichannel seismic reflection profiles in wilkes land show that extensive mass transport deposits at the base of the paleoslopes develop above a regional unconformity, wl-u3. on the continental shelf, wl-u3 truncates 300 to 600 m of strata and has been interpreted to separate preglacial strata below from glacial strata above (eittreim et al., 1995; escutia et al., 1997; escutia et al., 2005). extensive mass transport deposits in the wilkes land have irregular upper surfaces and commonly lens-shaped or wedge-shaped external geometries (fig. 18). internally, the mass transport deposits are mainly structureless, characterized by chaotic seismic facies and hyper- bolic reflections. their minimum run-out distances are 15 to 50 km, their width ranges from 5 to 13 km, and their thicknesses vary from 200 to 450 m

(2015) studied the stratigraphic interval of interest, deﬁning seven seismic facies that were used to infer a number of sedimentary subenviron- ments (i.e. channel-ﬁll, levees, lobes and mtcs). these subenvironments were then grouped into seven seismic units. ortiz-karpf et al. (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (a) (b) fig. 1. location and tectonic setting.

(2015) studied the stratigraphic interval of interest, deﬁning seven seismic facies that were used to infer a number of sedimentary subenviron- ments (i.e. channel-ﬁll, levees, lobes and mtcs). these subenvironments were then grouped into seven seismic units. ortiz-karpf et al. (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (a) (b) fig. 1. location and tectonic setting.

(2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (a) (b) fig. 1. location and tectonic setting.

(2007). by sorbonne universite user 59 interplay of mass-transport and turbidite-system deposits mixed contourite and debris-flow deposition, that take place during later glacial deposition. multichannel seismic reflection profiles in wilkes land show that extensive mass transport deposits at the base of the paleoslopes develop above a regional unconformity, wl-u3. on the continental shelf, wl-u3 truncates 300 to 600 m of strata and has been interpreted to separate preglacial strata below from glacial strata above (eittreim et al., 1995; escutia et al., 1997; escutia et al., 2005). extensive mass transport deposits in the wilkes land have irregular upper surfaces and commonly lens-shaped or wedge-shaped external geometries (fig. 18). internally, the mass transport deposits are mainly structureless, characterized by chaotic seismic facies and hyper- bolic reflections. their minimum run-out distances are 15 to 50 km, their width ranges from 5 to 13 km, and their thicknesses vary from 200 to 450 ms (about 170 to 380 m) (table 1; escutia et al., 2007). multi-event mass transport deposits at the base of the slope are observed and include deposits from wl-s4 to wl-s6, and possibly wl-s7 (figs. 18, 19). seismic units above the wl-u7 unconformity are not involved in any of the mass transport deposits, as indicated by downlap of prograding slope wedge clinoforms (i.e., seismic units wl-s8 and wl-s9) in the proximal parts of the mass transport deposits (fig. 18).

(2015) studied the stratigraphic interval of interest, deﬁning seven seismic facies that were used to infer a number of sedimentary subenviron- ments (i.e. channel-ﬁll, levees, lobes and mtcs). these subenvironments were then grouped into seven seismic units. ortiz-karpf et al. (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (2007). by sorbonne universite user 59 interplay of mass-transport and turbidite-system deposits mixed contourite and debris-flow deposition, that take place during later glacial deposition. multichannel seismic reflection profiles in wilkes land show that extensive mass transport deposits at the base of the paleoslopes develop above a regional unconformity, wl-u3. on the continental shelf, wl-u3 truncates 300 to 600 m of strata and has been interpreted to separate preglacial strata below from glacial strata above (eittreim et al., 1995; escutia et al., 1997; escutia et al., 2005). extensive mass transport deposits in the wilkes land have irregular upper surfaces and commonly lens-shaped or wedge-shaped external geometries (fig. 18). internally, the mass transport deposits are mainly structureless, characterized by chaotic seismic facies and hyper- bolic reflections. their minimum run-out distances are 15 to 50 km, their width ranges from 5 to 13 km, and their thicknesses vary from 200 to 450 ms (about 170 to 380 m) (table 1; escutia et al., 2007). multi-event mass transport deposits at the base of the slope are observed and include deposits from wl-s4 to wl-s6, and possibly wl-s7 (figs. 18, 19). seismic units above the wl-u7 unconformity are not involved in any of the mass transport deposits, as indicated by downlap of prograding slope wedge clinoforms (i.e., seismic units wl-s8 and wl-s9) in the proximal parts of the mass transport deposits (fig. 18).

(2015) studied the stratigraphic interval of interest, deﬁning seven seismic facies that were used to infer a number of sedimentary subenviron- ments (i.e. channel-ﬁll, levees, lobes and mtcs). these subenvironments were then grouped into seven seismic units. ortiz-karpf et al. (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (a) (b) fig. 1. location and tectonic setting.

these pass distally into smaller glide blocks and chaotic seismic facies inferred to be debrites. intermediate parts of the mass transport deposits have longitudinal linear features parallel to inferred flow direction. distal patterns consist of transverse compressive ridges. other mass transport deposits too large to be completely imaged within the 3d survey show internal facies, consisting of large angular glide blocks in a matrix of seismically visible smaller blocks and chaotic facies inferred to be debrites. multiple causes of mdts in this area are probable. in possible order of importance, these include tilting and oversteepening of sediments because of tectonic uplift, high sedimentation rates at the mouth of the canyon, and eustatic falls of sea level. key words: upper (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (2015) studied the stratigraphic interval of interest, deﬁning seven seismic facies that were used to infer a number of sedimentary subenviron- ments (i.e. channel-ﬁll, levees, lobes and mtcs). these subenvironments were then grouped into seven seismic units. ortiz-karpf et al. (2015) interpret that seismic unit d, which is located 300 –500 m below the seabed, is dominated by mtcs. in the study described here, unit d and older, underlying mtcs and their bound- ing surfaces were characterised and mapped in greater detail, and the chronology of mtc emplacement was assessed with respect to the development of the deep- water fold-and-thrust belt. based on the amplitude, continuity and conﬁguration of the reﬂections, and their external geometry, three mtc seismic facies are deﬁned (table 1). attribute extractions, including amplitude, dip and variance, were performed and integrated with variance and amplitude depth slices to deﬁne lateral facies changes and create seismic facies maps. kinematic indicators such as the orientation of the lateral scarps, onlap patterns, fold and fault vergence, grooves and megaclasts alignment ( sensu bull et al. , 2009) were inter- preted from maps and cross-sectional views. these kinematic indicators were used to infer mtc ﬂow directions and to link individual mtcs back to their source areas, thus enabling the investigation of the rela- tionship between fold-and-thrust belt growth, seabed deformation and mtc emplacement. (a) (b) fig. 1. location and tectonic setting.

ge from 100 m to 200 m. headward escarpments are well imaged in both map and cross-section views. proximal facies of the mass transport deposits includes rotated blocks and large angular glide blocks. these pass distally into smaller glide blocks and chaotic seismic facies inferred to be debrites. intermediate parts of the mass transport deposits have longitudinal linear features parallel to inferred flow direction. distal patterns consist of transverse compressive ridges. other mass transport deposits too large to be completely imaged within the 3d survey show internal facies, consisting of large angular glide blocks in a matrix of seismically visible smaller blocks and chaotic facies inferred to be debrites. multiple causes of mdts in this area are probable. in possible order of importance, these include tilting and oversteepening of sediments because of tectonic uplift, high sedimentation rates at the mouth of the canyon, and eustatic falls of sea level. key words: upper quaternary, seafloor, mass-transport deposits, mass transport deposits, base of slope, offshore niger delta, deepwater nigeria, leveed- channel deposits, sediment waves, seismic facies, debrites, digital enhancement, volume rendering, pressure ridges, lateral flow lines, shear zones, fault scarp, rotated blocks, thrust blocks mass-transport deposits in deepwater settings sepm special significant propor- tions of deepwater sediments worldwide. they are being more thoroughly studied than in the past because of hazards of mass failures of the continental slope and at deepwater drilling sites, as well as their significance in hydrocarbon exploration and devel- opment. mass transport deposits include a wide spectrum of gravity-induced deposits, including slides, slumps, and oned previously). the general architecture of this stratigraphic interval is illustrated by three regional seismic profiles, oriented approxi- mately parallel and perpendicular to the coastline (figs. 3, 4). the seismic character of this part of the stratigraphic column is marked by high-frequency, continuous, and moderate-ampli- tude reflections that are locally interbedded with discontinuous to transparent low-amplitude reflections (fig. 4). a series of discontinuities linked to well-defined incisional systems are vis- ible throughout the area of study (figs. 3, 4b). these systems have been described previously on the ecm (alonso et al., 1991; bertoni and cartwright, 2005), and are interpreted as slope- confined submarine canyons. for the purpose of seismic-stratigraphic analysis, three key seismic horizons (q-15, q-20, and q-30) have been mapped throughout the study area (figs. 3, 4). these horizons subdivide the interval of interest on the basis of changes in seismic ampli- tude, reflection continuity, and deformational structures. q-15 corresponds to a regional unconformity that appears as a con- tinuous high-amplitude reflection, and is locally onlapped by overlying reflections (dotted orange line in figures 3 and 4). q-20 is a continuous high-amplitude reflection that marks the lower- most limit of submarine mass-failure features in the area (dotted blue line in figures 3 and 4). q-30 is the base of the upper pleistocene–holocene section, and the lowermost limit of fluid- escape structures (dotted green line in figures 3 and 4). lithology of the succession is poorly constrained by sparse data, although it appears that it is composed mainly of deep marine, mostly fine- grained, clastic sediments (i.e., some sandstones, but mostly limestones and claystones) (e.g., melendez hevia and alvarez del buergo, 1996; maestro et al., 2002; frey-martínez et al., 2004; bertoni and cartwright, 2005).

mtcs. if total evacuation of the headwall and proximal area has occurred, the truncation of sediments in the headwall scarp may be difﬁcult to identify if inﬁlling by background sedi- mentation of similar dip and/or seismic facies character has occurred. the best way to proceed if such uncertainty exists is to identify the basal shear surface at some point below the main body of the mtc and attempt to trace it upslope to the headwall region, or utilize coherence or amplitude slices ﬂattened on the basal shear surface. 3.1.2. extensional ridges and blocks depending on the nature of the mtc under consideration, the headwall may be completely evacuated, with the basal shear plane exposed, as is the case in parts of the storegga slide main headwall (haﬂidason et al., 2004 ); or barely depleted, with material having undergone limited translation ( solheim et al., 2005 ). in most cases, headwall domains represent an intermediate between the above scenarios, with many studies describing examples where headwall regions are characterised by extensional features, typically deformed and translated, roughly square to rectangular ‘blocks’ or more laterally continuous ‘ridges’ separated by normal or listric fault grabens ( bøe et al., 2000; frey martinez et al., 2005; solheim et al., 2005; lastras et al., 2006 ). these represent discrete, detached units of translated material that have retained a high degree of internal coherency ( homza, 2004; lastras et al., 2006 ). the blocks may occur on a variety of scales and may undergo varying degrees of translation, with spacing, deformation and disintegration tend- ing to increase with distance away from the headwall scarp (laberg and vorren, 2000; gee et al., 2006 ). such blocks can be identiﬁed in planform from top mtc surface or in the case of relatively recent events, seabed time structure, amplitude or dip maps. time, stratal or coherency slices ﬂattened on the basal shear surface are also of use.

mtcs. if total evacuation of the headwall and proximal area has occurred, the truncation of sediments in the headwall scarp may be difﬁcult to identify if inﬁlling by background sedi- mentation of similar dip and/or seismic facies character has occurred. the best way to proceed if such uncertainty exists is to identify the basal shear surface at some point below the main body of the mtc and attempt to trace it upslope to the headwall region, or utilize coherence or amplitude slices ﬂattened on the basal shear surface. 3.1.2. extensional ridges and blocks depending on the nature of the mtc under consideration, the headwall may be completely evacuated, with the basal shear plane exposed, as is the case in parts of the storegga slide main headwall (haﬂidason et al., 2004 ); or barely depleted, with material having undergone limited translation ( solheim et al., 2005 ). in most cases, headwall domains represent an intermediate between the above scenarios, with many studies describing examples where headwall regions are characterised by extensional features, typically deformed and translated, roughly square to rectangular ‘blocks’ or more laterally continuous ‘ridges’ separated by normal or listric fault grabens ( bøe et al., 2000; frey martinez et al., 2005; solheim et al., 2005; lastras et al., 2006 ). these represent discrete, detached units of translated material that have retained a high degree of internal coherency ( homza, 2004; lastras et al., 2006 ). the blocks may occur on a variety of scales and may undergo varying degrees of translation, with spacing, deformation and disintegration tend- ing to increase with distance away from the headwall scarp (laberg and vorren, 2000; gee et al., 2006 ). such blocks can be identiﬁed in planform from top mtc surface or in the case of relatively recent events, seabed time structure, amplitude or dip maps. time, stratal or coherency slices ﬂattened on the basal shear surface are also of use.

o morphology, seismic profiles and cores show that large gullied canyons feed into a 30-km-long mass transport deposit sheet on the basin floor (table 1; nelson et al., 1991), whereas turbidite channel–levee systems (1 to 4 in fig. 8) are found downstream from the small canyons. seismic profiles show this mass transport deposit sheet as exhibiting irregular thickness of chaotic and transparent facies that have scoured into the underlying deposits (fig. 8c) (nelson et al., 1991). cores from the surface of the mass transport deposit sheet contain chaotic mixtures of unconsolidated clay clasts and chaotic sand deposits (nelson et al., 1991). seismic profiles downstream from the small canyons show surface and subsurface channel–levee systems (nelson and maldonado, 1988). cores from the channel floors contain thick (10–30 cm), graded turbidite sand beds. in contrast, the levees have thin-bedded (1–5 cm) turbidites (alonso and maldonado, 1990). we interpret that the location of the mass transport deposit sheet in the central ebro continental margin is related to the messinian subaerial ebro canyon, which underlies three gullied canyons located in this segment of the margin (figs. 7, 8). the messinian surface of the ebro subaerial canyon is nearly 3000 ms deep below the gullied canyons compared to the noncanyon messinian surface, which is 2000 ms deep below the north and south small canyons (1 to 4 in figs. 8b, 9a; escutia and maldonado, 1992). when the mediterranean sea nearly instantaneously refilled after the messinian salinity crisis, thick (750 m) deepwater pliocene clays were deposited rapidly on top of the subaerial gravels of the messinian ebro canyon (figs. 7, 8a; nelson and maldonado, 1990). as a result, the gullied central segment of the ebro margin, which overlies the thick muds of the messinian ebro canyon, apparently has less stability than the continental slope to the north and south.

o morphology, seismic profiles and cores show that large gullied canyons feed into a 30-km-long mass transport deposit sheet on the basin floor (table 1; nelson et al., 1991), whereas turbidite channel–levee systems (1 to 4 in fig. 8) are found downstream from the small canyons. seismic profiles show this mass transport deposit sheet as exhibiting irregular thickness of chaotic and transparent facies that have scoured into the underlying deposits (fig. 8c) (nelson et al., 1991). cores from the surface of the mass transport deposit sheet contain chaotic mixtures of unconsolidated clay clasts and chaotic sand deposits (nelson et al., 1991). seismic profiles downstream from the small canyons show surface and subsurface channel–levee systems (nelson and maldonado, 1988). cores from the channel floors contain thick (10–30 cm), graded turbidite sand beds. in contrast, the levees have thin-bedded (1–5 cm) turbidites (alonso and maldonado, 1990). we interpret that the location of the mass transport deposit sheet in the central ebro continental margin is related to the messinian subaerial ebro canyon, which underlies three gullied canyons located in this segment of the margin (figs. 7, 8). the messinian surface of the ebro subaerial canyon is nearly 3000 ms deep below the gullied canyons compared to the noncanyon messinian surface, which is 2000 ms deep below the north and south small canyons (1 to 4 in figs. 8b, 9a; escutia and maldonado, 1992). when the mediterranean sea nearly instantaneously refilled after the messinian salinity crisis, thick (750 m) deepwater pliocene clays were deposited rapidly on top of the subaerial gravels of the messinian ebro canyon (figs. 7, 8a; nelson and maldonado, 1990). as a result, the gullied central segment of the ebro margin, which overlies the thick muds of the messinian ebro canyon, apparently has less stability than the continental slope to the north and south.

hese deposits. mass-transport deposits can comprise sheets, lobes, and channel fills, and can reach 150 m or more in thickness. greater thicknesses are observed where successive flows are amalgamated. this paper documents both internal architectural or stratigraphic as well as external geomorphic attributes of such deposits, as expressed in outcrop and imaged by 3d seismic data. recognition of mass-transport deposits in outcrop is based on identification of bedding deformed by synsedimentary processes, with deformation ranging from minimal redistribution of large slide blocks to complete disaggregation typical of debris-flow deposit s. on seismic data, mass-transport deposits can be recognized by certain geomorphologic as well as stratigraphic distinguishing characteristics: basal linear grooved and scoured surfaces, hummocky relief at the top, and internal chaotic to transparent seismic facies, with internal thrust faulting common. key words: mass-transport deposits, mass transport deposits, debris flow, seismic stratigraphy, seismic geomorphology mass-transport deposits in deepwater settings sepm special publication no. 96, copyright © 2011 sepm (society for sedimentary geology), isbn 978-1-56576-287-9, p. 7–38. introduction mass movements of sediments form kilometer-scale features (fig. 1) that represent major subaerial and subaqueous geohazards and can comprise significant depositional elements, characteriz- ing marine slope and basin-floor systems. catastrophic conse- quences of mass-transport processes such as tsunamis, avalanches, major rock falls, and mudslides are dramatic (e.g., holmes, 1965; bolt et al., 1977; voight, 1978; brunsden and prior, 1984; fisher and smith, 1991; martinsen 1994; bondevik et al., 2003). in addi- tion, mass transport deposit of sediments can significantly affect stabil- ity of offshore installations (e.g., prior and coleman, 1982; solheim et al., 2005).

eismic units vi^ viii) are discussed brie£y in this section to explain some of the elements that in£uenced the distribution of gravity- induced deposits in the deep-marine margin of o¡shore t rinidad. isopach maps of seismic units vi^ viii show sig- ni¢cant variations in the location, geometry and extension of the depocentres that were developed in the study area during the last stages of basin in¢lling (fig. 5). generally speaking, these depocentres have an elongated geometry and present a ne^sw orientation that parallels the axis of the mud-volcano ridges. the depocentres were connected to the outer- shelf and upper- slope region by megachutes that were responsible for sediments funneling downslope (figs 5 and 6) (see also, moscardelli et al., 2006). the maps also reveal an overall migration of the depocentres from nw to se, as well as progressive thinning of the strati- graphic succession near the darien ridge area (fig. 5). the isopach map of seismic unit vi shows that the main depocentre during this phase was located in the nw cor- ner of the study area near darien ridge. darien and haydn megachutes were most likely acting as main feeders of the nw depocentre, whereas the callicore megachute was funneling sediments from the upper slope towards the central part of the basin (figs 5a and 6). the mtcs that are described in this paper are contained in the nw and central parts of seismic unit vi (mtc_2, mtc_2. 1, mtc_2.2, mtc_2.3 and mtc_2.4) (fig. 6). location and distribution of the main depocentres in seismic unit vii (fig. 5b) greatly di¡er from those of the previous basin con¢guration (fig. 5a). the isopach map of seismic unit vii (fig. 5b) shows that the areal extension of the nw depocentre was signi¢cantly reduced and new depocentres were relocated to the central and se parts of the basin.the central depocentre was located to the south of haydn ridge, where a 201 7 km 2 mtc (mtc_1) was de- posited (moscardelli et al., 2006).

from each other by continuous units of strong plan-parallel reﬂectors: as thick as 300 ms as in the case of that between am2 and am3; or as thick as 700 ms, as in the case of that between am1 and am2. these continuous strong plan-parallel units were seismically interpreted as a combination of turbiditic and hemipelagic deposition (figs. 8 and 9b). am1 is the basal megaslide, lying directly on horizon h3 (fig. 8). it is also the largest megaslide mapped throughout the basin, extending downslope for about 280 km in a general sen direction, presenting a maximum width of c. 250 km and covering a total area of approximately 67,000 km2 (table 1 and fig. 9a). the depositional area of am1 is located some 40e50 km downslope from the headscarps of the younger am2 (figs. 8 and 9), being mostly characterized by highly chaotic to transparent seismic facies which thicken signiﬁcantly basinwards and bulge up appreciably (maximum thickness of c. 778 m), creating a major positive topo- graphic feature over the coeval seaﬂoor. clear headwall scarps related to am1 are difﬁcult to identify (fig. 8), as no scars cutting into siliciclastic series in a plausible location and with plausible dimensions were found in spatial relation to this huge allochthonous mass. however, across the northwestern steep margin, am1 deposits are found some 100 km downslope from a large erosive area clearly recognizable along the slope, which merges downslope with the basal horizon h3, indi- cating that am1 could have slid away downslope from the dismantling of the mixed carbonate siliciclastic platform, leaving behind a large evacuation scar (figs. 8b and 9a). in some parts of the nw basin, slope scarps are even replaced directly downslope by detached blocks of high amplitude reﬂection, in continuity to which we ﬁnd the transparent am1 megaslide seaward from the fold-and-thrust belt system (figs. 11 and 9a). internal huge blocks of comparable very high amplitude reﬂections (up to 15e20 km wide) are preserved

g the upslope region, and compressional structures characterising the downslope region. many described mtcs do not ﬁt the upslope extension- downslope compression model, however, as it does not account for the huge variety and association of structures observed ( woodcock, 1979; farrell, 1984; elliot and williams, 1988; martinsen, 1989; martinsen and bakken, 1990; trincardi and argnani, 1990; o’leary, 1991; strachan, 2002a,b; lucente and pini, 2003; canals et al., 2004; frey martinez et al., 2005 ). such structures typically include folds, boudins and normal and reverse faults, with extensional deformation sometimes juxtaposed with, or even overprinted by, compression and vice-versa (farrell, 1984; martinsen and bakken, 1990; strachan, 2002a). for the purposes of the present study we have grouped the various kinematic indicators according to the domain in which they are most likely to occur within a mtc exhibiting a typical ‘tripartite’ anatomy ( martinsen, 1994; lastras et al., 2002 ): the headwall domain, translational domain and the toe domain ( fig. 2). although there may be some overlap, a clearly deﬁned classiﬁcation scheme is vital for the practical application of the presented work. all examples are illustrated with reference to a summary diagram (fig. 2), and key geometrical and geological criteria are summarised in fig. 3. 3.1. headwall domain this area encompasses the upslope, extension-dominated region of the mtc. two important kinematic indicators found in this domain are headwall scarps and extensional ridges and blocks . 3.1.1. headwall scarps headwall scarps are deﬁned as a boundary or scarp marking the upslope margin of a mtc, where the basal shear surface ramps up to cut stratigraphically higher, younger strata and intersect the surface. these are often conspicuous features that can be easily identiﬁed in both seismic section, and in planform using horizon maps.

from each other by continuous units of strong plan-parallel reﬂectors: as thick as 300 ms as in the case of that between am2 and am3; or as thick as 700 ms, as in the case of that between am1 and am2. horizon h3 (fig. 8). it is also the largest megaslide mapped throughout the basin, extending downslope for about 280 km in a general sen direction, presenting a maximum width of c. 250 km and covering a total area of approximately 67,000 km2 (table 1 and fig. 9a). the depositional area of am1 is located some 40e50 km downslope from the headscarps of the younger am2 (figs. 8 and 9), being mostly characterized by highly chaotic to transparent seismic facies which thicken signiﬁcantly basinwards and bulge up appreciably (maximum thickness of c. 778 m), creating a major positive topo- graphic feature over the coeval seaﬂoor. clear headwall scarps related to am1 are difﬁcult to identify (fig. 8), as no scars cutting into siliciclastic series in a plausible location and with plausible dimensions were found in spatial relation to this huge allochthonous mass. however, across the northwestern steep margin, am1 deposits are found some 100 km downslope from a large erosive area clearly recognizable along the slope, which merges downslope with the basal horizon h3, indi- cating that am1 could have slid away downslope from the dismantling of the mixed carbonate siliciclastic platform, leaving behind a large evacuation scar (figs. 8b and 9a). in some parts of the nw basin, slope scarps are even replaced directly downslope by detached blocks of high amplitude reﬂection, in continuity to which we ﬁnd the transparent am1 megaslide seaward from the fold-and-thrust belt system (figs. 11 and 9a). internal huge blocks of comparable very high amplitude reﬂections (up to 15e20 km wide) g the upslope region, and compressional structures characterising the downslope region. many described mtcs do not ﬁt the upslope extension- downslope compression model, however, as it does not account for the huge variety and association of structures observed ( woodcock, 1979; farrell, 1984; elliot and williams, 1988; martinsen, 1989; martinsen and bakken, 1990; trincardi and argnani, 1990; o’leary, 1991; strachan, 2002a,b; lucente and pini, 2003; canals et al., 2004; frey martinez et al., 2005 ). such structures typically include folds, boudins and normal and reverse faults, with extensional deformation sometimes juxtaposed with, or even overprinted by, compression and vice-versa (farrell, 1984; martinsen and bakken, 1990; strachan, 2002a). for the purposes of the present study we have grouped the various kinematic indicators according to the domain in which they are most likely to occur within a mtc exhibiting a typical ‘tripartite’ anatomy ( martinsen, 1994; lastras et al., 2002 ): the headwall domain, translational domain and the toe domain ( fig. 2). although there may be some overlap, a clearly deﬁned classiﬁcation scheme is vital for the practical application of the presented work. all examples are illustrated with reference to a summary diagram (fig. 2), and key geometrical and geological criteria are summarised in fig. 3. 3.1. headwall domain this area encompasses the upslope, extension-dominated region of the mtc. two important kinematic indicators found in this domain are headwall scarps and extensional ridges and blocks . 3.1.1. headwall scarps headwall scarps are deﬁned as a boundary or scarp marking the upslope margin of a mtc, where the basal shear surface ramps up to cut stratigraphically higher, younger strata and intersect the surface. these are often conspicuous features that can be easily identiﬁed in both seismic section, and in planform using horizon maps.

sheets on passive margins, which can run out hundreds of kilometers across the seafloor (as discussed later in the text) (table 1; e.g., walker and massingill, 1970; embley, 1976; damuth and embley, 1981; embley and jacobi, 1986). the slide blocks and hummocky surfaces of the mass transport deposit sheets are evident along the base of the oregon slope in the swath bathymetry (goldfinger et al., 2000) and gloria side-scan im- ages (fig. 6; eez scan 84 scientific staff, 1986). seismic facies and echo character from a wide variety of seismic profiles, including deep-tow side-scan sonar and 4.5 khz seismic profiles, show the chaotic and transparent facies of the mass transport deposits (goldfinger et al., 2000). in addition, sediment cores taken from these mass transport deposits (figs. 5, 6) contain the chaotic deposits of debris flows (goldfinger et al., 2000; nelson et al., 2000). a seismic reflector from deep-tow 4.5 khz profiles suggests that chaotic blocks from the 44 n slump (fig. 5) are correlative with the end of the missoula flood deposits (goldfinger et al., 2000; c. goldfinger, written communication, 2008), which oc- curred approximately 11,000 yr bp (e.g., baker and bunker, 1985). a similar age for the 44 n slump (~ 11,600 yr bp) also is suggested, because the 44 n slump blocks the astoria channel. downdip, this channel contains the latest pleistocene turbidites covered by holocene transgressive hemipelagic olive-gray clay with a basal age of 11,6
