hese deposits. mass-transport deposits can comprise sheets, lobes, and channel fills, and can reach 150 m or more in thickness. greater thicknesses are observed where successive flows are amalgamated. this paper documents both internal architectural or stratigraphic as well as external geomorphic attributes of such deposits, as expressed in outcrop and imaged by 3d seismic data. recognition of mass-transport deposits in outcrop is based on identification of bedding deformed by synsedimentary processes, with deformation ranging from minimal redistribution of large slide blocks to complete disaggregation typical of debris-flow deposit s. on seismic data, mass-transport deposits can be recognized by certain geomorphologic as well as stratigraphic distinguishing characteristics: basal linear grooved and scoured surfaces, hummocky relief at the top, and internal chaotic to transparent seismic facies, with internal thrust faulting common. key words: mass-transport deposits, mass transport deposits, debris flow, seismic stratigraphy, seismic geomorphology mass-transport deposits in deepwater settings sepm special publication no. 96, copyright © 2011 sepm (society for sedimentary geology), isbn 978-1-56576-287-9, p. 7–38. introduction mass movements of sediments form kilometer-scale features (fig. 1) that represent major subaerial and subaqueous geohazards and can comprise significant depositional elements, characteriz- ing marine slope and basin-floor systems. catastrophic conse- quences of mass-transport processes such as tsunamis, avalanches, major rock falls, and mudslides are dramatic (e.g., holmes, 1965; bolt et al., 1977; voight, 1978; brunsden and prior, 1984; fisher and smith, 1991; martinsen 1994; bondevik et al., 2003). in addi- tion, mass transport deposit of sediments can significantly affect stabil- ity of offshore installations (e.g., prior and coleman, 1982; solheim et al., 2005).

hese deposits. mass-transport deposits can comprise sheets, lobes, and channel fills, and can reach 150 m or more in thickness. greater thicknesses are observed where successive flows are amalgamated. this paper documents both internal architectural or stratigraphic as well as external geomorphic attributes of such deposits, as expressed in outcrop and imaged by 3d seismic data. recognition of mass-transport deposits in outcrop is based on identification of bedding deformed by synsedimentary processes, with deformation ranging from minimal redistribution of large slide blocks to complete disaggregation typical of debris-flow deposit s. on seismic data, mass-transport deposits can be recognized by certain geomorphologic as well as stratigraphic distinguishing characteristics: basal linear grooved and scoured surfaces, hummocky relief at the top, and internal chaotic to transparent seismic facies, with internal thrust faulting common. key words: mass-transport deposits, mass transport deposits, debris flow, seismic stratigraphy, seismic geomorphology mass-transport deposits in deepwater settings sepm special publication no. 96, copyright © 2011 sepm (society for sedimentary geology), isbn 978-1-56576-287-9, p. 7–38. introduction mass movements of sediments form kilometer-scale features (fig. 1) that represent major subaerial and subaqueous geohazards and can comprise significant depositional elements, characteriz- ing marine slope and basin-floor systems. catastrophic conse- quences of mass-transport processes such as tsunamis, avalanches, major rock falls, and mudslides are dramatic (e.g., holmes, 1965; bolt et al., 1977; voight, 1978; brunsden and prior, 1984; fisher and smith, 1991; martinsen 1994; bondevik et al., 2003). in addi- tion, mass transport deposit of sediments can significantly affect stabil- ity of offshore installations (e.g., prior and coleman, 1982; solheim et al., 2005).

1; frey martinez et al., 2006 ). in planform, a lateral margin may appear as a scarp or linear feature roughly parallel to the slope direction which separates a smooth, undeformed region of the seabed or top mtc age-equivalent horizon from the adjacent region that has been affected by failure ( fig. 6 a, b). conversely, they can also be expressed as raised, positive features due to localised or net accu- mulation of material in the translational or toe domain of the mtc (prior et al., 1984; trincardi and normark, 1989 ). a seismic section across a lateral margin may show a scarp of positive or negative relief, or in the case of a lateral margin with no discernable relief, a change in seismic facies from undeformed strata outside of the area affected by slope failure processes, to that of the disrupted facies symptomatic of mtcs ( fig. 6 a, b). in this respect, the iden- tiﬁcation of lateral margins becomes difﬁcult where the trans- lational domain does not exhibit a high degree of disruption. the example shown in fig. 6 a, b is taken from the southern margin of the storegga slide where material affected by instability in the storegga zone is juxtaposed with undeformed strata to the south. the identiﬁcation of lateral margins can be of great value to the kinematic study of mtcs, as they offer a primary constraint on the ﬂow direction of the mtc. where entire mtcs are imaged, the geometry and regional slope direction can be used to determine the overall translation direction ( masson et al., 1993). fig. 4a shows an image of the levant margin, which features a number of mtcs at the seabed ( frey martinez et al., 2006 ). a mtc array (labelled on fig. 4 a) features lateral margins that are conspicuous features in planform; generally dip-parallel, continuous and linear, but they do exhibit discontinuities and localised changes in trend. the lateral margins trend n–s, indicating that gross general transport also took place in this direction.

(2009) and alves (2015), the features close to the headwall scarp are interpreted as linear blocks accumulated in the extensional domain of mtda. the pointy features are interpreted as rafted blocks that can occur at any zone within mass transport deposits (alves, 2015); 'ridge- fig. 7. isochron thickness of gas-bearing strata (stacked enhanced seismic anomalies) in zone b. several depocenters are identi ﬁed and correlate with ﬂuid migration pathways (gas chimneys and faults). q. sun et al. / marine and petroleum geology 81 (2017) 17 e32 25 like' structures are often observed and usually rise over, or pierce, the overlying strata ( fig. 8 bec). at places, onlapping seismic re- ﬂections occur at the ﬂanks of these same ridges, indicating that the deposition of these onlapping strata occurred during, or immedi- ately after, the emplacement of mtda ( fig. 8 b and d). a steep headwall scarp is observed on seismic data, and has an elevation ranging from 60 to 95 m ( fig. 8). it is arcuate in plan view and extends from nw to se ( fig. 9 ). at this same scarp, mtda contacts with undeformed slope deposits that are observed to the east ( fig. 8 ced). in addition, a thin unit with near constant thick- ness (~65.0 m) drapes and overlies mtda. mtda has variable thickness, with an average value of 55.3 m (table 1). the maximum thickness of mass transport deposits is ~100 m and occurs against the headwall scarp ( fig. 8 a).

seismic interpretation of mass-transport deposits within the upper oligocene frio formation, south texas gulf coast osareni ogiesoba and ursula hammes abstract we integrated well logs and thr ee-dimensional seismic data to describe a wedge of deformed shallow frio rocks lying above a major bed-parallel decollement within the upper oligocene frio formation located between the houston and norias deltas on the south texas gulf coast. our analyses show that the identified deformed shallow frio rocks can be divided into proximal clay-rich and low-permeability sandstones charac- terized by discontinuous, mounded, and chaotic seismic events; near-proximal, clay-poor, and high-permeability sandstones characterized by parallel to subparallel bedded seismic events; and distal sand-, silt-, and mudstones composed of a mix of proximal and near-proximal rocks. all of the deformed rocks are composed of acoustic-impedance materials that are lower than those of the undeformed shallow frio and are underlain by low-velocity, overpressured, shale-rich rocks. the mecha- nism that triggered the collapse of the shallow frio and sub- sequent development of mass-transport deposits is attributed to an uprising, overpressured, shale-rich high and the devel- opment of a shelf-edge listric fault. proprietary biostratigraphic data show that the collapse of the shallow frio in areas be- tween the houston and norias deltas occurred between 27.5 and 25.3 ma— approximately the same time as the hackberry collapse in the mississippi delta. in the proximal area, inter- preted paleowater depths from biostratigraphic data based on benthic foraminifers range from 60 to 120 ft (20 –40 m) authors osareni ogiesoba /c24bureau of economic geology, jackson school of geosciences, uni- versity of texas at austin, austin, texas; osareni.ogiesoba@beg.utexas.edu osareni (chris) ogiesoba is a research associ- ate at the bureau of economic geology, univer- sity of texas. he holds a ph.d.

1; frey martinez et al., 2006 ). in planform, a lateral margin may appear as a scarp or linear feature roughly parallel to the slope direction which separates a smooth, undeformed region of the seabed or top mtc age-equivalent horizon from the adjacent region that has been affected by failure ( fig. 6 a, b). conversely, they can also be expressed as raised, positive features due to localised or net accu- mulation of material in the translational or toe domain of the mtc (prior et al., 1984; trincardi and normark, 1989 ). a seismic section across a lateral margin may show a scarp of positive or negative relief, or in the case of a lateral margin with no discernable relief, a change in seismic facies from undeformed strata outside of the area affected by slope failure processes, to that of the disrupted facies symptomatic of mtcs ( fig. 6 a, b). in this respect, the iden- tiﬁcation of lateral margins becomes difﬁcult where the trans- lational domain does not exhibit a high degree of disruption. the example shown in fig. 6 a, b is taken from the southern margin of the storegga slide where material affected by instability in the storegga zone is juxtaposed with undeformed strata to the south. the identiﬁcation of lateral margins can be of great value to the kinematic study of mtcs, as they offer a primary constraint on the ﬂow direction of the mtc. where entire mtcs are imaged, the geometry and regional slope direction can be used to determine the overall translation direction ( masson et al., 1993). fig. 4a shows an image of the levant margin, which features a number of mtcs at the seabed ( frey martinez et al., 2006 ). a mtc array (labelled on fig. 4 a) features lateral margins that are conspicuous features in planform; generally dip-parallel, continuous and linear, but they do exhibit discontinuities and localised changes in trend. the lateral margins trend n–s, indicating that gross general transport also took place in this direction.

1; frey martinez et al., 2006 ). in planform, a lateral margin may appear as a scarp or linear feature roughly parallel to the slope direction which separates a smooth, undeformed region of the seabed or top mtc age-equivalent horizon from the adjacent region that has been affected by failure ( fig. 6 a, b). conversely, they can also be expressed as raised, positive features due to localised or net accu- mulation of material in the translational or toe domain of the mtc (prior et al., 1984; trincardi and normark, 1989 ). a seismic section across a lateral margin may show a scarp of positive or negative relief, or in the case of a lateral margin with no discernable relief, a change in seismic facies from undeformed strata outside of the area affected by slope failure processes, to that of the disrupted facies symptomatic of mtcs ( fig. 6 a, b). in this respect, the iden- tiﬁcation of lateral margins becomes difﬁcult where the trans- lational domain does not exhibit a high degree of disruption. the example shown in fig. 6 a, b is taken from the southern margin of the storegga slide where material affected by instability in the storegga zone is juxtaposed with undeformed strata to the south. the identiﬁcation of lateral margins can be of great value to the kinematic study of mtcs, as they offer a primary constraint on the ﬂow direction of the mtc. where entire mtcs are imaged, the geometry and regional slope direction can be used to determine the overall translation direction ( masson et al., 1993). fig. 4a shows an image of the levant margin, which features a number of mtcs at the seabed ( frey martinez et al., 2006 ). a mtc array (labelled on fig. 4 a) features lateral margins that are conspicuous features in planform; generally dip-parallel, continuous and linear, but they do exhibit discontinuities and localised changes in trend. the lateral margins trend n–s, indicating that gross general transport also took place in this direction.

seismic interpretation of mass-transport deposits within the upper oligocene frio formation, south texas gulf coast osareni ogiesoba and ursula hammes abstract we integrated well logs and thr ee-dimensional seismic data to describe a wedge of deformed shallow frio rocks lying above a major bed-parallel decollement within the upper oligocene frio formation located between the houston and norias deltas on the south texas gulf coast. our analyses show that the identified deformed shallow frio rocks can be divided into proximal clay-rich and low-permeability sandstones charac- terized by discontinuous, mounded, and chaotic seismic events; near-proximal, clay-poor, and high-permeability sandstones characterized by parallel to subparallel bedded seismic events; and distal sand-, silt-, and mudstones composed of a mix of proximal and near-proximal rocks. all of the deformed rocks are composed of acoustic-impedance materials that are lower than those of the undeformed shallow frio and are underlain by low-velocity, overpressured, shale-rich rocks. the mecha- nism that triggered the collapse of the shallow frio and sub- sequent development of mass-transport deposits is attributed to an uprising, overpressured, shale-rich high and the devel- opment of a shelf-edge listric fault. proprietary biostratigraphic data show that the collapse of the shallow frio in areas be- tween the houston and norias deltas occurred between 27.5 and 25.3 ma— approximately the same time as the hackberry collapse in the mississippi delta. in the proximal area, inter- preted paleowater depths from biostratigraphic data based on benthic foraminifers range from 60 to 120 ft (20 –40 m) authors osareni ogiesoba /c24bureau of economic geology, jackson school of geosciences, uni- versity of texas at austin, austin, texas; osareni.ogiesoba@beg.utexas.edu osareni (chris) ogiesoba is a research associ- ate at the bureau of economic geology, univer- sity of texas. he holds a ph.d.

h non- enhanced seismic re ﬂections ( fig. 4 ). to the west, they contact with high-amplitude strata with a thickness reaching 230 m, and onlapping seismic re ﬂections being also observed ( fig. 4 b). to the north and east, the interpreted ensas are bounded by low- amplitude features ( fig. 4 e). however, their western limit is dif ﬁ- cult to identify because of the predominance of high-amplitude strata in this same area. thus, the black continuous line in fig. 4 b is the conservative limit of ensas to the west, providing a conservative area of 18 km 2, and a volume approaching 0.44 km 3 (fig. 4e; table 1). in zone b, acoustic anomalies observed on seismic and rms- amplitude data are vertically stacked ( figs. 5 e6). these stacked enhanced seismic anomalies (sesas) are trapped underneath chaotic mass transport deposits ( fig. 5aeb) and are sub-circular in plan view ( fig. 7). they occur along, or instead cross-cut, slope strata and seismic reﬂections that show a lateral inversion in polarity in these features (fig. 6ced). several chaotic and dimmed seismic reﬂections sourced from deeper strata are observed directly below the sesas (figs. 5aeb, 6 a). the thickness of sesas is variable and shows four maxima that correlate with the underlying chaotic and dimmed seismic re ﬂections ( figs. 5 e7). the sesas cover an area of 30.58 km2 (fig. 5c; table 1), abruptly terminate to the west where they are bounded by a large normal fault ( fig. 5aeb). negative seismic anomalies observed at the base of mass transport deposits are usually interpreted as basal shear zones, and are generated by differences in acoustic impedance between mass transport deposits and underlying strata ( dugan, 2012 ). therefore, the ensas observed in zone a occur in basal shear zones as documented in alves and lourenco (2010) and dugan (2012) . yet, they extend laterally beyond the mass transport deposits ( fig. 4 aed), a character suggesting they are not basal shear zones through their whole extent.

scarps can be isolated features or occur as series forming a step-like high relief (fig. 2f). conversely, in the se compartment, thrust belts are largely now inactivated and are located at shallower water depths, between c. 900 and 1400 m (fig. 1). the active thrust belt spans a narrow zone rarely wider than 10 km and is continuous for no more than a few tens of kilometres. the associated structural style is variable along strike, with the prevalence of zones of sea-ﬂoor structural uplift as a result of folding and/or faulting (fig. 5a); locally, active thrust faults can reach the sea ﬂoor, forming fault-related scarps up to 200 m high (fig. 5b). although these features are not as signiﬁcant as the spectacular relief mapped in the nw compartment, structural sea-ﬂoor uplift can nevertheless result in ﬂexure of sedimentary bedding along fold limbs, capable of elevating the sea bottom into ramp-like features as high as hundreds of metres (up to 300–350 m) over horizontal distances of only a few kilometres (figs 2e and 5a, b). a series of slope failure features and mass-transport deposits were seismically recognized along the fold-and-thrust belts of both the nw and se compartments. the main criteria for recognition of mass-transport processes were the existence of headwall features (erosional scarps and slide or rotated blocks; evans et al . 1996; mulder & cochonat 1996) and the presence of transparent to chaotic seismic facies with clear basal detach- ment surfaces (mulder & cochonat 1996; canals et al . 2004; sultan et al. 2004; evans et al. 2005; frey-martı´nez et al. 2006). seaward of the se compartment, mass-transport deposits were mapped in the study area downslope to around 2600 m water depth and can make up an upper remobilized sediment layer up to c. 300–600 m thick (figs 1 and 5a, b). slope failure features are developed along the sea-ﬂoor structural uplift that ﬂanks the lineaments of the fold-and-thrust belt (fig. 1).

mid-slope settings (fig. 19). external morphology seismic reflection data are better suited than outcrops for describing larger aspects of external as well as internal morphol- ogy of mass-transport deposits. table 1 summarizes the seismic stratigraphic criteria for recognition of mass-transport deposits. these criteria are discussed below. mass-transport deposits can assume a variety of shapes and sizes ranging from lobate to sheet to channel-form (posamentier et al., 2000; posamentier and kolla, 2003). figure 23 illustrates several lobate-form, deep-water mass-transport-deposit lobes. these lobes are characterized by relatively steep flanks (up to 20°), suggesting a flow mechanism that involved a relatively abrupt halt or en masse freezing of the flow. a similar, steep-flanked mass-transport de- posit is illustrated on the left side of figure 24. in contrast with these steep-sided debrites, a debrite lobe with tapered flanks is present on the right side of figure 24, giving the appearance of a deflated lobe. the gradient that characterizes the margins of these deposits reflects their rheology. mass-transport deposits also can be channelized (posamentier and kolla, 2003) and leveed (fig. 24). in some instances, channelized mass-transport deposits have opportu- nistically occupied an earlier-formed, basin-floor channel, likely formed by turbidity currents (fig. 25). most debris flows are characterized by a rugose external texture suggesting presence of large floating clasts (figs. 26, 27). a cluster of large clasts within a mass-transport deposit is shown in figure 17, with some clasts approaching ~ 500 m in diameter. a hybrid type of channelized, large-scale mass-transport deposit is relatively common in basin-floor settings. in low- gradient settings immediately outboard of the base of slope, a common aspect of large mass-transport deposits is the tendency to plow deeply into the substrate.

south china sea wu shi-guo1, qin zhi-liang1,2, wang da-wei1, peng xue-chao3, wang zhi-jun4, yao gen-shun5 1 institute of oceanology, the chinese academy of sciences, qingdao 266071, china 2 graduate university, the chinese academy of sciences, beijing 100049, china 3 institute of geological survey, guangzhou marine geology survey, guangzhou 510706, china 4 cnooc general research institute, beijing 100027, china 5 hangzhou institute of geology, petrochina, hangzhou 310023, china abstract mass transport deposits (mass transport deposits) are one kind of deepwater sedimentary systems driven by the gravity ﬂow action, and play an important role for the deep-water sedimentation in global continental margins. mass transport deposits are not only one of the most serious deep-water geo-hazards, but also have close relationship with the formation and accumulation of marine gas hydrates and deepwater hydrocarbon. based on the topographic and high resolution seismic data in the hydrocarbon exploration region, we identiﬁed the characteristics and distribution of mass transport deposits in the northern slope of the south china sea. mass transport deposits are characterized by apparent geomorphology and sedimentary structures. in mass transport deposits there are well developed extensional faults in the head and slides and turnover blocks in the middle. compressive structures and thrust faults are formed in the toe region of mass transport deposits. several mechanisms can account for development of mass transport deposits. however, baiyun mass transport deposits were inferred to be dominated by the dissolution of gas hydrate as suggested by the model of gas hydrate reservoirs and numerical modeling using the elastic-plastic ﬁnite element method for mass transport deposits in the baiyun sag.

mid-slope settings (fig. 19). external morphology seismic reflection data are better suited than outcrops for describing larger aspects of external as well as internal morphol- ogy of mass-transport deposits. table 1 summarizes the seismic stratigraphic criteria for recognition of mass-transport deposits. these criteria are discussed below. mass-transport deposits can assume a variety of shapes and sizes ranging from lobate to sheet to channel-form (posamentier et al., 2000; posamentier and kolla, 2003). figure 23 illustrates several lobate-form, deep-water mass-transport-deposit lobes. these lobes are characterized by relatively steep flanks (up to 20°), suggesting a flow mechanism that involved a relatively abrupt halt or en masse freezing of the flow. a similar, steep-flanked mass-transport de- posit is illustrated on the left side of figure 24. in contrast with these steep-sided debrites, a debrite lobe with tapered flanks is present on the right side of figure 24, giving the appearance of a deflated lobe. the gradient that characterizes the margins of these deposits reflects their rheology. mass-transport deposits also can be channelized (posamentier and kolla, 2003) and leveed (fig. 24). in some instances, channelized mass-transport deposits have opportu- nistically occupied an earlier-formed, basin-floor channel, likely formed by turbidity currents (fig. 25). most debris flows are characterized by a rugose external texture suggesting presence of large floating clasts (figs. 26, 27). a cluster of large clasts within a mass-transport deposit is shown in figure 17, with some clasts approaching ~ 500 m in diameter. a hybrid type of channelized, large-scale mass-transport deposit is relatively common in basin-floor settings. in low- gradient settings immediately outboard of the base of slope, a common aspect of large mass-transport deposits is the tendency to plow deeply into the substrate.

mid-slope settings (fig. 19). external morphology seismic reflection data are better suited than outcrops for describing larger aspects of external as well as internal morphol- ogy of mass-transport deposits. table 1 summarizes the seismic stratigraphic criteria for recognition of mass-transport deposits. these criteria are discussed below. mass-transport deposits can assume a variety of shapes and sizes ranging from lobate to sheet to channel-form (posamentier et al., 2000; posamentier and kolla, 2003). figure 23 illustrates several lobate-form, deep-water mass-transport-deposit lobes. these lobes are characterized by relatively steep flanks (up to 20°), suggesting a flow mechanism that involved a relatively abrupt halt or en masse freezing of the flow. a similar, steep-flanked mass-transport de- posit is illustrated on the left side of figure 24. in contrast with these steep-sided debrites, a debrite lobe with tapered flanks is present on the right side of figure 24, giving the appearance of a deflated lobe. the gradient that characterizes the margins of these deposits reflects their rheology. mass-transport deposits also can be channelized (posamentier and kolla, 2003) and leveed (fig. 24). in some instances, channelized mass-transport deposits have opportu- nistically occupied an earlier-formed, basin-floor channel, likely formed by turbidity currents (fig. 25). most debris flows are characterized by a rugose external texture suggesting presence of large floating clasts (figs. 26, 27). a cluster of large clasts within a mass-transport deposit is shown in figure 17, with some clasts approaching ~ 500 m in diameter. a hybrid type of channelized, large-scale mass-transport deposit is relatively common in basin-floor settings. in low- gradient settings immediately outboard of the base of slope, a common aspect of large mass-transport deposits is the tendency to plow deeply into the substrate.

acked allochthonous masses within the upper miocene-quaternary sedimentary record, they are best described as mass transport complexes (mtcs), and here- after renamed as: the amap�a megaslide complex (amc) and the par�a-maranh~ao megaslide complex (pmmc). 4.3.1. the amap�a megaslide complex the amap�a megaslide complex (amc) corresponds to a series of stacked megaslides, named amap�a after the adjacent coastal amap�a state in northern brazil (silva et al., 2010). the amc is composed of six major individual megaslides encompassing different stratigraphic levels, interlayered with undisturbed depo- sitional intervals which display either continuous or strong re- ﬂectors (fig. 8). several other smaller mdts could also be identiﬁed, but because they could not be correlated across the study area (because they were too thin or because of the lack of regional extent) they are not described in this paper. an acronym was assigned to each mappable megaslide, according to its position in the stratigraphic section (from the most ancient to the most recent; figs. 8 and 9 and table 1): am1 (amap�a megaslide 1); am2 (amap�a megaslide 2); am3 (amap�a megaslide 2); am4 (amap�a megaslide 4); am5 (amap�a megaslide 5) and am6 (amap�a megaslide 6). am1 to am6 are marked by seismically well-deﬁned basal d�ecollement surfaces (fig. 8), whereas their disturbed masses show seismic evidence of distinct degrees of displacements and disrup- tions, as indicated by a set of variable acoustic seismic facies types, such as: internal transparent to chaotic facies; or a combination of chaotic facies with local interbedded facies (fig.10). the megaslides lie either directly on the top of each other, as am4, am5 and am6 do, or may be separated from each other by continuous units of strong plan-parallel reﬂectors: as thick as 300 ms as in the case of that between am2 and am3; or as thick as 700 ms, as in the case of that between am1 and am2.

failure the interpretation presented suggests that the ecm is af- fected by processes of slope instability recorded by development of mass-transport deposits. seismic interpretation has demon- strated that slope instability affected the surficial and near- surface stratigraphic record of the ecm, the lubina mass transport deposit being the most obvious feature. the repeated occurrence of mass- wasting processes in the area raises the obvious question of what internal or external factors allowed this margin to be so suscep- tible to slope failure. numerous studies have demonstrated that slope instability is initiated when the downslope-oriented shear stress exceeds the shear strength (resisting stress) of the slope sediments (e.g., laberg and vorren, 2000). slope failure can hence be the result of a downslope-oriented increase in shear stress, a reduction in sediment strength, or a combination of both (lee et al., 1991). despite variability in regional geological processes, and inde- pendently of the scale of the mass-wasting event, slope instabil- ity is often triggered by variations in pore pressure. this trigger could result from underlying mechanisms, such as sedimen- tary, seismic-loading, gas-hydrate proces

seismic interpretation of mass-transport deposits within the upper oligocene frio formation, south texas gulf coast osareni ogiesoba and ursula hammes abstract we integrated well logs and thr ee-dimensional seismic data to describe a wedge of deformed shallow frio rocks lying above a major bed-parallel decollement within the upper oligocene frio formation located between the houston and norias deltas on the south texas gulf coast. our analyses show that the identified deformed shallow frio rocks can be divided into proximal clay-rich and low-permeability sandstones charac- terized by discontinuous, mounded, and chaotic seismic events; near-proximal, clay-poor, and high-permeability sandstones characterized by parallel to subparallel bedded seismic events; and distal sand-, silt-, and mudstones composed of a mix of proximal and near-proximal rocks. all of the deformed rocks are composed of acoustic-impedance materials that are lower than those of the undeformed shallow frio and are underlain by low-velocity, overpressured, shale-rich rocks. the mecha- nism that triggered the collapse of the shallow frio and sub- sequent development of mass-transport deposits is attributed to an uprising, overpressured, shale-rich high and the devel- opment of a shelf-edge listric fault. proprietary biostratigraphic data show that the collapse of the shallow frio in areas be- tween the houston and norias deltas occurred between 27.5 and 25.3 ma— approximately the same time as the hackberry collapse in the mississippi delta. in the proximal area, inter- preted paleowater depths from biostratigraphic data based on benthic foraminifers range from 60 to 120 ft (20 –40 m) authors osareni ogiesoba /c24bureau of economic geology, jackson school of geosciences, uni- versity of texas at austin, austin, texas; osareni.ogiesoba@beg.utexas.edu osareni (chris) ogiesoba is a research associ- ate at the bureau of economic geology, univer- sity of texas. he holds a ph.d.

ike directly across the depression and do not parallel the curvature of the bathymetric contours. the seismic proﬁles between 560-m and 590-m water depths show that the ridges evolve into rhythmic, undulating forms interpreted as folds, that die out at a water depth of about 650 m (fig. 17). sidescan-sonar images reveal numerous pock- marks on the seaﬂoor throughout the region. the pockmarks on the ‘humboldt slide’ are small depressions with a random and dense distribution. compared with the adjacent continental slope to the north, the ‘humboldt slide’ zone has a higher concentration of pockmarks (yun et al ., 1999), possibly indicating a greater tendency toward gas charging and strength reduction. the erosion and gully zone (fig. 18) extends between the 230-m and 380-m istobaths where huntec seismic proﬁles show truncations of shelf reﬂectors with an estimated 5–15 m of sediment missing. geotechnical tests (lee et al., 1981) from cores collected in the zone show that the sediment is overconsolidated, consistent with the loss of 15 m of sediment by erosion or slope failure. huntec seismic data show local hummocky deposits (< 5 m thick) that unconformably overlie the slope below the gullies (fig. 16). a surface deﬁning the upslope limit of crenulations cuts the slope sequence and crops out at the 380-m isobath (fig. 16). this exposed basal surface separates the sequence of slope-parallel-bedded, seaward-dipping reﬂectors that lie upslope from crenulated, back- tilted reﬂectors of what is interpreted to be the main slide mass. the basal surface is locally buried < 5 m near its upslope limit by disrupted reﬂectors, and dips 3°–4° seaward, parallel to the slope re- ﬂectors. farther downslope, the basal surface dips ~8° and cuts deeply into the slope section (fig. 16). according to gardner et al. (1999), the main body of the landslide is composed of a zone of back-tilted and gently folded blocks (fig. 15).

seismic interpretation of mass-transport deposits within the upper oligocene frio formation, south texas gulf coast osareni ogiesoba and ursula hammes abstract we integrated well logs and thr ee-dimensional seismic data to describe a wedge of deformed shallow frio rocks lying above a major bed-parallel decollement within the upper oligocene frio formation located between the houston and norias deltas on the south texas gulf coast. our analyses show that the identified deformed shallow frio rocks can be divided into proximal clay-rich and low-permeability sandstones charac- terized by discontinuous, mounded, and chaotic seismic events; near-proximal, clay-poor, and high-permeability sandstones characterized by parallel to subparallel bedded seismic events; and distal sand-, silt-, and mudstones composed of a mix of proximal and near-proximal rocks. all of the deformed rocks are composed of acoustic-impedance materials that are lower than those of the undeformed shallow frio and are underlain by low-velocity, overpressured, shale-rich rocks. the mecha- nism that triggered the collapse of the shallow frio and sub- sequent development of mass-transport deposits is attributed to an uprising, overpressured, shale-rich high and the devel- opment of a shelf-edge listric fault. proprietary biostratigraphic data show that the collapse of the shallow frio in areas be- tween the houston and norias deltas occurred between 27.5 and 25.3 ma— approximately the same time as the hackberry collapse in the mississippi delta. in the proximal area, inter- preted paleowater depths from biostratigraphic data based on benthic foraminifers range from 60 to 120 ft (20 –40 m) authors osareni ogiesoba /c24bureau of economic geology, jackson school of geosciences, uni- versity of texas at austin, austin, texas; osareni.ogiesoba@beg.utexas.edu osareni (chris) ogiesoba is a research associ- ate at the bureau of economic geology, univer- sity of texas. he holds a ph.d.

ike directly across the depression and do not parallel the curvature of the bathymetric contours. the seismic proﬁles between 560-m and 590-m water depths show that the ridges evolve into rhythmic, undulating forms interpreted as folds, that die out at a water depth of about 650 m (fig. 17). sidescan-sonar images reveal numerous pock- marks on the seaﬂoor throughout the region. the pockmarks on the ‘humboldt slide’ are small depressions with a random and dense distribution. compared with the adjacent continental slope to the north, the ‘humboldt slide’ zone has a higher concentration of pockmarks (yun et al ., 1999), possibly indicating a greater tendency toward gas charging and strength reduction. the erosion and gully zone (fig. 18) extends between the 230-m and 380-m istobaths where huntec seismic proﬁles show truncations of shelf reﬂectors with an estimated 5–15 m of sediment missing. geotechnical tests (lee et al., 1981) from cores collected in the zone show that the sediment is overconsolidated, consistent with the loss of 15 m of sediment by erosion or slope failure. huntec seismic data show local hummocky deposits (< 5 m thick) that unconformably overlie the slope below the gullies (fig. 16). a surface deﬁning the upslope limit of crenulations cuts the slope sequence and crops out at the 380-m isobath (fig. 16). this exposed basal surface separates the sequence of slope-parallel-bedded, seaward-dipping reﬂectors that lie upslope from crenulated, back- tilted reﬂectors of what is interpreted to be the main slide mass. the basal surface is locally buried < 5 m near its upslope limit by disrupted reﬂectors, and dips 3°–4° seaward, parallel to the slope re- ﬂectors. farther downslope, the basal surface dips ~8° and cuts deeply into the slope section (fig. 16). according to gardner et al. (1999), the main body of the landslide is composed of a zone of back-tilted and gently folded blocks (fig. 15).

ike directly across the depression and do not parallel the curvature of the bathymetric contours. the seismic proﬁles between 560-m and 590-m water depths show that the ridges evolve into rhythmic, undulating forms interpreted as folds, that die out at a water depth of about 650 m (fig. 17). sidescan-sonar images reveal numerous pock- marks on the seaﬂoor throughout the region. the pockmarks on the ‘humboldt slide’ are small depressions with a random and dense distribution. compared with the adjacent continental slope to the north, the ‘humboldt slide’ zone has a higher concentration of pockmarks (yun et al ., 1999), possibly indicating a greater tendency toward gas charging and strength reduction. the erosion and gully zone (fig. 18) extends between the 230-m and 380-m istobaths where huntec seismic proﬁles show truncations of shelf reﬂectors with an estimated 5–15 m of sediment missing. geotechnical tests (lee et al., 1981) from cores collected in the zone show that the sediment is overconsolidated, consistent with the loss of 15 m of sediment by erosion or slope failure. huntec seismic data show local hummocky deposits (< 5 m thick) that unconformably overlie the slope below the gullies (fig. 16). a surface deﬁning the upslope limit of crenulations cuts the slope sequence and crops out at the 380-m isobath (fig. 16). this exposed basal surface separates the sequence of slope-parallel-bedded, seaward-dipping reﬂectors that lie upslope from crenulated, back- tilted reﬂectors of what is interpreted to be the main slide mass. the basal surface is locally buried < 5 m near its upslope limit by disrupted reﬂectors, and dips 3°–4° seaward, parallel to the slope re- ﬂectors. farther downslope, the basal surface dips ~8° and cuts deeply into the slope section (fig. 16). according to gardner et al. (1999), the main body of the landslide is composed of a zone of back-tilted and gently folded blocks (fig. 15).

alysed. dip is calculated from the interpreted time structure map of the chosen horizon, and is useful for enhancing the appearance of laterally continuous geological features, such as faults, that may otherwise be overlooked (dalley et al., 1989 ). a coherency volume may be generated for a speciﬁed time interval and area, and so is free from interpretation bias. like the 3d seismic volume itself, it can be horizontally or stratigraphically sliced to enable the areal extent and lateral continuity of features to be examined. this technique allocates a degree of coherency to a region based on comparison of waveforms across adjacent traces, and gives apparent continuity to discontinuous features, such as faults and edges, irrespective of their orientation ( hart, 1999 ). seismic amplitude can vary due to a number of factors including porosity, ﬂuid content, bed thickness and geometry (hart, 1999 ). the presence of structures, sedimentological features and litho- logical changes may therefore cause organised amplitude patterns, such as linear or areal trends or polarity changes ( enachescu, 1993). following the mapping of a particular horizon, amplitude can be extracted along it and displayed as a continuous horizon map. amplitude can also be extracted from a speciﬁed time interval or window above, below or around a particular horizon. amplitudes can be added, regardless of their polarity, and a cumulative amplitude for the whole window is arrived at ( brown, 1999 ), providing more information for the speciﬁed interval which can be interpreted in a morphological sense. 2.3. geological setting the examples of kinematic indicators illustrated here are sourced from two study areas associated with proliﬁc slope insta- bility. the primary study area is the mid-norwegian continental margin ( fig. 1 a), with additional kinematic indicator examples taken from the levant basin ( fig. 1b). 2.3.1.

h non- enhanced seismic re ﬂections ( fig. 4 ). to the west, they contact with high-amplitude strata with a thickness reaching 230 m, and onlapping seismic re ﬂections being also observed ( fig. 4 b). to the north and east, the interpreted ensas are bounded by low- amplitude features ( fig. 4 e). however, their western limit is dif ﬁ- cult to identify because of the predominance of high-amplitude strata in this same area. thus, the black continuous line in fig. 4 b is the conservative limit of ensas to the west, providing a conservative area of 18 km 2, and a volume approaching 0.44 km 3 (fig. 4e; table 1). in zone b, acoustic anomalies observed on seismic and rms- amplitude data are vertically stacked ( figs. 5 e6). these stacked enhanced seismic anomalies (sesas) are trapped underneath chaotic mass transport deposits ( fig. 5aeb) and are sub-circular in plan view ( fig. 7). they occur along, or instead cross-cut, slope strata and seismic reﬂections that show a lateral inversion in polarity in these features (fig. 6ced). several chaotic and dimmed seismic reﬂections sourced from deeper strata are observed directly below the sesas (figs. 5aeb, 6 a). the thickness of sesas is variable and shows four maxima that correlate with the underlying chaotic and dimmed seismic re ﬂections ( figs. 5 e7). the sesas cover an area of 30.58 km2 (fig. 5c; table 1), abruptly terminate to the west where they are bounded by a large normal fault ( fig. 5aeb). negative seismic anomalies observed at the base of mass transport deposits are usually interpreted as basal shear zones, and are generated by differences in acoustic impedance between mass transport deposits and underlying strata ( dugan, 2012 ). therefore, the ensas observed in zone a occur in basal shear zones as documented in alves and lourenco (2010) and dugan (2012) . yet, they extend laterally beyond the mass transport deposits ( fig. 4 aed), a character suggesting they are not basal shear zones through their whole extent.

deposits (fig. 3). these maps were also helpful to recognise any changes in the geometry of mass transport deposits, areas with blocky strata, regions affected by extension, and basal ramps and ﬂats. length/width aspect ratios of the mass transport deposits were used to deduce their possible causal mechanisms and con- nection with the continental slope and shelf. root-mean square (rms) amplitude maps were generated to high- light the presence of high-amplitude strata and associated structural fabrics. rms amplitude maps calculate average amplitude values by squaring individual data samples over a deﬁned time window, boosting any high amplitude in the mapped interval (cf. brown, 2004). these attribute maps can emphasise structural fabric because seismic wave- lets are diminished across basal ramps as a result of the destructive interference of seismic energy (fairbairn and ward, 1984) and the in- complete reﬂection of energy from the fresnel zones on both sides of the ramps (townsend et al., 1998). rms amplitude maps helped the identiﬁcation of basal ramps and ﬂats, as well as any drag zones around growing diapirs. on rms amplitude maps, near-seaﬂoor uplift is shown as elliptical features around the salt diapirs, marked by differences in amplitude and character from those within it and the outer region. in addition, these same regions are characterised by ramps of variable dimensions (figs. 3, 5 and 8). time-structure maps were used to describe the morphological di- vision of individual mass transport deposits into their headwall, translational and toe do- mains. changes in dip associated with basal shear surfaces were underlined using time-dip maps (fig. 5). the latter maps highlight changes in dip of an interpreted seismic reﬂection. since ramps offset near-seaﬂoor strata, a continuous interpretation across the ramps will re- sult in a change in dip of the interpreted horizon, provided the vertical resolution is high enough to resolve the offset (yilmaz, 1987).

deposit a does not show remnant and rafted blocks but, instead, is crosscut by a pervasive fabric, comprising extensional faults and compressional ridges generated during the ris- ing of salt diapir b (figures 13b, 14b). faults are shown as low-amplitude lineaments on rms am- plitude maps, with high-amplitude strata separat- ing individual faults, i.e., reflecting an important contrast between faulted and nonfaulted strata (figures 13b, 14b). high-amplitude strata are likely to comprise interbedded sands and shales (fiduk et al., 2004) (figures 5b). the closely spaced faults, and moderately deformed strata separating them, denote limited movement of this mass transport deposit, which was confined to the south and west by ris- ing salt diapirs (figures 2c, 13b, 14b). the low- ermost mass transport deposit b comprises chaotic strata deformed and tilted on the flanks of the rising salt diapir b (figures 13b, 14b). we once again extracted data from seismic volumes 100 × 100 lines and 100 ms crossing the faulted, central region of the mass transport deposits (figure 16a, b). amplitude and dip values were extracted from the volume, and cde values were plotted in the ternary diagrams in figure 16c and d. strata in the faulted mass transport deposit a plots toward the left of the ternary diagram (as with mass transport deposits 5 and 6 in nankai and area 1 in southeast brazil), i.e., being predomi- nantly of the c3 to c2 types. importantly, the range in d is relatively wide in the faulted mass transport deposit a for relatively low e values, despite the sharp contrast in amplitude observed on rms amplitude maps (figure 16b). this latter character results in high-c strata in mass transport deposit a (figure 16a). steeply dipping strata in mass transport deposit b are of mod- erate to low amplitude and have been deformed by halokinesis and growth of the diapir (figures 13b, 14b, 16a).

top_chunks.text: rvey area is poor. channels up to 500 m wide, are commonly observed within this unit. these channels pre-date deformation and now provide useful kinematic markers for post-messinian faulting (fig. 4). thickness changes associated with these channels result in localised downlap and apparent onlap surfaces within unit pm1. these local thickness variations are related to deposition from the channels, and are not the result of syn-sedimentary structural growth. aside from the localised thickness variations associated with channel deposition, unit pm1 does not show any syn-kine- matic sedimentation and this unit is assumed to pre-date salt related deformation in this area. 3.1.2. post-messinian unit 2 (pm2) unit pm2 consists of low to medium amplitude, mainly continuous reﬂections, with localised packages of lower amplitude, chaotic reﬂections which pass laterally into more continuous units (fig. 5). unit pm2 contains several channel levee systems, which are larger and much more apparent on seismic sections that those described from within unit pm1. these channels are up to 2 km wide, and show clear, wedge shaped levee deposits which taper away from the channel axis. the ﬁll of the channel complexes within unit pm2 shows a variable seismic character ( fig. 5 ), with fig. 4. amplitude map of the top messinian horizon (top unit 2 in fig. 3a and b). this image shows the strike slip faulting and thrusting which affects the post-messinian sequence. channels provide useful markers for assessing the sense of offset of the strike slip fault systems which characterise this study area. fig. 5. representative seismic proﬁle through the pm2 interval showing channel levee systems with both high and low amplitude ﬁll characteristics. these channel systems are separated by packages of disturbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels a total area of approximately 67,000 km2 (table 1 and fig. 9a). the depositional area of am1 is located some 40e50 km downslope from the headscarps of the younger am2 (figs. 8 and 9), being mostly characterized by highly chaotic to transparent seismic facies which thicken signiﬁcantly basinwards and bulge up appreciably (maximum thickness of c. 778 m), creating a major positive topo- graphic (fig. 2). we suggest that sediment displacement, includ- ing folding and shear, was most likely caused by frictional resistance along the margin of the flow due to the difference in velocity between the flow and the ambient water and by the development of internal shear and thrust planes (e.g. mulder 2011). side-scan sonar records of muddy debris flows at the sea floor (masson et al. 1993) as well as 3d images displaying buried debris flows and/or mass transport deposits (bull et al. 2009) show that longitudinal shear may be pervasive and related to discrete flows with different velocities and timings (e.g. masson et al. 1993) or morphologically controlled zones of compression (gafeira et al. 2007). one of such zones might comprise the lateral ramp, and associated thrust anticline below, immediately se from site c0018 (fig. 6). what then was the overall control on the location of these internal zones of deformation within the failed succession? the zone of deformation involved layering (fig. 7). in a continental slope setting as exemplified by the nankai trough where the studied interval is characterized by a relatively uniform grain size distribution (fig. 2), the layering is interpreted to mainly involve changes in physical properties. these changes involve sediment porosity variations from fluctuations in sedimentation rates (af- fecting the bulk density), resulting in an acoustically laminated seismic signature (fig. 4). lower rates of sedimentation in general leads to lower porosity and higher undrained shear strength for fine-grained, siliciclastic sediments (see bartetzko and kopf (2007) for a review) and possibly also higher organic carbon content due to higher biological productivity of these periods. here, we suggest that this layering was the overall control on the location of internal zones of deformation, developing layers of higher porosity and lower shear strength (causing the observed scattering, fig. 2) exceeded by the shear stress during failure.

de a) low angle, b5° features around promontories (type i) and b) fault-controlled scarps created by the reactivation of radial faults and faulting of salt withdrawal basins (type ii) (fig. 6a and b). type i ramps are only found at the basal shear surface of mass transport deposit 2 while type ii ramps predominate at the base of the other mass transport deposits. in situations where adjacent ramps were antithetic, they formed promontories and adjacent coves were subsequently ﬁlled by de- bris ﬂow deposits (fig. 7b). both kinds of ramps inﬂuenced the distribu- tion of the mass transport deposits in distinct drag zones (fig. 9). table 1 seismic character and features of the mass transport deposits in the study area. mass transport deposit seismic unit age (mohriak, 2003; fiduk et al., 2004; mohriak, 2005) internal character and geometry associated salt diapirs headwall region basal shear features 1 h0 and h1 eocene continuous, high amplitude upper and basal surfaces. rafted blocks, slightly deformed blocks and debrites. d4 and d5 nw of diapir d5. striations, grooves, ramps. 2 h2 and h3 late eocene very discontinuous upper and lower boundaries; homogeneous chaotic reﬂections (debrites). d1, d2 and d3 headwall region not observed, interpreted as buried east of diapir d3. frontally conﬁned by ramps, promontories east of the mass transport deposit. condensed section in between promontories and basal ramps. 3 h4 and h5 oligocene–miocene large rafted blocks west of d5. hummocky upper surface and ramped basal surface. d1, d4 and d5 nw of diapir d5. ramps west of diapir d5. 4 h6 and h7 miocene continuous, high amplitude basal surface, with a moderate amplitude, hummocky upper surface. mass transport deposit comprises rafted blocks and debrites (chaotic reﬂections) d2 and d3 ne of diapir d2. minor topographic barriers, scarps, grooves and striations striking nw–se. table 2 aspect ratio and geometry of the mass transport deposits in the study area.

ike directly across the depression and do not parallel the curvature of the bathymetric contours. the seismic proﬁles between 560-m and 590-m water depths show that the ridges evolve into rhythmic, undulating forms interpreted as folds, that die out at a water depth of about 650 m (fig. 17). sidescan-sonar images reveal numerous pock- marks on the seaﬂoor throughout the region. the pockmarks on the ‘humboldt slide’ are small depressions with a random and dense distribution. compared with the adjacent continental slope to the north, the ‘humboldt slide’ zone has a higher concentration of pockmarks (yun et al ., 1999), possibly indicating a greater tendency toward gas charging and strength reduction. the erosion and gully zone (fig. 18) extends between the 230-m and 380-m istobaths where huntec seismic proﬁles show truncations of shelf reﬂectors with an estimated 5–15 m of sediment missing. geotechnical tests (lee et al., 1981) from cores collected in the zone show that the sediment is overconsolidated, consistent with the loss of 15 m of sediment by erosion or slope failure. huntec seismic data show local hummocky deposits (< 5 m thick) that unconformably overlie the slope below the gullies (fig. 16). a surface deﬁning the upslope limit of crenulations cuts the slope sequence and crops out at the 380-m isobath (fig. 16). this exposed basal surface separates the sequence of slope-parallel-bedded, seaward-dipping reﬂectors that lie upslope from crenulated, back- tilted reﬂectors of what is interpreted to be the main slide mass. the basal surface is locally buried < 5 m near its upslope limit by disrupted reﬂectors, and dips 3°–4° seaward, parallel to the slope re- ﬂectors. farther downslope, the basal surface dips ~8° and cuts deeply into the slope section (fig. 16). according to gardner et al. (1999), the main body of the landslide is composed of a zone of back-tilted and gently folded blocks (fig. 15).

of the southern bering sea extends from russia on the west to the umnak plateau of the aleutian island arc (fig. 2). the widest known submarine can- yons on earth are found along most of this margin. the exception is at the northwestern edge of the umnak plateau, where the more typical sized, 10-km-wide bering canyon is found (scholl et al., 1970; karl et al., 1996). in contrast to the bering canyon, navarin, pervenets, st. matthew, middle, zhemchug, and pribilof canyons vary from 50 to 150 km in width and 100 to 200 km in length (fig. 2; karl et al., 1996). the extensive gullied nature of these canyon walls and down-slope presence of mass transport deposits can be observed in the gloria side-scan sonar mosaics of the bering continental mar- gin and in seismic profiles (figs. 2, 3; see middle canyon floor; eez scan scientific staff, 1991). the irregular and steep axial gradients of these gullied canyons (9° to 5° downstream) also show evidence of the gullied and scarped morphology along the axes of the gigantic canyons (fig. 4b). in contrast, the less steep and gradual change in axial gradient from 5° to 1° in the bering canyon exhibits the typical regular graded profile of a canyon feeding downstream into the main active channel of a submarine fan, in this case the bering fan (figs. 2—(bf), 4b; carlson and karl, 1988). on the abyssal seafloor downstream from the gigantic gullied canyon mouths, a rough hummocky seafloor without obvious channels is observed in sonographs and seismic profiles (fig. 3; eez scan scientific staff, 1991; carlson et al., 1991). seismic profiles show erosional scarps from sediment failures along the canyon pathway and a hummocky surface from mass transport deposit sheets downstream on the abyssal seafloor (fig. 3; o morphology, seismic profiles and cores show that large gullied canyons feed into a 30-km-long mass transport deposit sheet on the basin floor (table 1; nelson et al., 1991), whereas turbidite channel–levee systems (1 to 4 in fig. 8) are found downstream from the small canyons. seismic profiles show this mass transport deposit sheet as exhibiting irregular thickness of chaotic and transparent facies that have scoured into the underlying deposits (fig. 8c) (nelson et al., 1991). cores from the surface of the mass transport deposit sheet contain chaotic mixtures of unconsolidated clay clasts and chaotic sand deposits (nelson et al., 1991). seismic profiles downstream from the small canyons show surface and subsurface channel–levee systems (nelson and maldonado, 1988). cores from the channel floors contain thick (10–30 cm), graded turbidite sand beds. in contrast, the levees have thin-bedded (1–5 cm) turbidites (alonso and maldonado, 1990). we interpret that the location of the mass transport deposit sheet in the central ebro continental margin is related to the messinian subaerial ebro canyon, which underlies three gullied canyons located in this segment of the margin (figs. 7, 8). the messinian surface of the ebro subaerial canyon is nearly 3000 ms deep below the gullied canyons compared to the noncanyon messinian surface, which is 2000 ms deep below the north and south small canyons (1 to 4 in figs. 8b, 9a; escutia and maldonado, 1992). when the mediterranean sea nearly instantaneously refilled after the messinian salinity crisis, thick (750 m) deepwater pliocene clays were deposited rapidly on top of the subaerial gravels of the messinian ebro canyon (figs. 7, 8a; nelson and maldonado, 1990). as a result, the gullied central segment of the ebro margin, which overlies the thick muds of the messinian ebro canyon, apparently has less stability than the continental slope to the north and south.

hese deposits. mass-transport deposits can comprise sheets, lobes, and channel fills, and can reach 150 m or more in thickness. greater thicknesses are observed where successive flows are amalgamated. this paper documents both internal architectural or stratigraphic as well as external geomorphic attributes of such deposits, as expressed in outcrop and imaged by 3d seismic data. recognition of mass-transport deposits in outcrop is based on identification of bedding deformed by synsedimentary processes, with deformation ranging from minimal redistribution of large slide blocks to complete disaggregation typical of debris-flow deposit s. on seismic data, mass-transport deposits can be recognized by certain geomorphologic as well as stratigraphic distinguishing characteristics: basal linear grooved and scoured surfaces, hummocky relief at the top, and internal chaotic to transparent seismic facies, with internal thrust faulting common. key words: mass-transport deposits, mass transport deposits, debris flow, seismic stratigraphy, seismic geomorphology mass-transport deposits in deepwater settings sepm special publication no. 96, copyright © 2011 sepm (society for sedimentary geology), isbn 978-1-56576-287-9, p. 7–38. introduction mass movements of sediments form kilometer-scale features (fig. 1) that represent major subaerial and subaqueous geohazards and can comprise significant depositional elements, characteriz- ing marine slope and basin-floor systems. catastrophic conse- quences of mass-transport processes such as tsunamis, avalanches, major rock falls, and mudslides are dramatic (e.g., holmes, 1965; bolt et al., 1977; voight, 1978; brunsden and prior, 1984; fisher and smith, 1991; martinsen 1994; bondevik et al., 2003). in addi- tion, mass transport deposit of sediments can significantly affect stabil- ity of offshore installations (e.g., prior and coleman, 1982; solheim et al., 2005).

top_chunks.text: aksu, 1987; masson et al., 2006; talling et al., 2014). hence, the recognition of sub- marine landslides on continental margins is important to: a) the recog- nition of areas prone to slope instability on modern continental slopes, b) the investigation of possible triggers of slope instability, and c) the recognition of global causes of submarine slope instability such as eustasy, tectonics and climatic events (vanneste et al., 2014). other fac- tors that have been proposed to trigger submarine landslides at a local scale include high sedimentation rates (leynaud et al., 2007; li et al., 2014), excess pore pressure (berndt et al., 2012), gas hydrate dissocia- tion (sultan et al., 2004) and earthquakes (sultan et al., 2004; zhao et al., 2015). multiple large-scale submarine landslides occurred in northwest africa during the quaternary (krastel et al. 2012). the most prominent submarine landslides in the region include the sahara slide complex (embley, 1982; gee et al., 1999; georgiopoulou et al., 2010), the mauritania slide complex (antobreh and krastel, 2007; henrich et al. 2008; förster et al. 2010), the cap blanc slide (krastel et al., 2006) and the dakar slide (meyer et al., 2012). the sahara slide complex is marine geology 393 (2017) 109–123 ⁎ corresponding author. e-mail address: li@geophysik.uni-kiel.de (w. li). http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.margeo.2016.11.013 0025-3227/© 2016 elsevier b.v. all rights reserved. contents lists available at sciencedirect marine geology journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/margo one of the largest known submarine slides in the world, and affected an area of 48,000 km2 offshore northwest africa (embley, 1982; fig. 1). during a period of rapid sea-level rise at ~50–60 ka, high primary pro- ductivity in surface waters offshore northwest africa resulted in the ac- cumulation of ﬁne-grained hemipelagites on the continental slope (bertrand et al., 1996; krastel et al., 2006).

top_chunks.text: dity current. in the example of the mississippi fan debris-ﬂow deposits, the presence of clasts demonstrates that the sediment ﬂow still retained competence and was not so energetic as to cause the clasts to disintegrate. triggers submarine landslides are triggered either by an increase in the driving stresses, a decrease in strength, or a combination of the two. the follow- ing possible triggers show the interplay of these factors. note that the relative importance of each of these triggers is not well understood. for ex- ample, in some environments one of these triggers will dominate, whereas in others a different trigger will be most signiﬁcant. sediment accumulation rapid sediment accumulation contributes to failure in several ways. first, as discussed above, when sedi- ment accumulates rapidly, most of the weight of newly added sediment is carried by pore-water pressures. the shear strength probably increases somewhat because some water will always be squeezed out, even if the coefﬁcient of consolida- tion ( cv) is low (i.e. relatively low permeability and/or high compressibility). however, the shear stress acting downslope increases more rapidly. as seen in eq. 1, the shear stress increases with the weight of sediment and is not inﬂuenced by pore pressure. the shear stress also may increase because more sediment may be deposited at the head of the sloping surface than at the toe. all three of the following processes push the slope toward failure: retarded strength development, increased devel- opment of shear stress because of thickness of the sediment body, and increased development of shear stress because of increases in the slope steepness. as discussed above, the mississippi delta is an ideal example of sediment failure induced by sedi- ment accumulation. coleman et al . (1993), prior & coleman (1978) and many other publications document a large variety of sediment failures on the mississippi prodelta (fig. 7).

top_chunks.text: aksu, 1987; masson et al., 2006; talling et al., 2014). hence, the recognition of sub- marine landslides on continental margins is important to: a) the recog- nition of areas prone to slope instability on modern continental slopes, b) the investigation of possible triggers of slope instability, and c) the recognition of global causes of submarine slope instability such as eustasy, tectonics and climatic events (vanneste et al., 2014). other fac- tors that have been proposed to trigger submarine landslides at a local scale include high sedimentation rates (leynaud et al., 2007; li et al., 2014), excess pore pressure (berndt et al., 2012), gas hydrate dissocia- tion (sultan et al., 2004) and earthquakes (sultan et al., 2004; zhao et al., 2015). multiple large-scale submarine landslides occurred in northwest africa during the quaternary (krastel et al. 2012). the most prominent submarine landslides in the region include the sahara slide complex (embley, 1982; gee et al., 1999; georgiopoulou et al., 2010), the mauritania slide complex (antobreh and krastel, 2007; henrich et al. 2008; förster et al. 2010), the cap blanc slide (krastel et al., 2006) and the dakar slide (meyer et al., 2012). the sahara slide complex is marine geology 393 (2017) 109–123 ⁎ corresponding author. e-mail address: li@geophysik.uni-kiel.de (w. li). http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.margeo.2016.11.013 0025-3227/© 2016 elsevier b.v. all rights reserved. contents lists available at sciencedirect marine geology journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/margo one of the largest known submarine slides in the world, and affected an area of 48,000 km2 offshore northwest africa (embley, 1982; fig. 1). during a period of rapid sea-level rise at ~50–60 ka, high primary pro- ductivity in surface waters offshore northwest africa resulted in the ac- cumulation of ﬁne-grained hemipelagites on the continental slope (bertrand et al., 1996; krastel et al., 2006).

top_chunks.text: aksu, 1987; masson et al., 2006; talling et al., 2014). hence, the recognition of sub- marine landslides on continental margins is important to: a) the recog- nition of areas prone to slope instability on modern continental slopes, b) the investigation of possible triggers of slope instability, and c) the recognition of global causes of submarine slope instability such as eustasy, tectonics and climatic events (vanneste et al., 2014). other fac- tors that have been proposed to trigger submarine landslides at a local scale include high sedimentation rates (leynaud et al., 2007; li et al., 2014), excess pore pressure (berndt et al., 2012), gas hydrate dissocia- tion (sultan et al., 2004) and earthquakes (sultan et al., 2004; zhao et al., 2015). multiple large-scale submarine landslides occurred in northwest africa during the quaternary (krastel et al. 2012). the most prominent submarine landslides in the region include the sahara slide complex (embley, 1982; gee et al., 1999; georgiopoulou et al., 2010), the mauritania slide complex (antobreh and krastel, 2007; henrich et al. 2008; förster et al. 2010), the cap blanc slide (krastel et al., 2006) and the dakar slide (meyer et al., 2012). the sahara slide complex is marine geology 393 (2017) 109–123 ⁎ corresponding author. e-mail address: li@geophysik.uni-kiel.de (w. li). http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.margeo.2016.11.013 0025-3227/© 2016 elsevier b.v. all rights reserved. contents lists available at sciencedirect marine geology journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/margo one of the largest known submarine slides in the world, and affected an area of 48,000 km2 offshore northwest africa (embley, 1982; fig. 1). during a period of rapid sea-level rise at ~50–60 ka, high primary pro- ductivity in surface waters offshore northwest africa resulted in the ac- cumulation of ﬁne-grained hemipelagites on the continental slope (bertrand et al., 1996; krastel et al., 2006).

the zone of deformation involved layering (fig. 7). in a continental slope setting as exemplified by the nankai trough where the studied interval is characterized by a relatively uniform grain size distribution (fig. 2), the layering is interpreted to mainly involve changes in physical properties. these changes involve sediment porosity variations from fluctuations in sedimentation rates (af- fecting the bulk density), resulting in an acoustically laminated seismic signature (fig. 4). lower rates of sedimentation in general leads to lower porosity and higher undrained shear strength for fine-grained, siliciclastic sediments (see bartetzko and kopf (2007) for a review) and possibly also higher organic carbon content due to higher biological productivity of these periods. here, we suggest that this layering was the overall control on the location of internal zones of deformation, developing layers of higher porosity and lower shear strength (causing the observed scattering, fig. 2) exceeded by the shear stress during failure.

mienert, 2004; smith et al., 2004). considering the above scenarios, it is essential to assess the impact of existing and future mass flows along the ecm, when siting platforms, drilling rigs, pipelines, and other field-develop- ment infrastructure. the area surrounding the lubina mass transport deposit requires a particular focused scrutiny. it is critical to avoid locations showing evidence of potential future collapse (e.g., retrogressive failure). such locations have been recognized mostly along the main headscarp and northern flank of the failed com- plex. if avoiding these locations is not possible, an alternative could be laying distribution facilities parallel to flow directions, whenever possible (e.g., robert bruce, personal communication). fig. 14.—conceptual model for slope failure and vertical fluid migration on the ecm. a) a failure plane is generated when elevated pore pressures develop along a specific shallow lithological boundary (i.e., overconsolidated or nonpermeable) and underlying sediment strength is reduced to the point where localized fracturing occurs. subsequently, opening-mode fractures propagate laterally at depth to the seafloor, following a shear-fracture mechanism. b) this creates a failure plane (basal shear surface) above which the overlying sedimentary section translates downslope, marking the initiation of slope failure (see text for further description). failure initiation fluid overpressures generated at this level retrogressive failure a b basal shear surface fluid migration pockmark mass-transport deposit lithological boundary 1000 m 100 m paleo-pockmark lithological boundary pockmark failure initiation fluid migration pockmark pockmark paleo-pockmark headscarp 1000 m jose frey

ral levees formed during lobe construction and channeled material down- slope between levee margins (fig. 6d). levees limited lateral spreading of the deposit and enhanced growth in the dip direction. the ﬁnal volumetric distribution was 40% contained in the lobe deposit, 59% in the source area, and 1% in a turbidity current ( fig. 7 ). we discuss the evolution of the retrogressive failure of experi- ment 3 in more detail ( fig. 10). within 5 s of ﬂow initiation, a prom- inent headscarp formed ~ 25 cm upslope of the gate ( fig. 10b). a zone of horst-graben structures and detached blocks developed between this headscarp and the gate. as each block detached from the main headscarp, it was progressively broken up into smaller blocks as it mi- grated through the system and accumulated at the back of the lobe deposit. with time, headwall retreat was balanced by downslope movement and growth of the lobe deposit. lateral levees formed 20 s after gate release ( fig. 10 c). after 2.6 min, the entire source area was an active zone of retrogressive failure ( fig. 10 d). the lobe continued to migrate downdip as it was pushed along by successive evacuated blocks accumulating at the rear. as the lobe was being pushed from behind, radial tension structures developed along the front ( fig. 10 d). the ﬁnal topography of the source area of experi- ment 3 re ﬂects the retrogressive failure process ( fig. 8a, c). fracture spacing is 2 –3 cm and fracture depth is 1 –2 cm. the lobe deposit of experiment 3 has a hummocky surface texture (figs. 6d, 9a, c and table 3). radial tension fractures occur along the perimeter of the lobe. the blocky surface topography is the result of the block-by-block construction process ( fig. 9 a–c). the l:w ratio for experiment 4 is 1:9, which indicates the longest dimension is the along- ﬂow direction and is nearly twice the width. this re ﬂects the role of the lateral levees that acted to funnel material down-dip and limited lateral growth.

canyons that trend in a west–east direction (figs. 3, 5). this association with a mass- failed deposit suggests an intrinsic control for these canyon areas to act as major fairways for mass failure, and is discussed in more detail later. architectural elements: description and interpretation headscarps.— a variance map (fig. 6) of the seafloor illustrates the planform geometry of the lubina mass transport deposit with exceptional detail. in figure 6, the various mass-wasting deposits constituting the failure com- plex in plan view exhibit lobe-like geometries of the headscarp. the headscarp appears as an abrupt offset of seafloor topography with two main salients (fig. 6,) suggesting that the lubina mass transport deposit consists of three mass-wasting deposits at least. each salient is separated by a distinct reentrant in the headscarp h1 to h3 in figure 6. these headscarps are confirmed in cross sections as erosional features, with ca. 20 to 30 m reduction of stratigraphic section (figs. 7, 8). 185 submarine slope failure and fluid migration processes on the ebro continental margin immediately downslope of the headscarp, there is a region of extensional thinning. this region is where the lubina mass transport deposit is cut by minor faults, with a distinct seafloor scarp of up to 30 m height. the geometry of these subsidiary faults bears a close relationship to the headscarp immediately updip. it is interpreted that these faults represent failure surfaces that propagated updip in a typical retrogressive sequence, as widely recognized in mass- wasting deposits (e.g., gee et al., 2005; lastras et al., 2004). upslope of the headscarp, the seafloor appears undeformed, suggesting that these updip areas have not been significantly affected by instability. toe region.— the toe regions of the various mass failures constituting the lubina mass transport deposit are difficult to distinguish, since they are to a great extent overlapping and are only partially covered by sei

direction. the peak in aspect ratio ( fig. 12 c) (experiment 3) is caused by lateral levees that funneled material in the downdip direction while simultaneously restricting lateral growth ( fig. 6d). at higher values of ff, the material yield strength is weak enough that the deposit can expand in the strike direction nearly as much as it can in the downdip direction (and no levees are formed), which results in aspect ratio only slightly above 1. deposit thickness increases slightly between experiments 2 and 3 but decreases for higher ff. this makes intuitive sense because yield strength decreases as ff increases. finally, mud ﬂow duration is short at low and high ff values and peaks at medium ff values. the peak value (experiment 3) re ﬂects the retrogressive failure that lasted nearly 12 min. this suggests the longest duration ﬂows correspond to retrogressive failure. if the initial ﬂow factor is too high, or too low, retrogressive failure cannot occur. the wide contrast in release mechanisms ( fig. 6), evacuation rate, (fig. 7 ) and style of deposition are important because knowledge of the initial slide acceleration and volume are critical components for modeling of the magnitude of slide-generated tsunami and impact force on seabed infrastructure ( bondevik et al., 2005; løvholt et al., 2005; zakeri et al., 2008 ). we observed two fundamentally different release mechanisms: the high ff experiment resulted in a high- velocity, high-volume ﬂow and deposited en masse , most of which occurred in the ﬁrst 10 s ( fig. 7). in contrast, the medium ff mudﬂow was a slow-velocity, low-volume retrogressive ﬂow that constructed the ﬁnal deposit as piece-by-piece accumulation of ~100 small detached blocks over a period of 11.8 min ( fig. 7 ). it is common to assume the total volume of a slide deposit was deposited by a single body, however it is clear that this assumption is not correct for retro- gressive events.

activity, tectonic background, sediments supply, and sea-level ﬂuctuations. recently there are some e-mail: swu@qdio.ac.cn wu s g et al.: analysis on seismic characteristics and triggering mechanisms of mass transport · · · 1057 new ﬁndings that the development of mass transport deposits is closely related to gas hydrate dissolution[8]. deepwater mass transport deposits are one of sediment diﬀusion patterns and play an important role in the research of global “source to sink”[9]. consequently, a deep study of characteristics, distribution and triggering mechanism will have both signiﬁcant theoretic values and wide potential applications. according to interpretations of seismic sections, mass transport deposits are common in neogene-quaternary strata, and in some places these sediments occupy main part of quaternary sequences[10,11]. carrying out this study is valuable to the process, transport mechanism and sequence style of deep-water mass transport deposits. based on analyses of new seismic proﬁles and multi-beam bathymetric data, this paper analyzes mass transport deposits in detail and discusses triggering mechanism of mass transport deposits of the northern south china sea. 2 regional geological setting three large deepwater basins, the qiongdongnan basin, pearl river mouth basin and taixinan basin, are distributed from west to east along the northern
