(in press ), this high-density layer does not have the commonly described erosive capability as often suggested (e.g. mulder and cochonat 1996; baas et al. 2009). fig. 1 a overview map showing storegga landslide and the bear island fan complex. b overview map showing the grand banks landslide (modified from piper and aksu ( 1987)) 1028 ocean dynamics (2010) 60:1027 –1046 2 case studies 2.1 the bear island fan complex extensive landslide activity characterises the huge depo- centres beyond the outlet of large ice streams terminating at the bear island fan (fig. 1a). a significant part of the sediments consists of well-defined debris lobes. the lobes in the uppermost part of these sediments were most likely deposited during the last glacial maximum. they are typically about 30 m thick and 10 km wide, and comprised of clay-rich material (laberg and v orren 2000;m a r re ta l . 2002).

( 1998), hydroplaning can start at froude numbers as low as 0.4. the densimetric froude numbers for the more clayey experimental slurries vary from 1.5 to 1.65. these values have been calculated assuming a density for the debris flow equal to the initial density of the debris flow slurry. for clay contents sufficiently high for the debris flows to remain coherent, such high froude number values cause the debris flow to hydroplane. as mentioned above, partial hydroplaning of the debris flow slurry was observed with low clay contents as well. 6.2 longitudinal deformation and velocity field development as seen from the high-speed camera measurements and piv analyses (figs. 7, 8 and 9), the internal velocities are very dependent on the composition of the flow and also vary within the body. the differential velocities result in internal deformation of the flowing materials. the velocity is in general higher in the head than in the body. this difference is especially large in the high clay flows (fig. 11). the higher velocity of the debris flow head compared to the body (which experiences higher bed friction) results in stretching and elongation of the flow. through comparison of the velocities in two adjacent cameras (50 cm apart), we get a measure of the amount of stretching throughout the body of the flow. at each camera position, the velocity field ( u(x, y, t), v(x, y, t)) is resolved as the debris flow slurry passes.

(fig. 2). we suggest that sediment displacement, includ- ing folding and shear, was most likely caused by frictional resistance along the margin of the flow due to the difference in velocity between the flow and the ambient water and by the development of internal shear and thrust planes (e.g. mulder 2011). side-scan sonar records of muddy debris flows at the sea floor (masson et al. 1993) as well as 3d images displaying buried debris flows and/or mass transport deposits (bull et al. 2009) show that longitudinal shear may be pervasive and related to discrete flows with different velocities and timings (e.g. masson et al. 1993) or morphologically controlled zones of compression (gafeira et al. 2007). one of such zones might comprise the lateral ramp, and associated thrust anticline below, immediately se from site c0018 (fig. 6). what then was the overall control on the location of these internal zones of deformation within the failed succession? the zone of deformation involved layering (fig. 7). in a continental slope setting as exemplified by the nankai trough where the studied interval is characterized by a relatively uniform grain size distribution (fig. 2), the layering is interpreted to mainly involve changes in physical properties. these changes involve sediment porosity variations from fluctuations in sedimentation rates (af- fecting the bulk density), resulting in an acoustically laminated seismic signature (fig. 4). lower rates of sedimentation in general leads to lower porosity and higher undrained shear strength for fine-grained, siliciclastic sediments (see bartetzko and kopf (2007) for a review) and possibly also higher organic carbon content due to higher biological productivity of these periods. here, we suggest that this layering was the overall control on the location of internal zones of deformation, developing layers of higher porosity and lower shear strength (causing the observed scattering, fig. 2) exceeded by the shear stress during failure.

episodes of deposition are correlated with the most rapid falls or rises of sea level. apparently, related gas-hydrate decomposi- tion, increases in deposition rates, change in location of depo- centers, and slope overloading result in episodes of massive sediment failures. global climate changes also caused temperate subpolar ice sheets on antarctica during the late oligocene to middle miocene that resulted in massive deposition of mass transport deposits on this margin, whereas later polar ice sheets favored the develop- ment of turbidite systems. mass transport deposits can have local controlling factors such as tectonic setting (e.g., bering margin), sediment supply (e.g., mississippi margin), or desiccation (e.g., ebro mar- gin) that influence their development in specific continental- margin locations. on passive margins, such as off the mississippi and amazon rivers, when their high rates and amount of sedi- ment deposition combine with growth faults and salt tectonics, mass transport deposit deposits become completely intermixed with turbidite deposits at all scales from basin-wide mass transport deposit sheets to individual beds a few centimeters thick. by sorbonne universite user c. hans nelson, carlota escutia, john e. damuth, and david c. twichell, jr. 62 acknowledgments we thank the many scientific staffs plus ship officers and crews who helped us during numerous oceanographic cruises that gathered the data for this paper. we also appreciate the following funding agencies that supported the cruises and scien- tific research with many grants: u.s. geological survey, national science foundation, consejo superior investigaciones de ciencias, ministerio de ciencias y educación, and the petroleum-industry- supported gulf intraslope basins consortium. discussions with oscar romero improved our chronology of climatic warming and glacial melt phases during the late pleistocene.

(iii) the along-strike relationships between the margin-scale tectonic regime, the ﬂuvial input and the architecture of the makran turbidite system at both the system and architectural element scales. regional setting geodynamic setting the makran accretionary prism results from the northward subduction of the arabian sea beneath the iranian and afghan continental blocks, now accreted to the eurasian continent (fig. 1). sub- duction started during late cretaceous times and continued fairly continuously until present times (kukowski et al., 2001; ellouz-zimmermann et al., 2007a; grando & mcclay, 2007). the western part of the arabian sea lithosphere belongs to the arabian plate, whereas the eastern part belongs to the indian plate; their present-day plate boundary runs along the dextral transform owen fracture zone (gordon & demets, 1989; fournier et al., 2001). the plate boundary shows a nearly east– west bend along the murray ridge before inter- secting the subduction boundary west of karachi city (ellouz-zimmermann et al., 2007b; fig. 1). the actual plate convergence rate has been esti- mated at 4 cm year )1 using classical plate mod- elling (demets et al., 1994), whereas recent space geodesy modelling and a gps-based model esti- mated the present-day velocities between 2æ5 cm year )1 in the western makran area and 3 cm year )1 in the eastern makran area (ellouz- zimmermann et al., 2007b; grando & mcclay, 2007). the makran subduction zone is considered as an area of important earthquake activity, and is a part of the two main tsunamigenic zones in the indian ocean (heidarzadeh et al., 2009). the a b fig. 1. (a) location map and physiography of the study area. compilation of multibeam bathymetry in the gulf of oman from the marabie (shom) and chamak (ifp) cruises, combined with the existing hydrosweep data (flueh et al., 1997). white dots indicate the location of sedimentary cores used in this study. (b) tectonic setting (sim- pliﬁed) of the gulf of oman. 378 j.

2011; strasser et al., 2011, 2012). seismic stratigraphic units in the nankai trough are shown in figure 5a and correlated with bore- hole data from iodp hole c0018a (expedition 333 scientists, 2011). in the itz, the largest mass transport deposit 6 has a maximum thickness of 182 m (597 ft) and an area approaching 20 km 2 (7.7 mi 2) (strasser et al., 2011). the mass transport deposit 6 divides the slope sedi- ments into two distinct subunits; unit ib, com- prising a sandy turbidite sequence, and unit ia with ash-bearing hemipelagites and multiple mass transport deposits (figures 4a, 5a). the larger mass transport deposit 6 has been drilled and cored at site c0018a, where it reaches a thick- ness of 61.5 m (201.7 ft), and was emplaced be- tween 0.85 and 1.05 ma (expedition 333 scien- tists, 2011; strasser et al., 2012). above this, mass transport deposit 5 comprises a younger instability episode and is part of unit ia (expedition 316 scientists, 2009a, b) (figures 4a, 5a). geological setting offshore southeast brazil the espírito santo basin is the northernmost of a series of upper jurassic –cretaceous rift basins developed in southeast brazil (chang et al., 1992) (figure 1c). following synrift extension, the early postrift geology of the basin was dominated by the accumulation of large volumes of aptian evap- orites, an event followed by the incision of sub- marine channel systems and the triggering of signif- icant mass-wasting events in the cenozoic (moreira and carminatti, 2004). from the late cretaceous onward, at least eight episodes of channel incision are recorded on the continental slope of espírito figure 5. (a) correlation panel between seismic data and key physi cal properties of mass transport deposits 5 and 6 at iodp site c0018a, nankai trough. note the contrasting seismic character of low-amplitud e strata in mass transport deposit 6 when compared with turbidite units in unit ib.

episodes of deposition are correlated with the most rapid falls or rises of sea level. apparently, related gas-hydrate decomposi- tion, increases in deposition rates, change in location of depo- centers, and slope overloading result in episodes of massive sediment failures. global climate changes also caused temperate subpolar ice sheets on antarctica during the late oligocene to middle miocene that resulted in massive deposition of mass transport deposits on this margin, whereas later polar ice sheets favored the develop- ment of turbidite systems. mass transport deposits can have local controlling factors such as tectonic setting (e.g., bering margin), sediment supply (e.g., mississippi margin), or desiccation (e.g., ebro mar- gin) that influence their development in specific continental- margin locations. on passive margins, such as off the mississippi and amazon rivers, when their high rates and amount of sedi- ment deposition combine with growth faults and salt tectonics, mass transport deposit deposits become completely intermixed with turbidite deposits at all scales from basin-wide mass transport deposit sheets to individual beds a few centimeters thick. by sorbonne universite user c. hans nelson, carlota escutia, john e. damuth, and david c. twichell, jr. 62 acknowledgments we thank the many scientific staffs plus ship officers and crews who helped us during numerous oceanographic cruises that gathered the data for this paper. we also appreciate the following funding agencies that supported the cruises and scien- tific research with many grants: u.s. geological survey, national science foundation, consejo superior investigaciones de ciencias, ministerio de ciencias y educación, and the petroleum-industry- supported gulf intraslope basins consortium. discussions with oscar romero improved our chronology of climatic warming and glacial melt phases during the late pleistocene.

ccumulation rate on the margin and that permeability barriers and lithological changes within the stratal architecture maintain each failure event some- what “conﬁned” within a discrete clinotheme. 6. conclusions the mtcs of the pb foredeep, investigated through a 3d geomor- phological approach coupled with a 2d seismic facies analysis and rollover trajectory analysis, have revealed that: • mtes can occur at any sea level position; the sea level does not ap- pear to act as a triggering mechanism in this framework. • the morphology of the mtc reﬂects the stratigraphy of the failed sec- tion and their source sedimentary environment (i.e., subaqueous delta, contouritic deposit, advection-dominated open slope depocenter). • the sediment failures are always conﬁned within a discrete clinotheme. the depth of rooting of each mass transport deposit is a further important controlling factor in the resultant deposit morphology, even within the same mass transport complex. in the pb foredeep, the main predisposing factor for the mtes ini- tiation is represented by a major increase in accumulation rate along the margin, which can occur irrespective of sea level variations. acknowledgments the authors would like to thank eni — exploration and production division, san donato milanese (italy) for sponsorship of this work and for the permission to publish these outcomes. we thank jasper knight (editor), michael strasser and an anonymous reviewer for their reviews that greatly improved the quality of the paper. references armitage, d.a., romans, b.w., covault, j.a., graham, s.a., 2009. the inﬂuence of mass transport deposit surface topography on the evolution of turbidite architecture: the sierra contreras, tres pasos formation (cretaceous), southern chile. journal of sedimentary research 79, 287–301. bull, s., cartwright, j., huuse, m., 2008. a review of kinematic indicators from mass transport complexes using 3d seismic data. marine and petroleum geology 26, 1–20.

picker- ing et al., 1989; clayton, 1994; droz et al., 1996; leeder, 1999), and kneller & buckee (2000) argue for the continuation of this wide usage. in the classiﬁcation scheme presented here, a turbidity current is deﬁned as a current in which ﬂuid turbulence is the main particle transport mechanism, although other mechanisms may also operate to varying degrees (see the variation in particle-support mechanism represented sche- matically in fig. 4). there is a continuum bet- ween concentrated density ﬂows and turbidity ﬂows; b) analyse the different types of mass movements that occurred in the investigated area; c) discuss the timing of slope failures; d) assess any geological hazards that may relate to the failure of upper headwall strata. this study contributes to a wider discussion about the stability of continental margins during the present-day relative sea-level highstand (e.g., owen et al., 2007; lee; 2009; smith et al., 2013). we show that it is crucial to investigate both landslide deposits, and their failure areas, in order to reconstruct the evolution of sub- marine slide complexes. 2. geological setting the northwest african continental margin is one of the best-studied passive margins in the world. earthquakes of magnitude m ≥ 7 have rarely been recorded south of the gulf of cadiz (seibold, 1982), but moderate earthquakes (4 ≤ m ≤ 6) are commonly observed in associa- tion with the reactivation of old weakness zones created during the opening of the atlantic ocean (hayes and rabinowitz, 1975; pereira and alves, 2011). the width of the continental shelf of northwest africa is generally 40–60 km, reaching a maximum width of n100 km offshore western sahara (fig. 1). the shelf break occurs at a water depth between 100 m and 200 m (fig. 1; wynn et al., 2000). the con- tinental slope dips 1° to 6° from a depth of 200 to 1500 m, while the continental rise is b1° beyond a depth of 4000 m. the northwest african continental margin has been affected by complex sediment transport processes since its inception (wynn et al., 2000; krastel et al., 2012). most of the continental margin of northwest africa is now arid and records limited sediment supply by rivers, even during past gla- cial times (weaver et al., 2000; wynn et al., 2000

[ 52] as shown earlier, most of the ﬂux of landslide material toward the deeper basin is controlled by the largest landslides that occur on passive margins, thus stressing the role of these preconditioning factors. this fact does not preclude that a majority of the landslides could ﬁnally be triggered by earth- quakes, as reported in section 3.5 (figure 12), but in passive margins, the ﬁnal trigger is marginal in controlling onset of slope failure. as said earlier, relatively small earthquakes could actually trigger large-magnitude slope failures if the right set of conditions (most likely related to sedimentation patterns and margin hydrogeology) exist in those margins. [ 53] recent work also suggests that, in opposition to the principles operating in turbidite paleoseismology, the earth- quake cycle and recurrence of major mass-wasting phenomena could be disconnected [ strasser et al ., 2012; völker et al ., 2011], implying that steady accumulation of sediments and buildup of speciﬁc slope conditions is a necessary prerequisite for large submarine landslides to occur. based on data from the middle america and central chile trench and forearc sys- tems, behrmann et al. [2014] even suggested that it takes 20 to 200 plate boundary earthquakes to set off a medium-sized (>10 km 2) or larger mass transport deposit. figure 4c shows that the largest mediterranean submarine slope failures occur in passive margins, where earthquakes of large magnitude are not present and recurrence of intraplate earthquakes is longer than in tectonically active margins. this distribution of slope failures means that, in passive margins, there must be pro- cesses at play, other than earthquakes, that precondition the slope for failure and that large slope failures can be triggered with much smaller ground motions (if any at all). the size of these failures also implies relatively homogeneous groundwa- ter conditions over large areas and highlights the si

ring the holocene, a time of rapid ice sheet decay, continental uplift and increased seismic activity, one of the most important triggering mechanisms for large failures during deglaciation processes. preconditioning factors such as weak layers related to contourite drifts and rapid loading by glacial sediments may enhance strain localization and creep processes on the slope. /c2112008 elsevier ltd. all rights reserved. 1. introduction the aim of this study is to present and discuss the large variety of mass transport deposit processes on glaciated and non-glaciated continental margins of the ne-atlantic ocean and mediterranean seas in rela- tion to seismic hazards, sediment properties, and sea level changes. the assessment of today’s submarine continental slope stability requires an understanding of what has caused submarine slope failures in the past. knowledge of preconditions of sediments to fail and their triggering mechanisms has improved signiﬁcantly following extensive studies conducted throughout the world. particularly the multidisciplinary investigations and interactions between academia and industry in studying the giant storegga slide complex of the mid-norwegian margin have revealed new insights into the occurrence and dynamics of mass transport deposit in relation to sedimentation and oceanographic processes, glacial history and seismicity, which together form a key study for slope failure on (formerly) glaciated margins (e.g. mienert, 2004; bryn et al., 2005a; solheim et al., 2005a, b ). potential preconditions to failure exist in the form of weak sediment layers, and they have been used to explain the architecture of the storegga slide ( bryn et al., 2003 ). however, the absence of other large (regional) scale slope failures in similar geological settings is difﬁcult to under- stand, and we need to shed more light on such complex, interacting processes.

and other features that disrupt the lateral continuity of seismic reflections. dip maps compute best-fit planes between im- mediate neighbour traces on a time or depth slice and calculate magnitude (gradient) of dip (brown, 2011). dip values are measured in degrees in re- lation to a horizontal plane. geological and geophysical background geological setting of southeast japan the nankai trough results from the subduction of the philippine sea plate beneath the eurasian plate along southeast japan (figure 1b). the study area is located in the imbricate thrust zone (itz) of the nankai trough, a highly deformed area of the con- tinental slope of southeast japan (moore et al., 2009) (figures 1b, 2a). here, the continental slope is dominated by a megasplay fault (msf) separating the itz from an inner forearc basin to the north- west of the study area (kumano basin, park et al., 2002; tobin and kinoshita, 2006) (figures 1b, 3a, 4a). seaward from the msf, a submarine channel system and recurrent mass transport deposits (mass transport deposits 1 to 6; expe- dition 333 scientists, 2011) were generated in what was interpreted as a broad zone of deformation (alves, 2013) (figures 3a, 4a). the present-day tectonic and depositional set- tings of the itz were initiated at approximately 2.2 ma in a frontal wedge-toe position (strasser et al., 2011). splay-fault movement was initiated at about 1.95 ma in the lower part of the wedge. ongoing megasplay slip occurs since about 1.55 ma (strasser et al., 2009). as a result of the complex interaction between fault-propagation folding, sea- floor instability, and faulting, the age of mass transport deposits sea- ward from the msf range from 2.87 ma to holocene (<100 yr b.p.) (kimura et al., 2011; strasser et al., 2011, 2012). seismic stratigraphic units in the nankai trough are shown in figure 5a and correlated with bore- hole data from iodp hole c0018a (expedition 333 scientists, 2011).

(4) can we use the seismic geomorphology of ancient mtcs to un- derstand the processes active at their time of deposition? (5) does each force trigger the same process for the given critical conditions of sediment stability? methodology and dat a sets the primary data set for this study of the deep-water ar- chitecture and nature of the o¡shoret rinidad continental margin are three- dimensional (3d) seismic re£ection data. gravity induced deposits mass transport complexturbidity current turbidite debris flow slump slide descriptive classificationgenetic classification shear failure along discrete shear planes with little or no internal deformation or rotation shear failure accompanied by rotation along discrete shear surfaces with various degrees of internal deformation shear distributed throughout the sediment mass. strength is principally from cohesion due to clay content. additional matrix support may come from buoyancy. plastic rheology and laminar state. transport mechanism supported by fluid turbulence (newtonian rheology) sedimentary structures essentially undeformed, continuous bedding plastic deformation particularly at the toe or base. plow structures, folds, tension faults, joints, slickensides, grooves, rotational blocks matrix supported, random fabric, clast size variable, matrix variable. rip ups, rafts, inverse grading and flow structures possible. normal size grading, sharp basal contacts, gradational upper contacts. seismically recognizable features (moscardelli et al., 2006; this work) continuous blocks without apparent internal deformation. high-amplitude, continuous reflections. compressional ridges, imbricate slides, irregular upper bedding contacts, duplex structures, contorted layers.

(2002) showed that submarine plunge pools at the base of the new jersey and california continental slope occur where the decrease in slope exceeds 4 ° . these authors proposed two scenarios for the formation of plunge pools. firstly, they could be related to the formation of hydraulic jumps at the break of slope, i.e. a change in the hydraulic regime from supercritical (i.e. for a froude num- ber, fr >1) to subcritical conditions ( fr <1). increase in turbulence in the vicinity of a jump could account for enhanced erosion and scouring (komar, 1973; garcia & parker, 1989; garcia, 1993; waltham, 2004), while enhanced sediment deposition (related to ﬂow deceleration and loss of capacity) occurs downstream. for given mag- nitudes of ﬂow depth, density and frictional forces, there is a critical change in slope at which hydraulic jumps can occur (theoretically ranging from ca 0æ05° to 1 æ2° ; komar, 1971). on present- day bathymetry, slope gradients are generally 7 ° to 12 ° in the proximal part of the knickpoint walls; they decrease towards ca 2t o3 ° near the base of slope and, ﬁnally, abruptly fall under 0 æ8° to 0 æ5° immediately downstream of the knick- point walls, where plunge pools form.

top_chunks.text: submarine landslides of the mediterranean sea: trigger mechanisms, dynamics, and frequency-magnitude distribution roger urgeles1 and angelo camerlenghi 2 received 10 january 2013; revised 17 november 2013; accepted 26 november 2013; published 26 december 2013. [1] submarine landslides are ubiquitous along mediterranean continental margins. with the aim of understanding mass-wasting processes and related hazard at the scale of a large marine basin encompassing multiple geological settings, we have compiled data on their geometry, age, and trigger mechanism with a geographic information system. the distribution of submarine landslides in the mediterranean reveals that major deltaic wedges have a higher density of large submarine landslides, while tectonically active margins are characterized by relatively small failures. in all areas, landslide size distributions display power law scaling for landslides > 1k m 3.w e ﬁnd consistent differences on the exponent of the power law (θ) depending on the tectonic setting. available age information suggests that failures exceeding 1000 km 3 are infrequent and may recur every ~40 kyr. smaller failures that can still cause signi ﬁcant damage might be relatively frequent (failures > 1k m3 may recur every 40 years). the database highlights that our knowledge of mass transport deposit activity with time is limited to a few tens of thousands of years. available data suggest that submarine landslides may preferentially occur during lowstand periods, but no ﬁrm conclusion can be made on this respect, as only 70 landslides (out of 696 in the database) have relatively accurate age determinations. the temporal pattern and changes in frequency-magnitude distribution suggest that sedimentation patterns and pore pressure development have had a major role in triggering slope failures and control the sediment ﬂux from mass transport deposit to the deep basin. citation: urgeles, r., and a.

(2004) are important, but they do not disprove a sedi- ment wave origin for the features. rather, they may imply that turbidity-current sediment waves can occur in a variety of environments, including shallow water, and that the resulting morphologies may be somewhat different. the adriatic crenula- tions do not show clear shear planes or a headwall scarp that would conﬁrm a landslide origin. they do, however, show some evidence of deformation at the base of their section and also possible ﬂuid- escape deformations within the crenulated sediment body.

eir significance in hydrocarbon exploration and devel- opment. mass transport deposits include a wide spectrum of gravity-induced deposits, including slides, slumps, and debrites, but generally excluding turbidites such as leveed-channel complexes and sheet deposits (moscardelli et al., 2006). terminology can be confusing (shanmugam et al., 1995). mass transport deposits and turbidites can occur inter- bedded in the same depositional regimes, and mass transport deposits can severely impact turbidite reservoir continuity and productivity (moscardelli et al., 2006). this paper illustrates seafloor examples of mass transport deposits and their interrelationships with turbidite leveed-channel complexes us- ing a 3d seismic survey in offshore deepwater nigeria. deposits illustrated are at or directly below the seafloor. high-frequency, near-surface 3d seismic data give depositional detail not possible in deeper data, and can serve as analogs for seismic interpretation at reservoir depths. sediment thicknesses and depths presented in isopach maps and seismic time sections are obtained from a depth-migrated seismic data set not presented in the paper. the seismic survey is approximately 100 km offshore and is approximately 35 km by 50 km in size (figs. 1, 2). sediments included in the survey occur in deep water at the toe of slope of the niger delta depocenter. they consist of upper quaternary slope, canyon, and basin deposits which are strongly controlled by underlying regional structural trends associated with the deposition of the niger delta (fig. 1). overall morphology of the present-day niger delta and re- lated deepwater sediments consists of shelf, slope, and basin- plain configuration, defined by seafloor bathymetric trends. well- defined seafloor structural trends suggest present-day structural activity, especially in the outer thrust trends (fig. 1) (mitchum and wach, 2002).

3d seismic interpretation of mass transport deposits: implications for basin analysis and geohazard evaluation j. frey-martínez abstract mass-transport deposits (mass transport deposits) are widely recognized from many continental margins and are an important component of slope systems. although mass transport deposits have been studied since the early 1920s, much of the research has been conducted on ancient features partially preserved at outcrop. the incompleteness of outcrop examples has been a persistent obstacle to a fuller, process based analy- sis of their causes, mechanisms, and results. in the last few decades, increasing use has been made of geophysical techniques such as 2d reflection seismology, sonar, and multibeam bathymetry to study modern mass transport deposits. many valuable insights have accrued from this approach, but it is, in essence, a two-dimensional analyti- cal framework, and suffers from many of the same limitations as the field-based approach. recent advent of 3d seismic technology offers a novel method for inves- tigations of both modern and subsurface mass transport deposits that promises to add significantly to the understanding of slope failure processes. modern, high-resolution 3d seismic surveys are now acquired on many continental margins for hydrocarbon exploration purposes, and often in areas that are or have been affected by slope failure. this means that the remarkable spatial resolving power of the 3d seismic method can be used to define the full areal extent and morphology of mass transport deposits with a precision that cannot be achieved with any other combination of methods. this paper illus- trates the potential for 3d seismic interpretation of mass transport deposits by describing a suite of complex examples from different continental margins worldwide. the application of seismic-based analyses for seafloor and near-surface geohazard evaluation asso- ciated with submarine slope failure is also discussed.

3d seismic interpretation of mass transport deposits: implications for basin analysis and geohazard evaluation j. frey-martínez abstract mass-transport deposits (mass transport deposits) are widely recognized from many continental margins and are an important component of slope systems. although mass transport deposits have been studied since the early 1920s, much of the research has been conducted on ancient features partially preserved at outcrop. the incompleteness of outcrop examples has been a persistent obstacle to a fuller, process based analy- sis of their causes, mechanisms, and results. in the last few decades, increasing use has been made of geophysical techniques such as 2d reflection seismology, sonar, and multibeam bathymetry to study modern mass transport deposits. many valuable insights have accrued from this approach, but it is, in essence, a two-dimensional analyti- cal framework, and suffers from many of the same limitations as the field-based approach. recent advent of 3d seismic technology offers a novel method for inves- tigations of both modern and subsurface mass transport deposits that promises to add significantly to the understanding of slope failure processes. modern, high-resolution 3d seismic surveys are now acquired on many continental margins for hydrocarbon exploration purposes, and often in areas that are or have been affected by slope failure. this means that the remarkable spatial resolving power of the 3d seismic method can be used to define the full areal extent and morphology of mass transport deposits with a precision that cannot be achieved with any other combination of methods. this paper illus- trates the potential for 3d seismic interpretation of mass transport deposits by describing a suite of complex examples from different continental margins worldwide. the application of seismic-based analyses for seafloor and near-surface geohazard evaluation asso- ciated with submarine slope failure is also discussed.

o morphology, seismic profiles and cores show that large gullied canyons feed into a 30-km-long mass transport deposit sheet on the basin floor (table 1; nelson et al., 1991), whereas turbidite channel–levee systems (1 to 4 in fig. 8) are found downstream from the small canyons. seismic profiles show this mass transport deposit sheet as exhibiting irregular thickness of chaotic and transparent facies that have scoured into the underlying deposits (fig. 8c) (nelson et al., 1991). cores from the surface of the mass transport deposit sheet contain chaotic mixtures of unconsolidated clay clasts and chaotic sand deposits (nelson et al., 1991). seismic profiles downstream from the small canyons show surface and subsurface channel–levee systems (nelson and maldonado, 1988). cores from the channel floors contain thick (10–30 cm), graded turbidite sand beds. in contrast, the levees have thin-bedded (1–5 cm) turbidites (alonso and maldonado, 1990). we interpret that the location of the mass transport deposit sheet in the central ebro continental margin is related to the messinian subaerial ebro canyon, which underlies three gullied canyons located in this segment of the margin (figs. 7, 8). the messinian surface of the ebro subaerial canyon is nearly 3000 ms deep below the gullied canyons compared to the noncanyon messinian surface, which is 2000 ms deep below the north and south small canyons (1 to 4 in figs. 8b, 9a; escutia and maldonado, 1992). when the mediterranean sea nearly instantaneously refilled after the messinian salinity crisis, thick (750 m) deepwater pliocene clays were deposited rapidly on top of the subaerial gravels of the messinian ebro canyon (figs. 7, 8a; nelson and maldonado, 1990). as a result, the gullied central segment of the ebro margin, which overlies the thick muds of the messinian ebro canyon, apparently has less stability than the continental slope to the north and south.

sis of a 3d seismic data set and a comparison with some recent results from outcrop studies, the aim of this paper is to elucidate the flow behaviour associated with the distal part of mass transport deposit 6 (hole c0018a; 127.55 to 188.57 m below seafloor (mbsf)). the scientific problems addressed in this paper include (a) what are the styles of mass transport deposit sediment deformation during its downslope flow? (b) does sediment deformation involve entrainment or simpler gravitational gliding under a ductile basal shear zone? and, (c) what is the role of the underlying substrate in controlling flow behaviour in mass transport deposit 6? site description iodp site c0018 is located in a quaternary slope basin on the footwall of the megasplay fault of the nankai trough subduction zone, se japan (fig. 1). the megasplay fault is interpreted to be a major ‘out-of-sequence’ thrust that may slip during large subduc- tion earthquakes (park et al. 2002; moore et al. 2007; strasser et al. 2009). the sediment of hole c0018a can be divided into two lithologic subunits (fig. 2). subunit 1a (0–190.65 mbsf) mainly comprises silty clay, interpreted to be hemipelagic mud with interbedded ash layers and is affected by mass transport deposits. subunit 1b (190.65–313.65 mbsf) comprises hemipelagic mud interbedded with a number of sandy turbidites (expedition 333 scientists 2011; strasser et al. 2014a) (fig. 2). six mass transport deposits were identified within lithological subunit 1a (fig. 2). the thickness of the mass transport deposits at the drill site varies from 50 to 61 m. deformation styles were highly variable and include zones of moderate to no deformation. the upper boundary was identified as a transition from undisturbed and subhorizontal, bioturbated sediments above and disturbed sediments below. the lower boundary is in most cases represented by an erosional boundary (expedition 333 scientists 2011).

7mtd character and genesis from outcrop and seismic data the character and genesis of submarine mass-transport deposits: insights from outcrop and 3d seismic data henry w. posamentier chevron energy technology company, 1500 louisiana street, houston, texas 77002, u.s.a. e-mail: henry.posamentier@chevron.com and ole j. martinsen statoilhydro research, p.o. box 7200, n-5020 bergen, norway e-mail: ojma@statoilhydro.com abstract: extensive deep-water mass-transport deposits are observed in both slope and basin-floor settings. a detailed understanding of mass-transport deposits, in terms of emplacement processes, depositional products, and their stratigraphic and geographic distribution, is vital because they can constitute a significant portion of the stratigraphic section in deep-water settings. in addition, ma ss-transport deposits can play a significant role in hydrocarbon exploration, inasmuch as they can constitute seal, reservoir, and possibly source facies under the right circumstances. different data types bring to light different aspects of mass-transport deposits. this paper focuses on insights derived from seismic and outcrop data. overall geometries and architecture of mass-transport deposits are readily observable in 3d seismic data; however, features below seismic resolution that are vital for process and lithologic understanding need to be observed in outcrop. integrating observations across a broad range of scales by linking seismic and outcrop observations constitutes an effective way of improving our understanding of when and where mass-transport deposits are likely to form. in addition, this linkage sheds light on details of internal architecture that commonly characterizes these deposits. mass-transport deposits can comprise sheets, lobes, and channel fills, and can reach 150 m or more in thickness. greater thicknesses are observed where successive flows are amalgamated.

7mtd character and genesis from outcrop and seismic data the character and genesis of submarine mass-transport deposits: insights from outcrop and 3d seismic data henry w. posamentier chevron energy technology company, 1500 louisiana street, houston, texas 77002, u.s.a. e-mail: henry.posamentier@chevron.com and ole j. martinsen statoilhydro research, p.o. box 7200, n-5020 bergen, norway e-mail: ojma@statoilhydro.com abstract: extensive deep-water mass-transport deposits are observed in both slope and basin-floor settings. a detailed understanding of mass-transport deposits, in terms of emplacement processes, depositional products, and their stratigraphic and geographic distribution, is vital because they can constitute a significant portion of the stratigraphic section in deep-water settings. in addition, ma ss-transport deposits can play a significant role in hydrocarbon exploration, inasmuch as they can constitute seal, reservoir, and possibly source facies under the right circumstances. different data types bring to light different aspects of mass-transport deposits. this paper focuses on insights derived from seismic and outcrop data. overall geometries and architecture of mass-transport deposits are readily observable in 3d seismic data; however, features below seismic resolution that are vital for process and lithologic understanding need to be observed in outcrop. integrating observations across a broad range of scales by linking seismic and outcrop observations constitutes an effective way of improving our understanding of when and where mass-transport deposits are likely to form. in addition, this linkage sheds light on details of internal architecture that commonly characterizes these deposits. mass-transport deposits can comprise sheets, lobes, and channel fills, and can reach 150 m or more in thickness. greater thicknesses are observed where successive flows are amalgamated.

upper unit (150 to 200 m) of parallel discontinuous reflectors still preserves the original layers; however, irregularities of the seafloor suggest a con- tinuous activity of the mass transport processes and associated deformation (fig. 3). both the headwall scarp and the displaced blocks are the source area for consid- erably more deformed mass transport deposits occurring downslope. these deposits are internally chaotic, suggesting debris flow, but locally present large displaced blocks that still maintain their internal layering (fig. 3). these deposits extend to water depths of 3,800 m. the megaslide is laterally and frontally confined, favoring the development of a series of reverse faults rooted on detachment levels that progressively become shallower, thus decreasing the thickness of the mobilized deposits from 1,000 m to about 300 m basinward. eventually they reach the seafloor forming pressure ridges (up to 50 m of relief) (fig. 4). fig. 3 headwall scarp, displaced and rotated blocks, debris flow deposits and preserved block (bl) over detachment surface (dotted line) in the upslope portion of the pará-maranhão megaslide fig. 4 pará-maranhão megaslide lateral confinement with reverse faults and pressure ridge megaslides in the foz do amazonas basin 587 2.2 the amapá megaslide complex to the nw of the amazon fan, the shelf-break is located under 200 m water deep, and the upper continental slope shows the highest local gradients in the foz do amazonas basin (circa 5.5°). a continuous erosive scarp, as high as 1,800 m, extends laterally along the upper continental slope for at least 120 km (fig. 2). beyond 2,000 m water depths, the seafloor is again smooth, with low gradients around 0.93°, in response to the deposition in the distal portions of the amazon fan. the megaslide deposits mapped in this region correspond to a complex of several mass transport deposits encompassing the upper sedimentary section between 1,800 to 2,700 m thick.

ﬁnd the transparent am1 megaslide seaward from the fold-and-thrust belt system (figs. 11 and 9a). internal huge blocks of comparable very high amplitude reﬂections (up to 15e20 km wide) are preserved as pre-failed stratigraphic layering within the transparent am1 allochthonous mass (figs. 8, 10a and 11). on the other hand, the upper part of the amc is composed of a stack of ﬁve closely-layered megaslides (am2-am6; figs. 8 and 9b). headwall scarps related to am2-am6 are clearly identiﬁed. the northwestern slope area is dominated by a steep nw-se-oriented faulted-erosive scarp (scarp a on fig. 8), which extends laterally for about 160 km, between c. 450-1200 m water depth (mean vertical relief of 750 m). on the lower slope lies a large rotated block (some 30 km wide) affected by numerous normal faults. am2-am6 headscarps are found just downslope from the rotated block as buried stepped scarps, resulting in paleorelief as high as ~150e300 m cutting into undisturbed layers. we can thus recog- nize a sharp transition between upslope undisturbed plan-parallel siliciclastic units and the chaotic and/or transparent seismic facies depicting these megaslides downslope (fig. 8). we can also observe that: (1) am2 stands as one of the largest siliciclastic units of the amc. it exhibits a tabular-like geometry (table 1 and fig. 9b). its internal seismic character is dominated by transparent facies, with the presence of local parallel-layered facies interpreted as preserved internal blocks, while its distal depositional units are extremely chaotic. these seismic and architectural characteristics point to a high degree of sedi- ment disruption, supporting the interpretation of am2 as predominantly liqueﬁed mass ﬂows (figs. 8 and 9b); (2) am3 and am4 slide along basal d�ecollement surfaces that shift upward or downward in the stratigraphy, depicting staircase morphologies (fig. 8). am3, the smallest megaslide in area (table 1 and fig.

postma and drinia 1993). the makrilia formation drapes the blocks and interfingers laterally with the kalamavka formation (alves and lourenço 2010). examples of non-entrenching landslide deposits are observed within silicilastic deposits, away from rafted blocks, including bed- parallel mass transport deposits transported over a sandy, mobile, detachment layer. the mass transport deposit in fig. 5a denotes a complex geometry, with internal folds in muddy strata interrupted by the injection of sandy mate- rial from the basal surface. the basal surface is, by itself, a bed- parallel feature formed of immature and poorly sorted sands and very fine pebbles. the mass transport deposit in fig. 5b comprises a series of deformed strata confined by a bed-parallel, sandy glide plane. in both non-entrained mass transport deposits, the basal glide plane becomes a low- angle truncation surface laterally in the succession, denoting very moderate erosion of seafloor strata during their deposition. other styles of failure have also been identified. figure 5c shows an example of a collapsed slide block, approximately 8.5 m tall, denoting a limited amount of entrenchment in slope strata. in this example, the block shows highly fractured breccia conglomerates at its base, hinting at the remobilization (and rolling) of the larger blocks over the slope siliciclastic substrate with

acked allochthonous masses within the upper miocene-quaternary sedimentary record, they are best described as mass transport complexes (mtcs), and here- after renamed as: the amap�a megaslide complex (amc) and the par�a-maranh~ao megaslide complex (pmmc). 4.3.1. the amap�a megaslide complex the amap�a megaslide complex (amc) corresponds to a series of stacked megaslides, named amap�a after the adjacent coastal amap�a state in northern brazil (silva et al., 2010). the amc is composed of six major individual megaslides encompassing different stratigraphic levels, interlayered with undisturbed depo- sitional intervals which display either continuous or strong re- ﬂectors (fig. 8). several other smaller mdts could also be identiﬁed, but because they could not be correlated across the study area (because they were too thin or because of the lack of regional extent) they are not described in this paper. an acronym was assigned to each mappable megaslide, according to its position in the stratigraphic section (from the most ancient to the most recent; figs. 8 and 9 and table 1): am1 (amap�a megaslide 1); am2 (amap�a megaslide 2); am3 (amap�a megaslide 2); am4 (amap�a megaslide 4); am5 (amap�a megaslide 5) and am6 (amap�a megaslide 6). am1 to am6 are marked by seismically well-deﬁned basal d�ecollement surfaces (fig. 8), whereas their disturbed masses show seismic evidence of distinct degrees of displacements and disrup- tions, as indicated by a set of variable acoustic seismic facies types, such as: internal transparent to chaotic facies; or a combination of chaotic facies with local interbedded facies (fig.10). the megaslides lie either directly on the top of each other, as am4, am5 and am6 do, or may be separated from each other by continuous units of strong plan-parallel reﬂectors: as thick as 300 ms as in the case of that between am2 and am3; or as thick as 700 ms, as in the case of that between am1 and am2.

acked allochthonous masses within the upper miocene-quaternary sedimentary record, they are best described as mass transport complexes (mtcs), and here- after renamed as: the amap�a megaslide complex (amc) and the par�a-maranh~ao megaslide complex (pmmc). 4.3.1. the amap�a megaslide complex the amap�a megaslide complex (amc) corresponds to a series of stacked megaslides, named amap�a after the adjacent coastal amap�a state in northern brazil (silva et al., 2010). the amc is composed of six major individual megaslides encompassing different stratigraphic levels, interlayered with undisturbed depo- sitional intervals which display either continuous or strong re- ﬂectors (fig. 8). several other smaller mdts could also be identiﬁed, but because they could not be correlated across the study area (because they were too thin or because of the lack of regional extent) they are not described in this paper. an acronym was assigned to each mappable megaslide, according to its position in the stratigraphic section (from the most ancient to the most recent; figs. 8 and 9 and table 1): am1 (amap�a megaslide 1); am2 (amap�a megaslide 2); am3 (amap�a megaslide 2); am4 (amap�a megaslide 4); am5 (amap�a megaslide 5) and am6 (amap�a megaslide 6). am1 to am6 are marked by seismically well-deﬁned basal d�ecollement surfaces (fig. 8), whereas their disturbed masses show seismic evidence of distinct degrees of displacements and disrup- tions, as indicated by a set of variable acoustic seismic facies types, such as: internal transparent to chaotic facies; or a combination of chaotic facies with local interbedded facies (fig.10). the megaslides lie either directly on the top of each other, as am4, am5 and am6 do, or may be separated from each other by continuous units of strong plan-parallel reﬂectors: as thick as 300 ms as in the case of that between am2 and am3; or as thick as 700 ms, as in the case of that between am1 and am2.

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

rvey area is poor. channels up to 500 m wide, are commonly observed within this unit. these channels pre-date deformation and now provide useful kinematic markers for post-messinian faulting (fig. 4). thickness changes associated with these channels result in localised downlap and apparent onlap surfaces within unit pm1. these local thickness variations are related to deposition from the channels, and are not the result of syn-sedimentary structural growth. aside from the localised thickness variations associated with channel deposition, unit pm1 does not show any syn-kine- matic sedimentation and this unit is assumed to pre-date salt related deformation in this area. 3.1.2. post-messinian unit 2 (pm2) unit pm2 consists of low to medium amplitude, mainly continuous reﬂections, with localised packages of lower amplitude, chaotic reﬂections which pass laterally into more continuous units (fig. 5). unit pm2 contains several channel levee systems, which are larger and much more apparent on seismic sections that those described from within unit pm1. these channels are up to 2 km wide, and show clear, wedge shaped levee deposits which taper away from the channel axis. the ﬁll of the channel complexes within unit pm2 shows a variable seismic character ( fig. 5 ), with fig. 4. amplitude map of the top messinian horizon (top unit 2 in fig. 3a and b). this image shows the strike slip faulting and thrusting which affects the post-messinian sequence. channels provide

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

rvey area is poor. channels up to 500 m wide, are commonly observed within this unit. these channels pre-date deformation and now provide useful kinematic markers for post-messinian faulting (fig. 4). thickness changes associated with these channels result in localised downlap and apparent onlap surfaces within unit pm1. these local thickness variations are related to deposition from the channels, and are not the result of syn-sedimentary structural growth. aside from the localised thickness variations associated with channel deposition, unit pm1 does not show any syn-kine- matic sedimentation and this unit is assumed to pre-date salt related deformation in this area. 3.1.2. post-messinian unit 2 (pm2) unit pm2 consists of low to medium amplitude, mainly continuous reﬂections, with localised packages of lower amplitude, chaotic reﬂections which pass laterally into more continuous units (fig. 5). unit pm2 contains several channel levee systems, which are larger and much more apparent on seismic sections that those described from within unit pm1. these channels are up to 2 km wide, and show clear, wedge shaped levee deposits which taper away from the channel axis. the ﬁll of the channel complexes within unit pm2 shows a variable seismic character ( fig. 5 ), with fig. 4. amplitude map of the top messinian horizon (top unit 2 in fig. 3a and b). this image shows the strike slip faulting and thrusting which affects the post-messinian sequence. channels provide

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

rvey area is poor. channels up to 500 m wide, are commonly observed within this unit. these channels pre-date deformation and now provide useful kinematic markers for post-messinian faulting (fig. 4). thickness changes associated with these channels result in localised downlap and apparent onlap surfaces within unit pm1. these local thickness variations are related to deposition from the channels, and are not the result of syn-sedimentary structural growth. aside from the localised thickness variations associated with channel deposition, unit pm1 does not show any syn-kine- matic sedimentation and this unit is assumed to pre-date salt related deformation in this area. 3.1.2. post-messinian unit 2 (pm2) unit pm2 consists of low to medium amplitude, mainly continuous reﬂections, with localised packages of lower amplitude, chaotic reﬂections which pass laterally into more continuous units (fig. 5). unit pm2 contains several channel levee systems, which are larger and much more apparent on seismic sections that those described from within unit pm1. these channels are up to 2 km wide, and show clear, wedge shaped levee deposits which taper away from the channel axis. the ﬁll of the channel complexes within unit pm2 shows a variable seismic character ( fig. 5 ), with fig. 4. amplitude map of the top messinian horizon (top unit 2 in fig. 3a and b). this image shows the strike slip faulting and thrusting which affects the post-messinian sequence. channels provide

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

top_chunks.text: urbed or parallel low amplitude reﬂections of uniform thickness. i.r. clark, j.a. cartwright / marine and petroleum geology 26 (2009) 1465–1482 1469 some channels having a high amplitude ﬁll of discontinuous reﬂections and others having a low amplitude, transparent ﬁll. high amplitude channel ﬁlls are often associated with development of mounds above the channel axis that may be due to differential compaction of the sand-rich channel ﬁll and the adjacent mud rich levee deposits (c.f. posamentier, 2003 ). the channel levee complexes are separated vertically by intervals of parallel reﬂec- tions of constant thickness ( fig. 5). these intervals likely represent periods of channel abandonment in this area. unit pm2 displays internal thickness variations related to channel levee complexes where thinning of the channel levees occurs away from the channel axis. this thinning is associated with local downlap of the levee reﬂections onto the pre-channel surface as well as downlap within the levee packages themselves (fig. 5 ). where subsequent folding has occurred, tilting of the channel levees in the vicinity of the fold limbs can appear similar to onlap onto the fold crest, and failure to recognise this can result in a misleading interpretation of structural timing. true syn-kine- matic intervals within unit pm2 are associated with expansion into the hangingwall and footwall synclines of thrust-related folds, and weakly developed onlap onto the fold limbs. these syn-kinematic intervals are not synchronous across the study area, but the largest, most continuous fold structures appear to have been the earliest to have been initiated. within unit pm2, growth packages are sepa- rated by intervals of parallel reﬂections of constant thickness, indicating that even after the onset of deformation, the growth of the thrust folds was episodic throughout the deposition of unit pm2. 3.1.3.

ar zone separating mass transport deposits 1 and 2. the yellow line marks the location of a longitudinal seismic profile (fig. 24) down the length of mass transport deposit 1. map is about 18 km wide. more deeply buried mass transport deposits underlying the mass transport deposits on the seafloor are illustrated by volume-rendered images. they show well-developed headward fault-scarp detachment surfaces. a distinct shear boundary flanks the eastern side of one flow, with an abrupt vertical edge. slide blocks sheared off the bounding wall are incorporated into the mass transport deposit. the development of succes- sive zones of mass transport deposits and slumped leveed-channel complexes considerably deeper than the illustrated units suggests a long- term sediment instability at the mouth of the canyon. both leveed-channel complexes and neighboring slope sediments are subject to slumping and incorporation into mass transport deposits in this unstable depositional environment. possible controls on the development of mass transport deposits are discussed below. discussion many authors have described the processes by which mass transport deposits are formed (summarized by moscardelli et al., 2006). several of these processes could have been acting together to produce mass transport deposits in the study area. most probable causes include: (1) contin- ued structural tilting of the seafloor towards the south, because of activity along toe thrusts of the niger delta (mitchum and wach, 2002); (2) high sedimentation rates producing instability in an apron focused at the canyon mouth; and (3) cyclical formation of mass transport deposits as part of the cyclical deposition associated with relative falls and rises of sea level. structural tilting of the sediments in the study area could produce major oversteepening of depositional slopes, leading to mass failure and downslope movement of sediments.

(2000) suggested that the older blanco slide in southern cascadia basin had an original run-out distance of 70 km, whereas the present observed run-out distance is 22 km (table 1). they assumed that this slide has an age of 1.2 million years and thus with a correction for plate convergence rates of 4 cm/yr over this time, the original toe of the landslide has been carried to its present position of 22 km by plate convergence. as previously described, the original ages ascribed to the cascadia basin mass transport deposit sheets may need significant correction. thus, the older blanco mass transport deposit sheet may not have extended as far as the 70 km run-out distance that goldfinger et al., (2000) projected. other evidence supports our observations that along the active tectonic continental margin of western north america, there are limited run-out distances of mass transport deposit sheets on the adjacent abyssal plains, compared to passive margins. in our studies, we observe that the active margin has mass transport deposit run-out distances on the abyssal plain of 5–80 km. in a plot of selected mass transport deposit sheets from a worldwide database, the active margins have maximum run-out lengths of 80 km, whereas the passive margins have maximum run-out lengths of ~ 1000 km across abyssal ocean floors (elverhøi et al., 2005).

deposits. messinian desiccation of the mediterranean sea caused a deeply eroded ebro subaerial canyon and an unstable central segment with an mass transport deposit sheet, whereas other stable ebro margin segments have only turbidite systems. in the northern gulf of mexico, the delta-fed mississippi fan and intraslope mini-basins contain mass transport deposits and turbidites that are equally intermixed from the largest scales with mass transport deposit sheets hundreds of kilometers long to the smallest scales with beds centimeters thick. in the antarctic wilkes land margin, global climate cooling caused a late oligocene to middle miocene time of temperate continental ice sheets that resulted in massive deposition of mass transport deposits on the margin, whereas later polar ice sheets favored development of turbidite systems. our case studies provide the following new insights: (1) mass transport deposits can dominate entire margins, dominate segments of a margin, be equally mixed with turbidites, or dominate a margin during some geologic times and not others; (2) on active tectonic margins with great earthquakes, the maximum run-out distances of mass transport deposit sheets across abyssal-basin floors are an order of magnitude less (~ 100 km) than on passive-margin settings (~ 1000 km), and the volumes of mass transport deposits are limited on the abyssal sea floor along active margins; (3) where the most precise radiocarbon ages are available, major mass transport deposit episodes of deposition are correlated with the most rapid falls or rises of sea level; (4) gullied canyons feeding mass transport deposit sheets have irregular and steep axial gradients (5–9°), whereas canyons feeding turbidite systems have a regular graded profile and less steep gradients (1 to 5°). our examples of mass transport deposit and turbidite systems provide analogues to help interpret ancient systems.

(2000) suggested that the older blanco slide in southern cascadia basin had an original run-out distance of 70 km, whereas the present observed run-out distance is 22 km (table 1). they assumed that this slide has an age of 1.2 million years and thus with a correction for plate convergence rates of 4 cm/yr over this time, the original toe of the landslide has been carried to its present position of 22 km by plate convergence. as previously described, the original ages ascribed to the cascadia basin mass transport deposit sheets may need significant correction. thus, the older blanco mass transport deposit sheet may not have extended as far as the 70 km run-out distance that goldfinger et al., (2000) projected. other evidence supports our observations that along the active tectonic continental margin of western north america, there are limited run-out distances of mass transport deposit sheets on the adjacent abyssal plains, compared to passive margins. in our studies, we observe that the active margin has mass transport deposit run-out distances on the abyssal plain of 5–80 km. in a plot of selected mass transport deposit sheets from a worldwide database, the active margins have maximum run-out lengths of 80 km, whereas the passive margins have maximum run-out lengths of ~ 1000 km across abyssal ocean floors (elverhøi et al., 2005).

deposits. messinian desiccation of the mediterranean sea caused a deeply eroded ebro subaerial canyon and an unstable central segment with an mass transport deposit sheet, whereas other stable ebro margin segments have only turbidite systems. in the northern gulf of mexico, the delta-fed mississippi fan and intraslope mini-basins contain mass transport deposits and turbidites that are equally intermixed from the largest scales with mass transport deposit sheets hundreds of kilometers long to the smallest scales with beds centimeters thick. in the antarctic wilkes land margin, global climate cooling caused a late oligocene to middle miocene time of temperate continental ice sheets that resulted in massive deposition of mass transport deposits on the margin, whereas later polar ice sheets favored development of turbidite systems. our case studies provide the following new insights: (1) mass transport deposits can dominate entire margins, dominate segments of a margin, be equally mixed with turbidites, or dominate a margin during some geologic times and not others; (2) on active tectonic margins with great earthquakes, the maximum run-out distances of mass transport deposit sheets across abyssal-basin floors are an order of magnitude less (~ 100 km) than on passive-margin settings (~ 1000 km), and the volumes of mass transport deposits are limited on the abyssal sea floor along active margins; (3) where the most precise radiocarbon ages are available, major mass transport deposit episodes of deposition are correlated with the most rapid falls or rises of sea level; (4) gullied canyons feeding mass transport deposit sheets have irregular and steep axial gradients (5–9°), whereas canyons feeding turbidite systems have a regular graded profile and less steep gradients (1 to 5°). our examples of mass transport deposit and turbidite systems provide analogues to help interpret ancient systems.

karl et al., 1996). in contrast to the bering canyon, navarin, pervenets, st. matthew, middle, zhemchug, and pribilof canyons vary from 50 to 150 km in width and 100 to 200 km in length (fig. 2; karl et al., 1996). the extensive gullied nature of these canyon walls and down-slope presence of mass transport deposits can be observed in the gloria side-scan sonar mosaics of the bering continental mar- gin and in seismic profiles (figs. 2, 3; carlson and karl, 1988). on the abyssal seafloor downstream from the gigantic gullied canyon mouths, a rough hummocky seafloor without obvious channels is observed in sonographs and seismic profiles (fig. 3; eez scan scientific staff, 1991; carlson et al., 1991). seismic profiles show erosional scarps from sediment failures along the canyon pathway and a hummocky surface from mass transport deposit sheets downstream on the abyssal seafloor (fig. 3;
