pressure ridges were also formed in the chaotic seismic facies interpreted as debrites. longitudinal linear features inter- preted as lateral flow lines were observed in some mass transport deposits. in addition, rotated blocks deforming sediment waves on levees of leveed-channel complexes were classified as mass transport deposits, because they are areally mappable and form a sequence-stratigraphic facies pattern on levee surfaces. study areas three key areas of the 3d seismic survey are described in greater detail to illustrate the various types of mass-transport deposits described in the study. area 1 is part of leveed-channel complex 1 (figs. 4–6). here, individual rotated blocks are formed by deformation of pre-existing sediment waves on the levee of a large leveed-channel complex. area 2 is east of the leveed- channel complexes, where two small, nearly complete mass transport deposits with headward escarpments, chaotic reflection patterns, inter- preted lateral flow lines, mounding, and compressive pressure ridges are interpreted as debrites (fig. 5). area 3 is in a central area, west of area 2 (fig. 5). here, portions of two relatively large surficial mass transport deposits contain large glide blocks on the seafloor in a fig. 4.—coherency map of the seafloor, overlaid by a diagram of leveed-channel complexes (channel fills are yellow and levees are brown), on and below the sea floor. channel fills and levees are numbered 1–5 from oldest to youngest. channel fills 1–3 are below the seafloor, and channel fills 4–5 are on the seafloor. wavy arcuate lines on the levee associated with channel fill 1 represent sediment waves which have been deformed by localized rotated blocks (study area 1). cross section (red line) shows location of figure 6. map is 35 km by 50 km in size. 89 seafloor mass-transport deposits, deepwater nigeria fig. 5.—coherency map of seafloor overlaid with diagram showing main areas of mass-transport deposits (in brown).

acked allochthonous masses within the upper miocene-quaternary sedimentary record, they are best described as mass transport complexes (mtcs), and here- after renamed as: the amap�a megaslide complex (amc) and the par�a-maranh~ao megaslide complex (pmmc). 4.3.1. the amap�a megaslide complex the amap�a megaslide complex (amc) corresponds to a series of stacked megaslides, named amap�a after the adjacent coastal amap�a state in northern brazil (silva et al., 2010). the amc is composed of six major individual megaslides encompassing different stratigraphic levels, interlayered with undisturbed depo- sitional intervals which display either continuous or strong re- ﬂectors (fig. 8). several other smaller mdts could also be identiﬁed, but because they could not be correlated across the study area (because they were too thin or because of the lack of regional extent) they are not described in this paper. an acronym was assigned to each mappable megaslide, according to its position in the stratigraphic section (from the most ancient to the most recent; figs. 8 and 9 and table 1): am1 (amap�a megaslide 1); am2 (amap�a megaslide 2); am3 (amap�a megaslide 2); am4 (amap�a megaslide 4); am5 (amap�a megaslide 5) and am6 (amap�a megaslide 6). am1 to am6 are marked by seismically well-deﬁned basal d�ecollement surfaces (fig. 8), whereas their disturbed masses show seismic evidence of distinct degrees of displacements and disrup- tions, as indicated by a set of variable acoustic seismic facies types, such as: internal transparent to chaotic facies; or a combination of chaotic facies with local interbedded facies (fig.10). the megaslides lie either directly on the top of each other, as am4, am5 and am6 do, or may be separated from each other by continuous units of strong plan-parallel reﬂectors: as thick as 300 ms as in the case of that between am2 and am3; or as thick as 700 ms, as in the case of that between am1 and am2.

xamples covering broad-scale examples of mass-transport deposits show that structural style, and thus classification, can vary greatly within the same units (e.g., prior et al., 1984; posamentier and kolla, 2003; posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; posamentier et al., 2000; posamentier and kolla, 2003; posamentier and walker, 2006). in the following sections, the most common processes that form mass-transport deposits are described to illustrate the main modes of gravitational sediment transport on subaqueous slopes. creep creep on subaqueous slopes is poorly studied and rarely identified compared to other mass-transport

by systematically slicing through the seismic data, selected deepwater stratigraphic elements are highlighted in order of depth (or time). the volume is best seen using a data set, flattened on the seafloor in order to stay as parallel as possible to stratigraphic elements. a seismic chair display illustrates a verti- cal section of four flattened volume-rendered layers a, b, c, and d from flattened depth layers reveal many aspects of the development of the mass transport deposits (fig. 26). these layers occur at depths below the seafloor from 125 m to 25 m, respec- tively, showing successively younger slices (oldest to youngest in fig. 26a–f). two portions of mass transport deposits (left and right in each image of fig. 26) are distinctly separated by the top of the underlying leveed-channel complex (visible in fig. 26 and described in fig. 22). the abrupt eastern boundary of the eastern mass transport deposit is distinct in slabs d through b (fig. 26), as is the northern detachment scar at the inception of the mass transport deposit. the seismic facies of the eastern mass transport deposit in proximal areas to the north is marked by fracturing and breakup of large rafted glide blocks of bedded material which appear to have moved only slightly, especially in older layers a and b. this pattern passes to the south into smaller blocks. well-developed transverse com- pressive pressure ridges also occur, especially at the distal end of the mass transport deposit. the eastern edge of the mass transport deposit is abrupt, as blocks of bedded material are sheared toe regions of the various mass failures constituting the lubina mass transport deposit are difficult to distinguish, since they are to a great extent overlapping and are only partially covered by seismic data. overall, the gross toe region for the entire mass-wasting deposit is recognized on the seafloor variance map as an area of noticeable seafloor roughness (fig. 6), which in cross section appears as short-wavelength and low-relief rugosity of the sea floor (fig. 7b). the precise geometry of this topographic irregu- larity cannot be described in detail, because of the limits of vertical and lateral seismic resolution. however, some of this rugosity has a ridge-like morphology, evident on the seafloor variance, and are interpreted as compressional ridges. lateral flanks.— the lateral flanks of the lubina mass transport deposit vary considerably, as seen on strike-oriented seismic profiles along the mass-failed deposit (figs. 3, 9). along the northern margin, flanks are seen as abrupt and steep (ca. 20°) limits between the highly chaotic seismic character within the mass-failed body and the unde- formed strata outside of the feature. in contrast, along the south- ern margin and toe regions, lateral flanks correspond to extensive areas where the failure complex thins progressively and is con- cordant with the underlying strata (fig. 9). this configuration suggests that sediment removal (i.e., undermining) of the main instability event triggered secondary minor slope failures along the northern flank of the lubina mass transport deposit. in contrast, it is also interpreted that the southeastern parts of the mass-failure com- plex were subsequently eroded at least partially by the reactiva- tion of a submarine channel. basal shear surface.— the basal shear surface of the lubina mass transport deposit can be traced continuously with a high degree of confidence over the entire 3d seismic volume.

deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; toe regions of the various mass failures constituting the lubina mass transport deposit are difficult to distinguish, since they are to a great extent overlapping and are only partially covered by seismic data. overall, the gross toe region for the entire mass-wasting deposit is recognized on the seafloor variance map as an area of noticeable seafloor roughness (fig. 6), which in cross section appears as short-wavelength and low-relief rugosity of the sea floor (fig. 7b). the precise geometry of this topographic irregu- larity cannot be described in detail, because of the limits of vertical and lateral seismic resolution. however, some of this rugosity has a ridge-like morphology, evident on the seafloor variance, and are interpreted as compressional ridges. lateral flanks.— the lateral flanks of the lubina mass transport deposit vary considerably, as seen on strike-oriented seismic profiles along the mass-failed deposit (figs. 3, 9). along the northern margin, flanks are seen as abrupt and steep (ca. 20°) limits between the highly chaotic seismic character within the mass-failed body and the unde- formed strata outside of the feature. in contrast, along the south- ern margin and toe regions, lateral flanks correspond to extensive areas where the failure complex thins progressively and is con- cordant with the underlying strata (fig. 9). this configuration suggests that sediment removal (i.e., undermining) of the main instability event triggered secondary minor slope failures along the northern flank of the lubina mass transport deposit. in contrast, it is also interpreted that the southeastern parts of the mass-failure com- plex were subsequently eroded at least partially by the reactiva- tion of a submarine channel. basal shear surface.— the basal shear surface of the lubina mass transport deposit can be traced continuously with a high degree of confidence over the entire 3d seismic volume.

toe regions of the various mass failures constituting the lubina mass transport deposit are difficult to distinguish, since they are to a great extent overlapping and are only partially covered by seismic data. overall, the gross toe region for the entire mass-wasting deposit is recognized on the seafloor variance map as an area of noticeable seafloor roughness (fig. 6), which in cross section appears as short-wavelength and low-relief rugosity of the sea floor (fig. 7b). the precise geometry of this topographic irregu- larity cannot be described in detail, because of the limits of vertical and lateral seismic resolution. however, some of this rugosity has a ridge-like morphology, evident on the seafloor variance, and are interpreted as compressional ridges. lateral flanks.— the lateral flanks of the lubina mass transport deposit vary considerably, as seen on strike-oriented seismic profiles along the mass-failed deposit (figs. 3, 9). along the northern margin, flanks are seen as abrupt and steep (ca. 20°) limits between the highly chaotic seismic character within the mass-failed body and the unde- formed strata outside of the feature. in contrast, along the south- ern margin and toe regions, lateral flanks correspond to extensive areas where the failure complex thins progressively and is con- cordant with the underlying strata (fig. 9). this configuration suggests that sediment removal (i.e., undermining) of the main instability event triggered secondary minor slope failures along the northern flank of the lubina mass transport deposit. in contrast, it is also interpreted that the southeastern parts of the mass-failure com- plex were subsequently eroded at least partially by the reactiva- tion of a submarine channel. basal shear surface.— the basal shear surface of the lubina mass transport deposit can be traced continuously with a high degree of confidence over the entire 3d seismic volume.

posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; toe regions of the various mass failures constituting the lubina mass transport deposit are difficult to distinguish, since they are to a great extent overlapping and are only partially covered by seismic data. overall, the gross toe region for the entire mass-wasting deposit is recognized on the seafloor variance map as an area of noticeable seafloor roughness (fig. 6), which in cross section appears as short-wavelength and low-relief rugosity of the sea floor (fig. 7b). the precise geometry of this topographic irregu- larity cannot be described in detail, because of the limits of vertical and lateral seismic resolution. however, some of this rugosity has a ridge-like morphology, evident on the seafloor variance, and are interpreted as compressional ridges. lateral flanks.— the lateral flanks of the lubina mass transport deposit vary considerably, as seen on strike-oriented seismic profiles along the mass-failed deposit (figs. 3, 9). along the northern margin, flanks are seen as abrupt and steep (ca. 20°) limits between the highly chaotic seismic character within the mass-failed body and the unde- formed strata outside of the feature. in contrast, along the south- ern margin and toe regions, lateral flanks correspond to extensive areas where the failure complex thins progressively and is con- cordant with the underlying strata (fig. 9). this configuration suggests that sediment removal (i.e., undermining) of the main instability event triggered secondary minor slope failures along the northern flank of the lubina mass transport deposit. in contrast, it is also interpreted that the southeastern parts of the mass-failure com- plex were subsequently eroded at least partially by the reactiva- tion of a submarine channel. basal shear surface.— the basal shear surface of the lubina mass transport deposit can be traced continuously with a high degree of confidence over the entire 3d seismic volume.

deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; posamentier et al., 2000; posamentier and kolla, 2003; posamentier and walker, 2006). in the following sections, the most common processes that form mass-transport deposits are described to illustrate the main modes of gravitational sediment transport on subaqueous slopes. creep creep on subaqueous slopes is poorly studied and rarely identified compared to other mass-transport

(2006), in which sediments were deformed into slump deposits with no original bedding planes preserved and, thus, causing the package to stand out prominently in seismic sections, the mass transport deposits discussed in this article are at a lesser degree of deformation. and as such, these sediments are not easily recognizable. another reason for the diffi- culty in recognizing the mass transport deposits is the depth of oc- currence. for example, when mass transport deposits get buried to depths of 7000 to 10,000 ft (2133–3048 m), some of the diagnostic features are obliterated because the sediments become compacted to such a degree that they end up paralleling the bedding plane. failure to recognize an mass transport deposit package could lead to inadequate production well planning, should there be a hydrocarbon field located within such mass transport deposits. for instance, because of reservoir compartmenta- lization, drilling vertical wells instead of horizontal wells to drain the reservoir would lead to early pressure decline and water-coning problems. how- ever, with careful mapping, using seismic attributes such as instantaneous phase and cosine of phase, and recognizing the decollement surface, mass transport deposit packages may be identified. acoustic impedance and petrophysical properties such as porosity, clay content, and permeability also play a key function in the recognition of mass transport deposits. deformation of shallow frio sediments is most likely related to basinwide sea level fall, during which the hackberry collapse at the 27.5-ma sequence boundary occurred (e.g., brown

posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; (1984) and nissen et al. (1999) (fig. 37). the striking linearity of grooves that are commonly observed at the bases of mass-transport deposits form because of the laminar rather th

deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

pressure ridges were also formed in the chaotic seismic facies interpreted as debrites. longitudinal linear features inter- preted as lateral flow lines were observed in some mass transport deposits. in addition, rotated blocks deforming sediment waves on levees of leveed-channel complexes were classified as mass transport deposits, because they are areally mappable and form a sequence-stratigraphic facies pattern on levee surfaces. study areas three key areas of the 3d seismic survey are described in greater detail to illustrate the various types of mass-transport deposits described in the study. area 1 is part of leveed-channel complex 1 (figs. 4–6). here, individual rotated blocks are formed by deformation of pre-existing sediment waves on the levee of a large leveed-channel complex. area 2 is east of the leveed- channel complexes, where two small, nearly complete mass transport deposits with headward escarpments, chaotic reflection patterns, inter- preted lateral flow lines, mounding, and compressive pressure ridges are interpreted as debrites (fig. 5). area 3 is in a central area, west of area 2 (fig. 5). here, portions of two relatively large surficial mass transport deposits contain large glide blocks on the seafloor in a fig. 4.—coherency map of the seafloor, overlaid by a diagram of leveed-channel complexes (channel fills are yellow and levees are brown), on and below the sea floor. channel fills and levees are numbered 1–5 from oldest to youngest. channel fills 1–3 are below the seafloor, and channel fills 4–5 are on the seafloor. wavy arcuate lines on the levee associated with channel fill 1 represent sediment waves which have been deformed by localized rotated blocks (study area 1). cross section (red line) shows location of figure 6. map is 35 km by 50 km in size. 89 seafloor mass-transport deposits, deepwater nigeria fig. 5.—coherency map of seafloor overlaid with diagram showing main areas of mass-transport deposits (in brown).

(2006), in which sediments were deformed into slump deposits with no original bedding planes preserved and, thus, causing the package to stand out prominently in seismic sections, the mass transport deposits discussed in this article are at a lesser degree of deformation. and as such, these sediments are not easily recognizable. another reason for the diffi- culty in recognizing the mass transport deposits is the depth of oc- currence. for example, when mass transport deposits get buried to depths of 7000 to 10,000 ft (2133–3048 m), some of the diagnostic features are obliterated because the sediments become compacted to such a degree that they end up paralleling the bedding plane. failure to recognize an mass transport deposit package could lead to inadequate production well planning, should there be a hydrocarbon field located within such mass transport deposits. for instance, because of reservoir compartmenta- lization, drilling vertical wells instead of horizontal wells to drain the reservoir would lead to early pressure decline and water-coning problems. how- ever, with careful mapping, using seismic attributes such as instantaneous phase and cosine of phase, and recognizing the decollement surface, mass transport deposit packages may be identified. acoustic impedance and petrophysical properties such as porosity, clay content, and permeability also play a key function in the recognition of mass transport deposits. deformation of shallow frio sediments is most likely related to basinwide sea level fall, during which the hackberry collapse at the 27.5-ma sequence boundary occurred (e.g., brown

xamples covering broad-scale examples of mass-transport deposits show that structural style, and thus classification, can vary greatly within the same units (e.g., prior et al., 1984; posamentier and kolla, 2003; posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; posamentier et al., 2000; posamentier and kolla, 2003; posamentier and walker, 2006). in the following sections, the most common processes that form mass-transport deposits are described to illustrate the main modes of gravitational sediment transport on subaqueous slopes. creep creep on subaqueous slopes is poorly studied and rarely identified compared to other mass-transport

posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; formed and deformed (mass- moved) shallow frio rocks. the frio formation in our work area was grossly divided into three parts based on environmental consideration: (1) shallow frio, (2) mf, and (3) deep frio (figure 3). this article focuses on the shallow frio. because of geologic complexities, the shal- low frio is further subdivided into (1) undeformed and (2) deformed (mass-transported) strata. key seismic lines and locations of wells used in the following discussion are shown in figure 4 .w i t h the exception of well h, every well has a p-wave sonic log. results upper oligocene: undeformed shallow frio the undeformed shallow frio (usf) formation on the south texas gulf coast is composed of high- stand systems tracts consisting of paralic sequences made up of alternating transgressive and regressive sandstones and shales (e.g., galloway et al., 1982; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). it is bound at the base by sb4 and at the top by sb5 (figure 5 ). seismically, these usf sedimentary deposits (figure 5 ) appear as parallel and contin- uous events even across fault boundaries (e.g., tyler and ambrose, 1986; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). the interval is less faulted than the middle and lower frio ( figure 5), where listric faults abound, most of which die out beneath the shallow frio interval. although most faults are small and normal in our project area, these parallel evenly deposited beds become abruptly disturbed eastward and southeastward (figures 5, 6) and are expressed in highly distorted and deformed beds that contrast sharply against layered beds. as such, the deformed rocks are described as a separate package, and we refer to these deposits as mass transport deposits (or as the deformed shallow frio, figures 5 , 6). sitting unconformably on the mass transport deposits is the anahuac shale (as) ( figures 5 –7), which is characterized figure 5.

(2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

formed and deformed (mass- moved) shallow frio rocks. the frio formation in our work area was grossly divided into three parts based on environmental consideration: (1) shallow frio, (2) mf, and (3) deep frio (figure 3). this article focuses on the shallow frio. because of geologic complexities, the shal- low frio is further subdivided into (1) undeformed and (2) deformed (mass-transported) strata. key seismic lines and locations of wells used in the following discussion are shown in figure 4 .w i t h the exception of well h, every well has a p-wave sonic log. results upper oligocene: undeformed shallow frio the undeformed shallow frio (usf) formation on the south texas gulf coast is composed of high- stand systems tracts consisting of paralic sequences made up of alternating transgressive and regressive sandstones and shales (e.g., galloway et al., 1982; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). it is bound at the base by sb4 and at the top by sb5 (figure 5 ). seismically, these usf sedimentary deposits (figure 5 ) appear as parallel and contin- uous events even across fault boundaries (e.g., tyler and ambrose, 1986; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). the interval is less faulted than the middle and lower frio ( figure 5), where listric faults abound, most of which die out beneath the shallow frio interval. although most faults are small and normal in our project area, these parallel evenly deposited beds become abruptly disturbed eastward and southeastward (figures 5, 6) and are expressed in highly distorted and deformed beds that contrast sharply against layered beds. as such, the deformed rocks are described as a separate package, and we refer to these deposits as mass transport deposits (or as the deformed shallow frio, figures 5 , 6). sitting unconformably on the mass transport deposits is the anahuac shale (as) ( figures 5 –7), which is characterized figure 5.

deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

formed and deformed (mass- moved) shallow frio rocks. the frio formation in our work area was grossly divided into three parts based on environmental consideration: (1) shallow frio, (2) mf, and (3) deep frio (figure 3). this article focuses on the shallow frio. because of geologic complexities, the shal- low frio is further subdivided into (1) undeformed and (2) deformed (mass-transported) strata. key seismic lines and locations of wells used in the following discussion are shown in figure 4 .w i t h the exception of well h, every well has a p-wave sonic log. results upper oligocene: undeformed shallow frio the undeformed shallow frio (usf) formation on the south texas gulf coast is composed of high- stand systems tracts consisting of paralic sequences made up of alternating transgressive and regressive sandstones and shales (e.g., galloway et al., 1982; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). it is bound at the base by sb4 and at the top by sb5 (figure 5 ). seismically, these usf sedimentary deposits (figure 5 ) appear as parallel and contin- uous events even across fault boundaries (e.g., tyler and ambrose, 1986; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). the interval is less faulted than the middle and lower frio ( figure 5), where listric faults abound, most of which die out beneath the shallow frio interval. although most faults are small and normal in our project area, these parallel evenly deposited beds become abruptly disturbed eastward and southeastward (figures 5, 6) and are expressed in highly distorted and deformed beds that contrast sharply against layered beds. as such, the deformed rocks are described as a separate package, and we refer to these deposits as mass transport deposits (or as the deformed shallow frio, figures 5 , 6). sitting unconformably on the mass transport deposits is the anahuac shale (as) ( figures 5 –7), which is characterized figure 5.

deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

pressure ridges were also formed in the chaotic seismic facies interpreted as debrites. longitudinal linear features inter- preted as lateral flow lines were observed in some mass transport deposits. in addition, rotated blocks deforming sediment waves on levees of leveed-channel complexes were classified as mass transport deposits, because they are areally mappable and form a sequence-stratigraphic facies pattern on levee surfaces. study areas three key areas of the 3d seismic survey are described in greater detail to illustrate the various types of mass-transport deposits described in the study. area 1 is part of leveed-channel complex 1 (figs. 4–6). here, individual rotated blocks are formed by deformation of pre-existing sediment waves on the levee of a large leveed-channel complex. area 2 is east of the leveed- channel complexes, where two small, nearly complete mass transport deposits with headward escarpments, chaotic reflection patterns, inter- preted lateral flow lines, mounding, and compressive pressure ridges are interpreted as debrites (fig. 5). area 3 is in a central area, west of area 2 (fig. 5). here, portions of two relatively large surficial mass transport deposits contain large glide blocks on the seafloor in a fig. 4.—coherency map of the seafloor, overlaid by a diagram of leveed-channel complexes (channel fills are yellow and levees are brown), on and below the sea floor. channel fills and levees are numbered 1–5 from oldest to youngest. channel fills 1–3 are below the seafloor, and channel fills 4–5 are on the seafloor. wavy arcuate lines on the levee associated with channel fill 1 represent sediment waves which have been deformed by localized rotated blocks (study area 1). cross section (red line) shows location of figure 6. map is 35 km by 50 km in size. 89 seafloor mass-transport deposits, deepwater nigeria fig. 5.—coherency map of seafloor overlaid with diagram showing main areas of mass-transport deposits (in brown).

formed and deformed (mass- moved) shallow frio rocks. the frio formation in our work area was grossly divided into three parts based on environmental consideration: (1) shallow frio, (2) mf, and (3) deep frio (figure 3). this article focuses on the shallow frio. because of geologic complexities, the shal- low frio is further subdivided into (1) undeformed and (2) deformed (mass-transported) strata. key seismic lines and locations of wells used in the following discussion are shown in figure 4 .w i t h the exception of well h, every well has a p-wave sonic log. results upper oligocene: undeformed shallow frio the undeformed shallow frio (usf) formation on the south texas gulf coast is composed of high- stand systems tracts consisting of paralic sequences made up of alternating transgressive and regressive sandstones and shales (e.g., galloway et al., 1982; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). it is bound at the base by sb4 and at the top by sb5 (figure 5 ). seismically, these usf sedimentary deposits (figure 5 ) appear as parallel and contin- uous events even across fault boundaries (e.g., tyler and ambrose, 1986; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). the interval is less faulted than the middle and lower frio ( figure 5), where listric faults abound, most of which die out beneath the shallow frio interval. although most faults are small and normal in our project area, these parallel evenly deposited beds become abruptly disturbed eastward and southeastward (figures 5, 6) and are expressed in highly distorted and deformed beds that contrast sharply against layered beds. as such, the deformed rocks are described as a separate package, and we refer to these deposits as mass transport deposits (or as the deformed shallow frio, figures 5 , 6). sitting unconformably on the mass transport deposits is the anahuac shale (as) ( figures 5 –7), which is characterized figure 5.

(2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; deposit facies were preferentially deposited in different quadrants of drag zones. the estimated axial ratios of drag zones were es- timated to be b1.5, 1.5–2.0, and 2.00; with the long axes mainly oriented in nw–se direction. additionally, the location of drag zones and mass transport deposit fa- cies was inﬂuenced by the position of basal ramps. the orientation (ϕ) of the long axes and axial ratios of the drag zone were important parameters for investigating the strain history of the paleo seaﬂoor and the mass transport deposits. these zones are strain markers, which could only be analysed by estima- tion of their aspect ratios. drag zones, though elliptical in map view, can- not be considered as strain ellipses, as the pre-requisite for hypothetical representation of the zone as initially circular objects cannot be adequate- ly justiﬁed from seismic. if it were possible to identify the elliptical drag zone in attribute data from near-horizontal section through the seismic volume, there would be no way to characterise the intermediate axis suf- ﬁciently to carry out a strain analysis. in this work we identiﬁed three statistical parameters (angle of dip, length along strike, orientation) deﬁning the geometry of basal ramps, and two types of ramps. type i is promontory-related and type ii is fault-controlled. promontories are linked with very high-amplitude reﬂections, characteristic of bright spots. this implies that promontories in mass transport deposit 1 and mass transport deposit 2 can comprise potential exploration targets, similar to features described as ‘erosional shadow remnants’ by moscardelli et al. (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

formed and deformed (mass- moved) shallow frio rocks. the frio formation in our work area was grossly divided into three parts based on environmental consideration: (1) shallow frio, (2) mf, and (3) deep frio (figure 3). this article focuses on the shallow frio. because of geologic complexities, the shal- low frio is further subdivided into (1) undeformed and (2) deformed (mass-transported) strata. key seismic lines and locations of wells used in the following discussion are shown in figure 4 .w i t h the exception of well h, every well has a p-wave sonic log. results upper oligocene: undeformed shallow frio the undeformed shallow frio (usf) formation on the south texas gulf coast is composed of high- stand systems tracts consisting of paralic sequences made up of alternating transgressive and regressive sandstones and shales (e.g., galloway et al., 1982; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). it is bound at the base by sb4 and at the top by sb5 (figure 5 ). seismically, these usf sedimentary deposits (figure 5 ) appear as parallel and contin- uous events even across fault boundaries (e.g., tyler and ambrose, 1986; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). the interval is less faulted than the middle and lower frio ( figure 5), where listric faults abound, most of which die out beneath the shallow frio interval. although most faults are small and normal in our project area, these parallel evenly deposited beds become abruptly disturbed eastward and southeastward (figures 5, 6) and are expressed in highly distorted and deformed beds that contrast sharply against layered beds. as such, the deformed rocks are described as a separate package, and we refer to these deposits as mass transport deposits (or as the deformed shallow frio, figures 5 , 6). sitting unconformably on the mass transport deposits is the anahuac shale (as) ( figures 5 –7), which is characterized figure 5.

formed and deformed (mass- moved) shallow frio rocks. the frio formation in our work area was grossly divided into three parts based on environmental consideration: (1) shallow frio, (2) mf, and (3) deep frio (figure 3). this article focuses on the shallow frio. because of geologic complexities, the shal- low frio is further subdivided into (1) undeformed and (2) deformed (mass-transported) strata. key seismic lines and locations of wells used in the following discussion are shown in figure 4 .w i t h the exception of well h, every well has a p-wave sonic log. results upper oligocene: undeformed shallow frio the undeformed shallow frio (usf) formation on the south texas gulf coast is composed of high- stand systems tracts consisting of paralic sequences made up of alternating transgressive and regressive sandstones and shales (e.g., galloway et al., 1982; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). it is bound at the base by sb4 and at the top by sb5 (figure 5 ). seismically, these usf sedimentary deposits (figure 5 ) appear as parallel and contin- uous events even across fault boundaries (e.g., tyler and ambrose, 1986; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). the interval is less faulted than the middle and lower frio ( figure 5), where listric faults abound, most of which die out beneath the shallow frio interval. although most faults are small and normal in our project area, these parallel evenly deposited beds become abruptly disturbed eastward and southeastward (figures 5, 6) and are expressed in highly distorted and deformed beds that contrast sharply against layered beds. as such, the deformed rocks are described as a separate package, and we refer to these deposits as mass transport deposits (or as the deformed shallow frio, figures 5 , 6). sitting unconformably on the mass transport deposits is the anahuac shale (as) ( figures 5 –7), which is characterized figure 5.

posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; posamentier et al., 2000; posamentier and kolla, 2003; posamentier and walker, 2006). in the following sections, the most common processes that form mass-transport deposits are described to illustrate the main modes of gravitational sediment transport on subaqueous slopes. creep creep on subaqueous slopes is poorly studied and rarely identified compared to other mass-transport

formed and deformed (mass- moved) shallow frio rocks. the frio formation in our work area was grossly divided into three parts based on environmental consideration: (1) shallow frio, (2) mf, and (3) deep frio (figure 3). this article focuses on the shallow frio. because of geologic complexities, the shal- low frio is further subdivided into (1) undeformed and (2) deformed (mass-transported) strata. key seismic lines and locations of wells used in the following discussion are shown in figure 4 .w i t h the exception of well h, every well has a p-wave sonic log. results upper oligocene: undeformed shallow frio the undeformed shallow frio (usf) formation on the south texas gulf coast is composed of high- stand systems tracts consisting of paralic sequences made up of alternating transgressive and regressive sandstones and shales (e.g., galloway et al., 1982; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). it is bound at the base by sb4 and at the top by sb5 (figure 5 ). seismically, these usf sedimentary deposits (figure 5 ) appear as parallel and contin- uous events even across fault boundaries (e.g., tyler and ambrose, 1986; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). the interval is less faulted than the middle and lower frio ( figure 5), where listric faults abound, most of which die out beneath the shallow frio interval. although most faults are small and normal in our project area, these parallel evenly deposited beds become abruptly disturbed eastward and southeastward (figures 5, 6) and are expressed in highly distorted and deformed beds that contrast sharply against layered beds. as such, the deformed rocks are described as a separate package, and we refer to these deposits as mass transport deposits (or as the deformed shallow frio, figures 5 , 6). sitting unconformably on the mass transport deposits is the anahuac shale (as) ( figures 5 –7), which is characterized figure 5.

toe regions of the various mass failures constituting the lubina mass transport deposit are difficult to distinguish, since they are to a great extent overlapping and are only partially covered by seismic data. overall, the gross toe region for the entire mass-wasting deposit is recognized on the seafloor variance map as an area of noticeable seafloor roughness (fig. 6), which in cross section appears as short-wavelength and low-relief rugosity of the sea floor (fig. 7b). the precise geometry of this topographic irregu- larity cannot be described in detail, because of the limits of vertical and lateral seismic resolution. however, some of this rugosity has a ridge-like morphology, evident on the seafloor variance, and are interpreted as compressional ridges. lateral flanks.— the lateral flanks of the lubina mass transport deposit vary considerably, as seen on strike-oriented seismic profiles along the mass-failed deposit (figs. 3, 9). along the northern margin, flanks are seen as abrupt and steep (ca. 20°) limits between the highly chaotic seismic character within the mass-failed body and the unde- formed strata outside of the feature. in contrast, along the south- ern margin and toe regions, lateral flanks correspond to extensive areas where the failure complex thins progressively and is con- cordant with the underlying strata (fig. 9). this configuration suggests that sediment removal (i.e., undermining) of the main instability event triggered secondary minor slope failures along the northern flank of the lubina mass transport deposit. in contrast, it is also interpreted that the southeastern parts of the mass-failure com- plex were subsequently eroded at least partially by the reactiva- tion of a submarine channel. basal shear surface.— the basal shear surface of the lubina mass transport deposit can be traced continuously with a high degree of confidence over the entire 3d seismic volume.

posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000; (2006). in addition, the drag zones mapped in this work are sites of recur- ring mass transport deposit events, and such areas should be avoided when planning well trajectories, especially when these zones are in front of salt diapirs. if located on the proximal part of the diapirs, they can act as a structural barrier to remobilised mass transport deposits.

formed and deformed (mass- moved) shallow frio rocks. the frio formation in our work area was grossly divided into three parts based on environmental consideration: (1) shallow frio, (2) mf, and (3) deep frio (figure 3). this article focuses on the shallow frio. because of geologic complexities, the shal- low frio is further subdivided into (1) undeformed and (2) deformed (mass-transported) strata. key seismic lines and locations of wells used in the following discussion are shown in figure 4 .w i t h the exception of well h, every well has a p-wave sonic log. results upper oligocene: undeformed shallow frio the undeformed shallow frio (usf) formation on the south texas gulf coast is composed of high- stand systems tracts consisting of paralic sequences made up of alternating transgressive and regressive sandstones and shales (e.g., galloway et al., 1982; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). it is bound at the base by sb4 and at the top by sb5 (figure 5 ). seismically, these usf sedimentary deposits (figure 5 ) appear as parallel and contin- uous events even across fault boundaries (e.g., tyler and ambrose, 1986; barnaby et al., 1998; brown et al., 2004). the interval is less faulted than the middle and lower frio ( figure 5), where listric faults abound, most of which die out beneath the shallow frio interval. although most faults are small and normal in our project area, these parallel evenly deposited beds become abruptly disturbed eastward and southeastward (figures 5, 6) and are expressed in highly distorted and deformed beds that contrast sharply against layered beds. as such, the deformed rocks are described as a separate package, and we refer to these deposits as mass transport deposits (or as the deformed shallow frio, figures 5 , 6). sitting unconformably on the mass transport deposits is the anahuac shale (as) ( figures 5 –7), which is characterized figure 5.

(2006), in which sediments were deformed into slump deposits with no original bedding planes preserved and, thus, causing the package to stand out prominently in seismic sections, the mass transport deposits discussed in this article are at a lesser degree of deformation. and as such, these sediments are not easily recognizable. another reason for the diffi- culty in recognizing the mass transport deposits is the depth of oc- currence. for example, when mass transport deposits get buried to depths of 7000 to 10,000 ft (2133–3048 m), some of the diagnostic features are obliterated because the sediments become compacted to such a degree that they end up paralleling the bedding plane. failure to recognize an mass transport deposit package could lead to inadequate production well planning, should there be a hydrocarbon field located within such mass transport deposits. for instance, because of reservoir compartmenta- lization, drilling vertical wells instead of horizontal wells to drain the reservoir would lead to early pressure decline and water-coning problems. how- ever, with careful mapping, using seismic attributes such as instantaneous phase and cosine of phase, and recognizing the decollement surface, mass transport deposit packages may be identified. acoustic impedance and petrophysical properties such as porosity, clay content, and permeability also play a key function in the recognition of mass transport deposits. deformation of shallow frio sediments is most likely related to basinwide sea level fall, during which the hackberry collapse at the 27.5-ma sequence boundary occurred (e.g., brown

posamentier and walker, 2006). analysis of 3d seismic data allows a full spatial view of mass-transport deposits, particularly where they are located on or near the seafloor. the principal direction of movement can be readily interpreted from these data, though locally within the mass-transport deposits the direction of movement can vary considerably both as a result of local slopes (prior and coleman, 1979) and because of internal kinematics (lewis, 1971; martinsen, 1989, 1994). based both on outcrop data and in deeper seismic data, the overall direction of movement, and consequently paleoslope, can be difficult to assess (fig. 4; woodcock, 1979; martinsen and collinson, 2002; strachan and alsop, 2006). in outcrop examples of mass-transport deposits, interpretations of paleoslope orientation must be made on measurements of all directional structures in as many mass-transport deposits as possible rather than on single observations (cf. martinsen et al., 2000; martinsen and collinson, 2002; martinsen et al., 2003). core data can be useful to prove the presence of mass-transport deposits in deeply buried stratigraphy with poor seismic reso- lution, but direction of movement is usually impossible to attain, even with high-resolution dipmeter log data, due to the extensive deformation. basal grooves observed on seismic data can be a direct indication of flow direction (brami et al., 2000;
